items.stem: The P–V diagram shows an ideal Otto cycle for 0.25 mol of monatomic gas (γ = 5/3) in a variable-volume optical pressure cell, compressing adiabatically from V_max = 4.5 × 10⁻³ m³ (at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa) to V_min = 1.5 × 10⁻³ m³, heating isochorically to 1.123 × 10⁶ Pa, expanding adiabatically to 4.5 × 10⁻³ m³, and cooling isochorically back to state A. Calculate the cycle efficiency η = W_net / Q_in.
items.workedSolution: For an ideal monatomic Otto cycle (γ = 5/3), η = 1 − (V_min / V_max)^(γ − 1) = 1 − (1.5 × 10⁻³ / 4.5 × 10⁻³)^(2/3) = 0.519 (equivalently W_net / Q_in = 583.2 / 1.123 × 10³ = 0.519).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates the closed adiabatic heat-engine cycle to obtain 0.519 (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses exponent 1 instead of γ − 1 = 2/3 in the Otto efficiency relation η = 1 − (V_min / V_max)^(γ − 1).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Computes Carnot efficiency 1 − T_A / T_C between extreme cycle temperatures instead of Otto efficiency.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Raises V_min / V_max to γ = 5/3 rather than γ − 1 = 2/3.

items.stem: Spectroscopic thermometry confirms that Argon-40 (Ar) atoms (molar mass 0.04 kg mol⁻¹) in a sealed quartz spectroscopy cell are equilibrated at 820 K. Use Boltzmann constant 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ and elementary charge 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Determine the mean kinetic energy per atom expressed in eV.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes T = 820 K into the monatomic kinetic-theory energy relation to obtain 0.106 eV (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Evaluates (1/2) k_B T / e for a single degree of freedom instead of three.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes k_B T / e and omits the 3/2 translational factor.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Doubles the 3/2 factor to 3 k_B T / e by omitting the 1/2 in kinetic energy.

items.stem: Starting at 184 K in a thermal-energy-storage phase-change capsule, 1.25 kg of ethanol absorbs heat, crosses its 351 K boiling point (specific latent heat of vaporization L_v = 8.46 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹), and finishes as vapour at 381 K. With c_liquid = 2440 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and c_vapour = 1600 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, how much energy was supplied?
items.workedSolution: Sensible heating: Q_sens = 1.25 × 2440 × (351 − 184) + 1.25 × 1600 × (381 − 351) = 5.694 × 10⁵ J. Latent heat on plateau: Q_lat = mL = 1.25 × 8.46 × 10⁵ = 1.058 × 10⁶ J. Total Q = 1.63 × 10⁶ J.

markScheme.criterion: Sums sensible mcΔT stages and latent heat mL to obtain 1.63 × 10⁶ J (D).

items.stem: Radiometric observations characterise a spherical main-sequence stellar photosphere (ideal blackbody, area 3.6 × 10¹⁸ m², surface temperature 3600 K) from a separation d = 8.5 × 10¹⁰ m. Taking Wien's constant b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K, what is the peak emission wavelength λ_max in nanometres?
items.workedSolution: By Wien's displacement law, λ_max = b / T = (2.90 × 10⁻³) / 3600 = 8.056 × 10⁻⁷ m = 806 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates the blackbody radiation law in SI units to obtain 806 nm (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Inverts Wien's displacement law by dividing T by b instead of b by T.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts 273.15 from the kelvin temperature before applying Wien's law.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies Wien's constant b by T instead of dividing b by T.

items.stem: Within a closed noble-gas power-conversion loop, 1.4 mol of monatomic working gas completes a four-stage Carnot engine loop between a hot reservoir at 277 °C and a cold sink at 87 °C (take T(K) = θ(°C) + 273.15), expanding from 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ to 7.0 × 10⁻³ m³ while in contact with the hot source (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; net work output by the gas positive).

markScheme.criterion: Converts temperatures to kelvin and applies 1 − T_C / T_H.
Obtains 0.345.
Uses Q_H = nRT_H ln(V_B / V_A).
Obtains 8.02 × 10³ J.
Multiplies η by Q_H (or evaluates Q_H − Q_C).
Obtains 2.77 × 10³ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the thermal efficiency η of the Carnot cycle.
Calculate the thermal energy Q_H absorbed from the hot reservoir during the isothermal expansion A → B.
Determine the net mechanical work W_net done by the gas per cycle.

items.stem: During an instrument check, a rigid stainless-steel vacuum-calibration tank of internal volume 0.06 m³ contains 2.8 mol of Argon-40 (Ar) (molar mass 0.04 kg mol⁻¹) at 310 K (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹). What is the pressure inside the chamber?
items.workedSolution: From the ideal gas equation p = nRT / V = (2.8 × 8.31 × 310) / 0.06 = 1.20 × 10⁵ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Applies p = nRT / V in SI units to obtain 1.20 × 10⁵ Pa (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies nRT by volume V instead of dividing nRT by V.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts 273.15 from an already-kelvin temperature before applying pV = nRT.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the amount of substance n in p = nRT / V, solving for 1 mol instead of the given molar amount.

items.stem: A 0.16 kg copper cup (specific heat 385 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) inside a lagged benchtop thermal-equilibrium chamber contains 0.22 kg of ethanol (2440 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) equilibrated at 290 K. Engineers transfer a 0.36 kg glass sample (840 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 475 K into the liquid with zero external heat loss.
items.workedSolution: (a) Solving the enthalpy balance yields T_eq = 352 K. (b) Heat released by the hot solid Q_lost = m_s c_s (T_s − T_eq) = 3.72 × 10⁴ J. (c) Heat gained by the ethanol Q_liq = m_l c_liq (T_eq − T_l) = 3.33 × 10⁴ J.

markScheme.criterion: Sets up full calorimetry heat-balance equation.
Obtains 352 K.
Evaluates m_s c_s (T_s − T_eq).
Obtains 3.72 × 10⁴ J.
Evaluates m_l c_liq (T_eq − T_l).
Obtains 3.33 × 10⁴ J.

items.stem: A four-stroke marine diesel engine with 6 cylinders runs at 40.0 rev s⁻¹ with an indicator loop area of 720 J per cylinder and delivers an output shaft torque of 280 N m. Calculate the friction power lost within the engine.
items.workedSolution: $P_{\mathrm{ind}} = 720 \times (40.0/2) \times 6 = 86.4\text{ kW}$. $P_{\mathrm{brake}} = T\omega = 280 \times 2\pi(40.0) = 70.4\text{ kW}$. Friction power $P_{\mathrm{fric}} = P_{\mathrm{ind}} - P_{\mathrm{brake}} = 16.0 kW$.

markScheme.criterion: Friction power equals 16.0 kW.

items.stem: In an enthalpy-rate experiment using a guarded electrical immersion-heating vessel, an electrical immersion heater of input power 900 W and thermal transfer efficiency 0.75 supplies energy on a 0.75 kg sample of aluminium, changing its temperature from 896 K to 959 K across its 933.5 K phase boundary. Adopt c_solid = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, c_liquid = 1180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, and L_f = 3.97 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) P_eff = η P = 675 W. (b) Δt_f = m L_f / P_eff = 441 s. (c) Total energy Q_total = 3.456 × 10⁵ J, giving t_total = Q_total / P_eff = 512 s.

markScheme.criterion: Multiplies heater power P by efficiency η.
Obtains 675 W.
Divides m L_f by P_eff.
Obtains 441 s.
Computes Q_total and divides by P_eff.
Obtains 512 s.

Calculate the duration of the isothermal melting plateau at 933.5 K.
Determine the total time required for the temperature to change from 896 K to 959 K.
workingSteps: Q_total = m c_solid (933.5 − 896) + m L_f + m c_liquid (959 − 933.5) = 3.456 × 10⁵ J.

items.stem: In a high-efficiency reciprocating research engine cylinder, 0.4 mol of an ideal monatomic gas undergoes the clockwise closed heat-engine cycle A → B → C → D → A: isobaric expansion A → B at 6.3 × 10⁵ Pa from 1.8 × 10⁻³ m³ to 7.2 × 10⁻³ m³, isochoric cooling B → C to 1.8 × 10⁵ Pa, isobaric compression C → D at 1.8 × 10⁵ Pa back to 1.8 × 10⁻³ m³, and isochoric heating D → A to 6.3 × 10⁵ Pa. Take work done by the gas as positive.
items.workedSolution: (a) W_net = (P_high − P_low)(V_max − V_min) = 2.43 × 10³ J. (b) Q_in = Q_DA + Q_AB = (3/2)(P_high − P_low)V_min + (5/2)P_high(V_max − V_min) = 9.72 × 10³ J. (c) η = W_net / Q_in = 0.250.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates enclosed loop area (P_high − P_low)(V_max − V_min).
Obtains 2.43 × 10³ J.
Identifies heat input on both D → A (isochoric) and A → B (isobaric).
Uses monatomic factors (3/2) on D → A and (5/2) on A → B.
Obtains Q_in = 9.72 × 10³ J.
Divides W_net from (a) by Q_in from (b).
Obtains 0.250.

parts.prompt: Calculate the net mechanical work W_net done by the gas in one complete cycle.
Calculate the total thermal energy Q_in supplied to the monatomic gas during the heating stages D → A and A → B.
Determine the thermal efficiency η of this cycle.

items.stem: A calorimetry experiment records the cooling curve shown in the figure as 0.38 kg of molten solidified myristic ester freezes at 62 °C and cools in solid form down to 23 °C. The solid has specific heat capacity 1690 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and specific latent heat of fusion 1.88 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. When previously melted from 23 °C using a 115 W immersion heater, the heating setup operated at 83% thermal efficiency. Separately, a rigid argon thermal test vessel holds a fixed mass of ideal gas at 118 kPa and 23 °C before warming at constant volume to 118 °C (use T / K = θ / °C + 273.2).
items.workedSolution: (a)(i) Q₁ = m c Δθ = 0.38 × 1690 × (62 − 23) = 2.505 × 10⁴ J ≈ 2.50 × 10⁴ J. (a)(ii) Q_melt = m L_f = 7.144 × 10⁴ J; Q_total = 9.649 × 10⁴ J ≈ 9.65 × 10⁴ J. (a)(iii) mean molecular kinetic energy stays constant while intermolecular potential energy changes to overcome or form intermolecular bonds. (a)(iv) temperature remains constant along a horizontal plateau during freezing before falling smoothly toward ambient temperature. (b)(i) T₁ = 296.2 K, T₂ = 391.2 K, so p₂ = 118 × (391.2 / 296.2) = 155.8 kPa ≈ 156 kPa. (b)(ii) faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Q = m c Δθ = 0.38 × 1690 × 39.
Correctly computes 2.50 × 10⁴ J (4 s.f. 2.505 × 10⁴ J).
Computes latent energy Q_melt = 7.144 × 10⁴ J and sums Q_warm + Q_melt.
Shows 4 s.f. value 9.649 × 10⁴ J rounding cleanly to 9.65 × 10⁴ J.
States that temperature and mean molecular kinetic energy remain constant along the plateau.
Explains that intermolecular potential energy changes as bonds are weakened, broken, or formed.
States accurately that temperature remains constant along a horizontal plateau during freezing before falling smoothly toward ambient temperature.
Converts both temperatures using T = θ + 273.2 (296.2 K and 391.2 K) and applies p₂ = p₁ T₂ / T₁.
Evaluates final gas pressure = 156 kPa (4 s.f. 155.8 kPa).

Explains via Newton second law that faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area (no credit for quoting pV = nRT alone).

items.stem: Why can the compression stroke inside a high-speed internal combustion cylinder be approximated as adiabatic even though the cylinder walls are metal and not perfectly insulated?
items.workedSolution: Because the stroke completes in milliseconds, rapid change allows negligible thermal energy transfer between gas and surroundings ($Q \approx 0$).

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that rapid change allows negligible thermal energy transfer between gas and surroundings.

options.label: A
options.text: Rapid change allows negligible thermal energy transfer between gas and surroundings.

options.label: B
options.text: Metal cylinder walls conduct heat rapidly enough to hold gas temperature constant.
options.distractorRationale: Describes an isothermal limit, the opposite of adiabatic.

options.label: C
options.text: Piston motion cancels thermal conduction by reversing the temperature gradient.
options.distractorRationale: Compressing gas raises temperature above the wall temperature.

options.label: D
options.text: Ideal gases cannot transfer thermal energy while their pressure is rising.
options.distractorRationale: Heat transfer depends on temperature difference and time, not pressure direction.

items.stem: An open glass U-tube contains seawater of known density ρ₂ = 1030 kg m⁻³ in its lower bend and right arm. An immiscible sample of mineral oil of unknown density ρ₁ is poured into the left arm until equilibrium is reached as illustrated. Above the horizontal interface datum P–Q, the left oil column stands h₁ = 0.26 m tall while the right seawater column stands h₂ = 0.187 m tall (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). What is the density ρ₁ of the unknown mineral oil?
items.workedSolution: Pressures at P and Q on the same horizontal datum are equal: p₀ + ρ₁ g h₁ = p₀ + ρ₂ g h₂ ⇒ ρ₁ = ρ₂ (h₂ / h₁) = 1030 × (0.187 / 0.26) = 740.8 kg m⁻³ ≈ 741 kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Correct unknown density ρ₁ = 741 kg m⁻³.

items.stem: A pharmaceutical cold-storage unit operates as a refrigerator between an interior at 266 K and a room at 296 K. Calculate the maximum theoretical coefficient of performance $\mathrm{COP}_{\mathrm{ref}}$ of the unit.
items.workedSolution: $\mathrm{COP}_{\mathrm{ref,max}} = \frac{T_{\mathrm{C}}}{T_{\mathrm{H}} - T_{\mathrm{C}}} = \frac{266}{296 - 266} = 8.87$.

markScheme.criterion: Maximum refrigerator COP equals 8.87.

items.stem: A sample of 0.35 mol of ideal gas in a closed noble-gas power-conversion loop undergoes an isobaric expansion from state A (1.4 × 10⁵ Pa, 6.0 × 10⁻³ m³) to state B (9.0 × 10⁻³ m³), followed by an isochoric rise to 3.36 × 10⁵ Pa at state C. Given R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, find the absolute temperature at B.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates PV / (nR) at the target state to obtain 433 K (C).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Stops after computing the initial temperature T_A = P_A V_A / (nR) without scaling by V_B / V_A.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the final temperature T_C at state C rather than the intermediate temperature T_B.

items.stem: Inside a sealed quartz spectroscopy cell of fixed volume 0.025 m³, 2 mol of ideal Neon-20 (Ne) gas (M = 20.2 g mol⁻¹) is heated at constant volume from T₁ = 250 K to T₂ = 625 K, producing the two speed distributions shown. Use R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (kinetic-theory pressure relation: pV = ⅓ N m v_rms²).

markScheme.criterion: Uses v_rms = √(3RT₁ / M) with M in kg mol⁻¹.
Obtains 555 m s⁻¹.
Applies p = nRT₁ / V.
Obtains 1.66 × 10⁵ Pa.
Scales v_rms by √(T₂ / T₁) or re-evaluates √(3RT₂ / M).
Obtains 878 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the root-mean-square speed v_rms of the Neon-20 (Ne) atoms at T₁ = 250 K.
Calculate the gas pressure inside the vessel at T₁ = 250 K.
Determine the new root-mean-square speed of the atoms when heated to T₂ = 625 K.

items.stem: In an infrared energy-balance investigation, a deep-space probe aluminium-kapton radiator fin of surface area 12 m² and greybody emissivity e = 0.92 has a uniform temperature of 298 K while exchanging radiation with an ambient environment at 240 K. Take b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.
items.workedSolution: (a) λ_max = b / T = 9.73 × 10⁻⁶ m. (b) Gross emitted power P_emitted = e σ A T⁴ = 4.94 × 10³ W. (c) Net radiative loss P_net = e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴) = 2.86 × 10³ W.

markScheme.criterion: Uses λ_max = (2.90 × 10⁻³) / T.
Obtains 9.73 × 10⁻⁶ m.
Uses P_emitted = e σ A T⁴.
Obtains 4.94 × 10³ W.
Evaluates e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴).
Obtains 2.86 × 10³ W.

parts.prompt: Calculate the peak infrared wavelength λ_max emitted by the surface.
Calculate the gross thermal power emitted by the greybody surface.
Determine the net rate of radiative thermal energy loss to the 240 K surroundings.
workingSteps: P_net = e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴) = 2.86 × 10³ W.

items.stem: Coupled thermally to a 310 K reservoir, 1.2 mol of ideal gas confined in a laboratory heat-engine indicator rig with low-friction seals expands slowly from 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ at A to 6.0 × 10⁻³ m³ at B (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; define work done by the gas as positive).
items.workedSolution: (a) P_B = nRT / V_B = 5.15 × 10⁵ Pa. (b) W_by = nRT ln(V_B / V_A) = 3.40 × 10³ J. (c) Since ΔU = 0, Q = W_by and ΔS = Q / T = 11.0 J K⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses P_B = nRT / V_B.
Obtains 5.15 × 10⁵ Pa.
Evaluates nRT ln(V_B / V_A).
Obtains 3.40 × 10³ J.
Uses ΔS = Q / T with Q = W_by.
Obtains 11.0 J K⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the final pressure P_B of the gas in state B.
Calculate the work done by the gas during the reversible isothermal expansion A → B.
Determine the change in entropy ΔS of the gas during A → B.
workingSteps: Since ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas isotherm, Q = W_by.

items.stem: Inside a low-heat-capacity polymeric calorimetry beaker, 0.035 kg of ice initially at 263.15 K is added to 0.58 kg of liquid water at 318.15 K. Take melting point T_m = 273.15 K, c_ice = 2100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, c_water = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, and L_f = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. Neglecting external heat losses, what is the final equilibrium temperature T_eq?
items.workedSolution: Energy to warm and melt all ice at 273.15 K: Q_1+2 = 0.035 × 2100 × (273.15 − 263.15) + 0.035 × 3.34 × 10⁵ = 1.243 × 10⁴ J. Energy balance with warm water: m_w c_w (318.15 − T_eq) = Q_1+2 + m_ice c_w (T_eq − 273.15), giving T_eq = 311 K.

markScheme.criterion: Includes sub-zero ice warming, fusion latent heat, and meltwater warming to obtain 311 K (B).

items.stem: A monatomic ideal gas (0.6 mol) in a closed-cycle Stirling regenerator test cell transitions from state A (1.5 × 10⁵ Pa, 4.5 × 10⁻³ m³) to state B (3.75 × 10⁵ Pa, 4.5 × 10⁻³ m³) and then to state C (3.75 × 10⁵ Pa, 9.9 × 10⁻³ m³). Defining work done on the gas as positive (ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW), calculate the total thermal energy ΔQ absorbed by the gas over A → B → C.
items.workedSolution: Along A → B → C, work done on the gas is ΔW = 0 − P_B(V_C − V_B) = -2.025 × 10³ J. Total internal energy change ΔU = (3/2)(P_C V_C − P_A V_A) = 4.556 × 10³ J. By the first law ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW, thermal energy supplied is ΔQ = ΔU − ΔW = 6.58 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates the first-law energy transfer with consistent work sign to obtain 6.58 × 10³ J (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Reverses the sign of expansion work ΔW in ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW, adding negative ΔW instead of evaluating ΔQ = ΔU − ΔW.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes only the total internal energy change ΔU_AC and omits the boundary work done during B → C.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the monatomic 3/2 factor in ΔU = (3/2)(P_C V_C − P_A V_A).

markScheme.criterion: Finds specific heat capacity c = 2.10e+3 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the isothermal constant $p(V + V_0)$ in kPa cm³.
Convert this product $pV_{\mathrm{total}}$ into SI base-derived units (J).
workingSteps: $1\text{ kPa cm}^3 = 10^3\text{ Pa}\times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^3 = 10^{-3}\text{ J}$, so $pV = 4.58 J$.

parts.prompt: Predict the graduated scale reading $V_2$ at $p_2 = 182$ kPa.
Explain why pressure must be changed slowly with pauses before reading, and how plotting $1/p$ against $V$ determines $V_0$ graphically.
parts.expectedAnswer: change the pressure slowly and wait for thermal equilibrium so the trapped air temperature remains constant and isothermal boyle behaviour holds; plotting 1/p against V produces a straight line whose negative horizontal intercept equals −V₀.

Rearranging p(V + V₀) = C gives 1/p = V/C + V₀/C, which cuts the V-axis at −V₀.

options.text: Because air remains an ideal gas right down to −273 °C without liquefying.
options.distractorRationale: Real air liquefies around −196 °C, so absolute zero must be obtained by linear extrapolation from room-to-hot water temperatures.

options.label: C

items.workedSolution: (a) P₁ = 106 W. (b) P₂ = 253 W; eliminating H gives c = (P₂ − P₁) / [(ṁ₂ − ṁ₁)Δθ] = 2.44e+3 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. (c) H = P₁ − ṁ₁cΔθ = 8.80 W. (d) identical inlet and outlet temperatures keep thermal energy loss rate to the surroundings constant so heat loss cancels upon subtraction.

Obtains specific heat capacity c = 2.44e+3 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Substitutes back to find H = 8.80 W.

items.stem: Consider N molecules of an ideal monatomic gas, each of mass m, sealed inside a cubic container of side L and volume V = L³, as illustrated.
items.workedSolution: elastic wall collision reverses velocity giving momentum change minus two m u, Newton second and third laws give wall force, and isotropic random motion gives the one-third factor in pV equals one-third N m c rms squared. A single molecule travelling with x-velocity +u rebounds elastically from the wall face of area L², reversing velocity to −u for a momentum change Δp = −2mu. The time between consecutive impacts on the same face is the round trip t = 2L / u. By Newton's second law the mean force exerted by the wall on the molecule is F = Δp / t = −mu² / L, and by Newton's third law the molecule exerts an equal and opposite outward force +mu² / L on the wall, producing pressure p₁ = F / L² = mu² / L³ = mu² / V. Summing over all N molecules gives pV = Nm⟨u²⟩. Because molecular motion is random with all three orthogonal directions equally likely, ⟨u²⟩ = ⟨v²⟩ = ⟨w²⟩ = (1/3) c_rms², yielding pV = (1/3) N m c_rms². Key assumptions: negligible molecular volume relative to container volume, negligible intermolecular forces except during elastic collisions, negligible collision duration compared with time between collisions, and large N moving randomly.

markScheme.criterion: L1a: States molecule collides elastically with wall so velocity reverses from +u to −u, giving momentum change Δp = −2mu (do not award without direction reversal).
L1b: Finds time between collisions with the same wall as round-trip t = 2L / u.
L2a: Applies Newton's second law F = Δp / t = mu² / L AND explicitly invokes Newton's third law for the equal and opposite force exerted on the wall.
L2b: Divides force by wall area L² to obtain single-molecule pressure p₁ = mu² / L³ = mu² / V and sums over N molecules to get pV = Nm⟨u²⟩.
L3a: Justifies factor 1/3 explicitly from random isotropic motion making x, y, z directions equally likely so ⟨u²⟩ = ⟨v²⟩ = ⟨w²⟩ = (1/3) c_rms² → pV = (1/3) N m c_rms².
L3b: States at least three kinetic theory assumptions (negligible molecular volume, negligible intermolecular forces except during collisions, negligible collision duration, elastic collisions).

parts.expectedAnswer: elastic wall collision reverses velocity giving momentum change minus two m u, Newton second and third laws give wall force, and isotropic random motion gives the one-third factor in pV equals one-third N m c rms squared. A single molecule travelling with x-velocity +u rebounds elastically from the wall face of area L², reversing velocity to −u for a momentum change Δp = −2mu. The time between consecutive impacts on the same face is the round trip t = 2L / u. By Newton's second law the mean force exerted by the wall on the molecule is F = Δp / t = −mu² / L, and by Newton's third law the molecule exerts an equal and opposite outward force +mu² / L on the wall, producing pressure p₁ = F / L² = mu² / L³ = mu² / V. Summing over all N molecules gives pV = Nm⟨u²⟩. Because molecular motion is random with all three orthogonal directions equally likely, ⟨u²⟩ = ⟨v²⟩ = ⟨w²⟩ = (1/3) c_rms², yielding pV = (1/3) N m c_rms². Key assumptions: negligible molecular volume relative to container volume, negligible intermolecular forces except during elastic collisions, negligible collision duration compared with time between collisions, and large N moving randomly.

L2: Round-trip time t = 2L/u, Newton's 2nd law F = Δp/t = mu²/L, Newton's 3rd law on wall, and pressure p = F/L² = mu²/V.
L3: Sum over N molecules, apply 3D isotropy ⟨u²⟩ = ⟨v²⟩ = ⟨w²⟩ = (1/3) c_rms², and state ideal-gas assumptions.

items.stem: A student investigates Boyle's law using a sealed glass air column over an oil reservoir connected to a foot pump and Bourdon pressure gauge.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 Model Response: Wear safety goggles and never exceed the manufacturer's maximum safe pressure on the glass tube. Ensure the sealed column contains a fixed mass of dry air with no valve leaks. Pump oil slowly to increase pressure in small steps across at least six widely spaced pressures. After each step, wait for thermal equilibrium so heat generated by compression dissipates and the air returns to constant room temperature. Read the volume at the bottom/flat level of the oil meniscus strictly at eye level to eliminate parallax, alongside the Bourdon gauge reading. Repeat measurements while slowly releasing pressure to verify no air escaped. Plot absolute pressure p against 1/V; a straight line passing through the origin verifies p ∝ 1/V (constant pV).

markScheme.criterion: States safety precaution: wear safety goggles and keep pressure strictly below the glass tube's maximum limit.
Confirms fixed mass of trapped dry air (sealed system, repeat readings during decompression to verify zero leakage).
Changes pressure slowly and pauses between readings so compressed air returns to constant room temperature (isothermal).
Reads volume meniscus perpendicularly at eye level (eliminating parallax) across >= 6 pressure-volume pairs.
Plots pressure p against 1/V (or 1/p against V when accounting for tubing dead volume).
States clearly that a straight best-fit line passing through the origin confirms Boyle's law (pV = constant).

parts.prompt: Describe how to perform this investigation safely and accurately to verify Boyle's law graphically, stating precautions, measurements, thermal controls, and graphical proof. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: Wear safety goggles and avoid exceeding the maximum safe pressure rating of the glass column; change the pressure slowly and wait for thermal equilibrium so the trapped air temperature remains constant and isothermal boyle behaviour holds; read the oil meniscus at eye level across at least six pressure steps, verify zero gas leakage by checking original readings on decompression, and plot p against 1/V to verify a straight line through the origin.
workingSteps: Level 1: Safety goggles, do not exceed pressure limit, ensure valve sealed so gas mass is fixed.
Level 2: Change pressure slowly, wait 1–2 min for thermal equilibration, read oil meniscus at eye level (no parallax) + Bourdon gauge across >= 6 readings.
Level 3: Repeat on decompression to check for leaks/hysteresis, plot p vs 1/V (straight line through origin confirms pV = const; or 1/p vs V to find dead volume).

items.stem: A Year 13 class determines an experimental value for absolute zero using a vertical glass capillary tube containing air trapped by a bead of concentrated sulfuric acid immersed in a water bath.
items.workedSolution: Level 3 Model Response: Wear safety goggles and handle the concentrated sulfuric acid bead and hot water with care. Fasten a uniform-bore open-topped capillary tube alongside a millimetre ruler inside a tall beaker so the entire trapped air column remains completely submerged. The concentrated sulfuric acid bead acts as a movable frictionless seal keeping the air at constant atmospheric pressure while simultaneously absorbing water vapour to keep the air dry. Begin with hot water around 85 °C (or heat gradually from ice-cold water), stir the water bath thoroughly before every reading so the thermometer and trapped air share the exact same uniform temperature, and view the bottom of the acid bead perpendicularly at eye level to eliminate parallax. Record at least six pairs of (θ, L) down to near 10 °C. Because the capillary cross-section is uniform, V ∝ L; plot L against θ / °C, draw a straight line of best fit, and extrapolate (or compute −L₀/gradient) to L = 0 to estimate absolute zero near −273 °C.

markScheme.criterion: States safety precautions for corrosive concentrated sulfuric acid (goggles/gloves) and scalding water.
Submerges the entire trapped air column completely inside the water bath alongside a millimetre scale.
Explains both roles of concentrated H₂SO₄: traps air at constant atmospheric pressure AND dries the air (removes water vapour).
Stirs the water bath thoroughly before every reading so water temperature is uniform and equals trapped air temperature.
Reads column length L (noting V ∝ L for uniform bore) and temperature θ at eye level across >= 6 temperatures over a wide range.
Plots L against θ / °C and extrapolates the best-fit straight line to L = 0 (or evaluates −L₀ / gradient) to find absolute zero near −273 °C.

parts.prompt: Explain how to carry out this practical safely and accurately to determine absolute zero graphically, detailing apparatus setup, safety, chemical and thermal precautions, and extrapolation. [6 marks]
parts.expectedAnswer: Wear safety goggles and acid-resistant gloves when handling the corrosive H₂SO₄ bead and hot water; the concentrated sulfuric acid bead traps dry air at constant atmospheric pressure and absorbs water vapour while stirring the water bath keeps temperature uniform; submerge the entire trapped air column below water level beside a ruler, record column length L and temperature θ across at least six temperatures from ice water to 85 °C, plot L against θ, and extrapolate linearly to L = 0 to find absolute zero near −273 °C.
workingSteps: Level 1: Goggles + care with corrosive H₂SO₄ and scalding water; open-topped uniform capillary tube fully submerged.
Level 2: Acid bead maintains constant atmospheric pressure AND dries trapped air; stir bath thoroughly before reading θ and L at eye level.
Level 3: Record >= 6 points over wide temperature range (e.g. 10–85 °C), plot L vs θ (V ∝ L for uniform bore), extrapolate linearly to L = 0 (or calculate θ₀ = θ₁ − L₁/m).

items.stem: On the P–V diagram for a high-efficiency reciprocating research engine cylinder, 1.2 mol of ideal monatomic gas (adiabatic index 5/3) undergoes adiabatic expansion A → B from (5.5 × 10⁵ Pa, 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³) to 0.01 m³, followed by isobaric compression B → C to 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³ and isochoric regeneration C → A. Adopt positive work for expansion by the gas.
items.workedSolution: (a) Adiabatic relation gives P_B = 5.46 × 10⁴ Pa. (b) Isochoric heat input Q_in = 1.86 × 10³ J. (c) By cyclic energy conservation ΔU_cycle = 0, W_net = Q_in − Q_out = 835 J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies P V^(5/3) = const along A → B.
Obtains 5.46 × 10⁴ Pa.
Uses Q_in = (3/2) ΔP V on the isochoric heating leg.
Obtains 1.86 × 10³ J.
Evaluates W_net = Q_in − Q_out (or sums leg works).
Obtains 835 J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the pressure P_B of the gas at state B.
Calculate the thermal energy Q_in absorbed by the gas during the isochoric heating leg.
workingSteps: On C → A (constant V = 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³, P_C = P_B), Q_in = ΔU_CA = (3/2)(P_A − P_B) V_A = 1.86 × 10³ J.

parts.prompt: Determine the net mechanical work W_net done by the gas per cycle.
workingSteps: Heat rejected on isobaric leg B → C is Q_out = (5/2) P_B (V_B − V_C) = 1.023 × 10³ J; W_net = Q_in − Q_out = 835 J.

items.stem: Within a semiconductor lithography purge canister, low-pressure monatomic Krypton-84 (Kr) gas (M = 0.0838 kg mol⁻¹) is held at 440 K. Data: k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹, 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) E_k,avg = (3/2) k_B T = 0 J. (b) Dividing by 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C gives 0.0569 eV. (c) v_rms = √(3RT / M) = 362 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies E_k = (3/2) k_B T in kelvin.
Obtains 0 J.
Divides energy in joules by elementary charge e.
Obtains 0.0569 eV.
Evaluates v_rms = √(3RT / M).
Obtains 362 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the mean translational kinetic energy of a single atom in joules.
Convert this mean translational kinetic energy into electronvolts.
Determine the root-mean-square speed of the Krypton-84 (Kr) atoms.

items.stem: In a thermal-energy-storage phase-change capsule, 0.65 kg of aluminium is heated continuously from 894 K in the solid state to 1019 K in the liquid state across its melting point at 933.5 K. Use c_solid = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, c_liquid = 1180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, and specific latent heat of fusion L_f = 3.97 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) Q_sens = m c_solid ΔT₁ + m c_liquid ΔT₂ = 8.87 × 10⁴ J. (b) Plateau latent energy Q_lat = m L = 2.58 × 10⁵ J. (c) Total thermal energy Q_total = Q_sens + Q_lat = 3.47 × 10⁵ J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates m c₁ ΔT₁ + m c₂ ΔT₂.
Obtains 8.87 × 10⁴ J.
Evaluates m L on the phase-change plateau.
Obtains 2.58 × 10⁵ J.
Sums sensible and latent energies.
Obtains 3.47 × 10⁵ J.

items.stem: Modelled as an ideal blackbody (emissivity = 1), an incandescent refractory-metal calibration sphere has radiating surface area 1.8 × 10¹⁸ m² and surface temperature 8800 K. Its thermal spectrum is shown in the figure, and a detector is positioned at distance d = 6.8 × 10¹¹ m. Take b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.
items.workedSolution: (a) λ_max = b / T = 3.30 × 10⁻⁷ m. (b) P = σ A T⁴ = 6.12 × 10²⁶ W. (c) I = P / (4π d²) = 105 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies λ_max = (2.90 × 10⁻³) / T.
Obtains 3.30 × 10⁻⁷ m.
Applies P = σ A T⁴.
Obtains 6.12 × 10²⁶ W.
Divides P by 4π d².
Obtains 105 W m⁻².

items.stem: The diagram shows a reversible Carnot cycle A → B → C → D → A for 1.4 mol of monatomic ideal gas in a cryocooler compression cylinder containing monatomic working gas coupled to a hot reservoir at 464 K and a cold sink at 290 K, with isothermal expansion from 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ to 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³. Taking R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, what magnitude of thermal energy Q_C is rejected to the cold sink per cycle?
items.workedSolution: During isothermal compression C → D at T_C = 290 K, V_C / V_D = V_B / V_A, so heat rejected to the cold sink is Q_C = nRT_C ln(V_B / V_A) = 2.34 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Carnot thermodynamics in kelvin to obtain 2.34 × 10³ J (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses log₁₀(V_B / V_A) instead of ln(V_B / V_A) in Q_C = nRT_C ln(V_B / V_A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes net work W_net = Q_H − Q_C instead of the rejected heat Q_C.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes the heat absorbed Q_H from the hot reservoir instead of the heat Q_C rejected to the cold sink.

items.stem: A sample of 2.8 mol of monatomic Neon-20 (Ne) gas (molar mass 20.2 g mol⁻¹) is sealed inside a semiconductor lithography purge canister of constant volume 0.016 m³ at 310 K. Take R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) p = nRT / V = (2.8 × 8.31 × 310) / 0.016 = 4.51 × 10⁵ Pa. (b) Single-atom mass m = M / N_A = 0 kg. (c) Density ρ = nM / V = 3.53 kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes Kelvin temperature into p = nRT / V.
Obtains 4.51 × 10⁵ Pa.
Converts molar mass to kg mol⁻¹ and divides by Avogadro constant.
Obtains 0 kg.
Evaluates ρ = nM / V in SI units.
Obtains 3.53 kg m⁻³.

items.stem: In a calorimetry run using a low-heat-capacity polymeric calorimetry beaker, a 0.18 kg cylinder of copper (c = 385 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 440 K is quenched in 0.55 kg of mineral oil (c = 1960 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 294 K. During mixing, 650 J of thermal energy escapes to the surroundings. Find T_eq at thermal equilibrium.
items.workedSolution: Enthalpy balance: m_s c_s (T_s − T_eq) = m_l c_l (T_eq − T_l) + 650, giving T_eq = 302.3 K. Therefore T_eq = 302 K.

markScheme.criterion: Applies calorimetry energy balance to obtain 302 K (B).

items.stem: During a testbed trial of a four-cylinder four-stroke petrol test engine (4 cylinders) running at 55.0 rev s⁻¹, each cylinder indicator loop encloses 460 J. The dynamometer records a brake torque of 118 N m while fuel of calorific value 4.40 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹ enters at 3.30 × 10⁻³ kg s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) $P_{\mathrm{ind}} = 50.6 kW$. (b) $P_{\mathrm{brake}} = 40.8 kW$. (c) $\eta_{\mathrm{th}} = \frac{P_{\mathrm{ind}}}{P_{\mathrm{in}}} = 34.8%$. (d) $\eta_{\mathrm{mech}} = \frac{P_{\mathrm{brake}}}{P_{\mathrm{ind}}} = 80.6%$ (overall $\eta_{\mathrm{ov}} = \eta_{\mathrm{th}} \eta_{\mathrm{mech}} = 28.1%$).

markScheme.criterion: Applies four-stroke firing frequency $f/2$ times loop area times cylinder count.
Obtains $P_{\mathrm{ind}} = 50.6 kW$.
Applies $P_{\mathrm{brake}} = T(2\pi f)$.
Obtains $P_{\mathrm{brake}} = 40.8 kW$.
Computes $P_{\mathrm{in}} = \text{CV} \times \dot{m}$ and writes $\eta_{\mathrm{th}} = P_{\mathrm{ind}}/P_{\mathrm{in}}$.
Obtains $\eta_{\mathrm{th}} = 34.8%$.
Uses $\eta_{\mathrm{mech}} = P_{\mathrm{brake}}/P_{\mathrm{ind}}$.
Obtains $\eta_{\mathrm{mech}} = 80.6%$.

items.stem: In a micro-electro-mechanical gas spring cavity, 1.5 mol of a monatomic ideal gas executes a clockwise closed cycle A → B → C → D → A between pressures 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa and 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa and volumes 1.2 × 10⁻³ m³ and 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³ (A → B isobaric expansion at 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa, B → C isochoric cooling, C → D isobaric compression at 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa, D → An isochoric heating). Taking net work done by the gas as positive, what is the net mechanical work output W_net per cycle?
items.workedSolution: Net work done by the gas equals the enclosed rectangular area: W_net = (P_high − P_low)(V_max − V_min) = (3.0 × 10⁵ − 1.5 × 10⁵)(3.0 × 10⁻³ − 1.2 × 10⁻³) = 270 J.

markScheme.criterion: Computes netWorkJ correctly for the closed rectangular cycle to obtain 270 J (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies the enclosed loop area by an extraneous 3/2 internal-energy factor.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates only the expansion work along A → B and forgets to subtract the compression work along C → D.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes P_B V_B − P_D V_D instead of the enclosed rectangular loop area (P_high − P_low)(V_max − V_min).

items.stem: A calorimetry experiment records the cooling curve shown in the figure as 0.42 kg of molten laboratory cetyl alcohol freezes at 54 °C and cools in solid form down to 20 °C. The solid has specific heat capacity 1580 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and specific latent heat of fusion 1.42 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. When previously melted from 20 °C using a 92 W immersion heater, the heating setup operated at 76% thermal efficiency. Separately, a rigid oxygen-free nitrogen bulb holds a fixed mass of ideal gas at 104 kPa and 20 °C before warming at constant volume to 96 °C (use T / K = θ / °C + 273.2).
items.workedSolution: (a)(i) Q₁ = m c Δθ = 0.42 × 1580 × (54 − 20) = 2.256 × 10⁴ J ≈ 2.26 × 10⁴ J. (a)(ii) Q_melt = m L_f = 5.964 × 10⁴ J; Q_total = 8.220 × 10⁴ J ≈ 8.22 × 10⁴ J. (a)(iii) mean molecular kinetic energy stays constant while intermolecular potential energy changes to overcome or form intermolecular bonds. (a)(iv) temperature remains constant along a horizontal plateau during freezing before falling smoothly toward ambient temperature. (b)(i) T₁ = 293.2 K, T₂ = 369.2 K, so p₂ = 104 × (369.2 / 293.2) = 131.0 kPa ≈ 131 kPa. (b)(ii) faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Q = m c Δθ = 0.42 × 1580 × 34.
Correctly computes 2.26 × 10⁴ J (4 s.f. 2.256 × 10⁴ J).
Computes latent energy Q_melt = 5.964 × 10⁴ J and sums Q_warm + Q_melt.
Shows 4 s.f. value 8.220 × 10⁴ J rounding cleanly to 8.22 × 10⁴ J.
States that temperature and mean molecular kinetic energy remain constant along the plateau.
Explains that intermolecular potential energy changes as bonds are weakened, broken, or formed.
States accurately that temperature remains constant along a horizontal plateau during freezing before falling smoothly toward ambient temperature.
Converts both temperatures using T = θ + 273.2 (293.2 K and 369.2 K) and applies p₂ = p₁ T₂ / T₁.
Evaluates final gas pressure = 131 kPa (4 s.f. 131.0 kPa).

Explains via Newton second law that faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area (no credit for quoting pV = nRT alone).

items.stem: Inside a frictionless piston-cylinder assembly on a thermodynamics test bench, 0.4 mol of an ideal monatomic gas (adiabatic index γ = 5/3) initially at P_A = 6.0 × 10⁵ Pa and V_A = 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³ is reversibly and adiabatically expanded to V_B = 0.01 m³. Take R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the final pressure P_B in state B?
items.workedSolution: For a monatomic adiabatic process, P_B = P_A (V_A / V_B)^(5/3) = 6.0 × 10⁵ × (2.5 × 10⁻³ / 0.01)^(5/3) = 5.95 × 10⁴ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Applies P V^(5/3) = const to obtain 5.95 × 10⁴ Pa (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses the diatomic adiabatic index γ = 7/5 instead of γ = 5/3 for a monatomic gas.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Treats the process as isothermal (P_A V_A = P_B V_B) rather than adiabatic (P_A V_A^(5/3) = P_B V_B^(5/3)).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the adiabatic exponent, using 3/5 instead of γ = 5/3.

items.stem: A cylinder holds 0.200 mol of dry air ($\gamma = 1.40$) initially at pressure 420 kPa and volume 1.40 × 10⁻³ m³. The gas undergoes an adiabatic change to a final volume of 4.20 × 10⁻³ m³. Take $R = 8.31\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$ and apply $Q = \Delta U + W$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $p_2 = 90.2 kPa$. (b) $T_2 = \frac{p_2 V_2}{nR} = 228 K$. (c) Work done by gas $W = 523 J$. (d) Change in internal energy $\Delta U = −523 J$.

markScheme.criterion: Applies the governing pressure-volume relation $p_1 V_1^{\gamma} = p_2 V_2^{\gamma}$.
Obtains $p_2 = 90.2 kPa$.
Applies $pV = nRT$ with $R = 8.31\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$.
Obtains $T_2 = 228 K$.
Evaluates mechanical work done by the gas with correct sign.
Obtains $W = 523 J$.
Applies $Q = \Delta U + W$ with $Q = 0$ for an adiabatic process.
Obtains $\Delta U = −523 J$.

parts.prompt: Calculate the final pressure of the gas in kPa.
Determine the final thermodynamic temperature of the gas in kelvin.
Calculate the work done BY the gas during the change, stating its sign clearly.
Hence calculate the change in internal energy $\Delta U$ of the gas.
workingSteps: For an adiabatic change $Q = 0$, so $\Delta U = -W = −523 J$.

options.label: A
options.text: Gas molecules are arranged in collapsible hollow crystal layers that fold under pressure.
options.distractorRationale: Gases possess no crystal structure or layered lattice.

options.label: B
options.text: The gas molecules themselves shrink dramatically in physical diameter whenever external pressure rises.
options.distractorRationale: Compression reduces inter-molecular spacing, not the intrinsic size of individual molecules.

options.label: C
options.text: The right-hand gaseous state is readily compressed because large empty spaces between widely separated molecules allow the gas volume to decrease easily under pressure.

options.label: D
options.text: Attractive intermolecular forces pull the gas molecules together whenever the piston moves inward.
options.distractorRationale: Intermolecular attractions in a dilute gas are negligible compared with thermal kinetic energy.

items.stem: The diagram shows an illuminated smoke-cell experiment alongside a magnified eyepiece view tracking one bright suspended particle from P to W. How does the observed motion of the illuminated specks change if the fluid inside the sealed cell is warmed uniformly to a higher temperature?
items.workedSolution: If the sealed cell is warmed uniformly to a higher steady temperature, higher temperature increases average molecular speed so collisions become more frequent and vigorous and the erratic motion becomes faster.

markScheme.criterion: If the sealed cell is warmed uniformly to a higher steady temperature, higher temperature increases average molecular speed so collisions become more frequent and vigorous and the erratic motion becomes faster.

options.label: A
options.text: The erratic motion slows down and stops because warmer fluid molecules expand and lock together.
options.distractorRationale: Higher temperature raises molecular kinetic energy and speeds up Brownian agitation.

options.label: B
options.text: If the sealed cell is warmed uniformly to a higher steady temperature, higher temperature increases average molecular speed so collisions become more frequent and vigorous and the erratic motion becomes faster.

options.label: C
options.text: All specks begin moving together in a single straight line away from the microscope lens.
options.distractorRationale: Uniform warming intensifies random isotropic motion rather than creating a single-direction beam.

options.label: D
options.text: The motion remains completely unchanged because temperature does not affect molecular speeds.
options.distractorRationale: Mean kinetic energy of fluid molecules is directly proportional to thermodynamic temperature.

items.stem: The pressure–temperature (P–T) diagram shows a two-stage process A → B → C for 0.2 mol of an ideal gas sealed inside a variable-volume optical pressure cell. At state A, the pressure is 1.6 × 10⁵ Pa and the volume is 6.0 × 10⁻³ m³. Process A → B is an isobaric expansion to volume 9.0 × 10⁻³ m³, and process B → C is an isochoric heating to pressure 3.84 × 10⁵ Pa. Take R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) T_A = P_A V_A / (nR) = 578 K. (b) Isobaric expansion gives T_B = T_A (V_B / V_A) = 866 K. (c) Isochoric heating gives T_C = T_B (P_C / P_A) = 2.08 × 10³ K.

markScheme.criterion: Uses T_A = P_A V_A / (nR).
Obtains 578 K.
Applies V_B / T_B = V_A / T_A or P_A V_B / (nR).
Obtains 866 K.
Applies P_C / T_C = P_B / T_B or P_C V_B / (nR).
Obtains 2.08 × 10³ K.

parts.prompt: Calculate the initial temperature T_A of the gas in state A.
Determine the temperature T_B at the end of the isobaric expansion A → B.
workingSteps: By Charles's law at constant pressure, T_B = T_A (V_B / V_A) = 866 K.

parts.prompt: Calculate the final temperature T_C in state C after the isochoric stage B → C.

items.stem: An experiment records the molecular speed distribution of 0.5 mol of Xenon-131 (Xe) gas (molar mass 131.3 g mol⁻¹) occupying 0.04 m³ in a sealed borosilicate acoustic-thermometry sphere at 250 K (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (kinetic-theory pressure relation: pV = ⅓ N m v_rms²)). Which value equals the rms speed of the atoms?
items.workedSolution: Convert molar mass to SI units: M = 0.1313 kg mol⁻¹. Using v_rms = √(3RT / M) at T = 250 K gives v_rms = √(3 × 8.31 × 250 / 0.1313) = 218 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates √(3RT / M) with M in kg mol⁻¹ to obtain 218 m s⁻¹ (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes molar mass in g mol⁻¹ instead of kg mol⁻¹ into √(3RT / M), underestimating v_rms by a factor of √1000 ≈ 31.6.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 3 from the three translational degrees of freedom, evaluating √(RT / M).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses a factor of 2 instead of 3, computing the most probable speed v_p = √(2RT / M) rather than v_rms.

items.stem: In a climate radiative-transfer model, a polar sea-ice radiative-balance monitoring sector of area 1.2 m² and surface emissivity e = 0.95 is at 298 K while exchanging thermal infrared radiation with an effective surrounding environment at 240 K. Taking σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, what is the net rate of radiative energy loss P_net from the surface?
items.workedSolution: Net radiative power loss P_net = e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴) = 0.95 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 1.2 × ((298)⁴ − (240)⁴) = 295 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴) to obtain 295 W (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Evaluates e σ A (T − T_amb)⁴ instead of e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴), a classic fourth-power algebra error.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the greybody emissivity factor e (< 1) from P_net = e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates gross emitted power e σ A T⁴ and ignores incoming radiation absorbed from the surroundings at T_amb.

items.stem: A thermal bath keeps 1.2 mol of ideal gas in a precision pneumatic actuator chamber sealed with a movable piston at 350 K during a reversible expansion from 5.0 × 10⁻³ m³ to 0.01 m³ (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹). What is the thermal energy Q supplied to the gas (equal to work done by the gas)?
items.workedSolution: At constant temperature T = 350 K, ΔU = 0 and W_by = Q = nRT ln(V_B / V_A) = 1.2 × 8.31 × 350 × ln(0.01 / 5.0 × 10⁻³) = 2.42 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates W = nRT ln(V_B / V_A) to obtain 2.42 × 10³ J (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes log₁₀(V_B / V_A) instead of ln(V_B / V_A).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Treats pressure as remaining constant at P_A, computing P_A(V_B − V_A) instead of ∫ P dV = nRT ln(V_B / V_A).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Adds U = (3/2)nRT to isothermal work, overlooking that ΔU = 0 at constant temperature.

items.stem: During a latent-heat experiment in a well-insulated copper-lined laboratory calorimeter, 0.035 kg of cold ice (268.15 K, c = 2100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) melts completely after immersion in 0.68 kg of water (348.15 K, c = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹), with T_m = 273.15 K, L_f = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹, and zero heat loss to the room.
items.workedSolution: (a) Q_lat = m_ice L_f = 1.17 × 10⁴ J. (b) Full enthalpy balance yields T_eq = 340 K. (c) Heat released by warm water = 2.19 × 10⁴ J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates m_ice L_f.
Obtains 1.17 × 10⁴ J.
Balances ice warming, melting, and meltwater warming against warm water cooling.
Obtains 340 K.
Evaluates m_water c_water (T_water − T_eq).
Obtains 2.19 × 10⁴ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the latent thermal energy required solely to melt all the ice once it reaches 273.15 K.
Calculate the final thermal equilibrium temperature T_eq of the water.
workingSteps: m_water c_water (348.15 − T_eq) = m_ice c_ice (273.15 − 268.15) + Q_lat + m_ice c_water (T_eq − 273.15).

parts.prompt: Determine the total thermal energy released by the initially warm water.

items.stem: Inside a variable-volume optical pressure cell, 1.5 mol of monatomic ideal gas undergoes two sequential processes plotted on the P–V graph: isochoric heating from A (1.2 × 10⁵ Pa, 3.5 × 10⁻³ m³) to B (2.4 × 10⁵ Pa, 3.5 × 10⁻³ m³), followed by isobaric expansion to C (2.4 × 10⁵ Pa, 0.0112 m³). Use ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW with work done on the gas (ΔW) and heat transferred into the gas (ΔQ) taken as positive.
items.workedSolution: (a) Work is done only along B → C: ΔW = −P_B(V_C − V_B) = -1.85 × 10³ J. (b) ΔU_AC = (3/2)(P_C V_C − P_A V_A) = 3.40 × 10³ J. (c) By ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW, total heat supplied ΔQ = ΔU_AC − ΔW = 5.25 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies ΔW_AB = 0 and computes ΔW = −P_B(V_C − V_B).
Obtains -1.85 × 10³ J.
Applies ΔU = (3/2)(P_C V_C − P_A V_A).
Obtains 3.40 × 10³ J.
Applies ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW ⇒ ΔQ = ΔU_AC − ΔW to obtain total heat supplied.
Obtains 5.25 × 10³ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the total mechanical work done on the gas ΔW along path A → B → C (including its sign).
Calculate the total change in internal energy ΔU of the monatomic gas between state A and state C.
workingSteps: For a monatomic ideal gas, U = (3/2) PV, so ΔU_AC = (3/2)(P_C V_C − P_A V_A).

parts.prompt: Determine the total thermal energy ΔQ supplied to the gas over the complete path A → B → C.
workingSteps: By the first law of thermodynamics (ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW), ΔQ = ΔU_AC − ΔW = 3.402 × 10³ − (-1.848 × 10³) = 5.25 × 10³ J.

items.stem: After switching on the immersion heater in a continuous-flow calorimeter, how does the experimenter verify that steady-state conditions have been reached before collecting the outflow liquid?
items.workedSolution: Only when the outlet temperature remains constant over time indicating thermal equilibrium before recording mass flow rate is zero net energy stored in the apparatus. Therefore the correct statement is: Check that the outlet temperature remains constant over time indicating thermal equilibrium before recording mass flow rate

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: outlet temperature remains constant over time indicating thermal equilibrium before recording mass flow rate.

items.stem: Which set of microscopic assumptions underpins the kinetic theory model of an ideal gas?
items.workedSolution: Standard A-Level kinetic theory assumes negligible molecular volume compared with container volume, negligible intermolecular forces except during elastic collisions, and negligible collision duration. Therefore the correct statement is: Molecules are assumed to have negligible molecular volume compared with container volume, negligible intermolecular forces except during elastic collisions, and negligible collision duration

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: negligible molecular volume compared with container volume, negligible intermolecular forces except during elastic collisions, and negligible collision duration.

options.text: Molecules are assumed to move at identical speeds, attract strongly at long range, and occupy half the container volume.
options.distractorRationale: Contradicts Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution, zero attractions, and negligible molecular volume.

options.label: C
options.text: Molecules are assumed to undergo inelastic collisions with the walls while spending most of their time in contact with other molecules.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses both elastic collisions and negligible collision duration.

options.label: D
options.text: Molecules are assumed to have zero mass, move strictly along one axis, and obey gravitational attraction between neighbours.
options.distractorRationale: Molecules have finite mass m and isotropic 3D motion.

items.stem: In Required Practical 8 (Boyle's law), dry air is trapped in a graduated tube above oil with a connecting dead volume $V_0 = 1.5$ cm³. At gauge-corrected absolute pressure $p_1 = 112$ kPa, the graduated scale reads $V_1 = 36.0$ cm³. After compressing slowly to $p_2 = 210$ kPa at constant temperature, what graduated volume $V_2$ is read?
items.workedSolution: Total initial volume $V_{\mathrm{total}} = 36 + 1.5 = 37.5$ cm³. Thus $pV = 112\times 10^3 \times 37.5\times 10^{-6} = 4.20 J$, and at 210 kPa the tube reads $V_2 = 18.5 cm³$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly evaluates v2Cm3 $= 18.5 cm³$.

items.stem: In Required Practical 8 (Charles's law), a dry air sample trapped by a concentrated sulfuric acid bead inside a uniform vertical capillary tube is heated in a water bath. Two points on the best-fit straight line of air column length $L$ against temperature $\theta$ are $(18\ ^\circ\text{C}, 112.0\text{ mm})$ and $(82\ ^\circ\text{C}, 136.8\text{ mm})$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $m = 0.388 mm °C⁻¹$. (b) $L_0 = 105 mm$. (c) Absolute zero $= -271 °C$. (d) the concentrated sulfuric acid bead traps dry air at constant atmospheric pressure and absorbs water vapour while stirring the water bath keeps temperature uniform.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates $\Delta L / \Delta\theta$.
Gradient $m = 0.388 mm °C⁻¹$.
Substitutes into $L_0 = L_1 - m\theta_1$.
Length at 0 °C $= 105 mm$.
Sets $L = 0$ to solve $\theta = -L_0 / m$.
Extrapolated absolute zero $= -271 °C$.
Bead traps fixed mass of air at constant atmospheric pressure.
Concentrated sulfuric acid absorbs water vapour / keeps air dry.
Thorough stirring keeps water bath uniform so thermometer reads true air temperature.

items.stem: Thermal engineers calibrate a battery-cooling glycol mixture by running two different mass flow rates through a constant-head calorimeter. items.workedSolution: (a) P₁ = 186 W. (b) P₂ = 366 W; eliminating H gives c = (P₂ − P₁) / [(ṁ₂ − ṁ₁)Δθ] = 3.60e+3 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. (c) H = P₁ − ṁ₁cΔθ = 6.00 W. (d) identical inlet and outlet temperatures keep thermal energy loss rate to the surroundings constant so heat loss cancels upon subtraction.

Correct Run 1 power P₁ = 186 W.
Calculates Run 2 power P₂ = 366 W and Δθ = 10.0 K.
Applies simultaneous elimination P₂ − P₁ = (ṁ₂ − ṁ₁) c Δθ.
Obtains specific heat capacity c = 3.60e+3 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Substitutes back to find H = 6.00 W.

Concludes identical inlet and outlet temperatures keep thermal energy loss rate to the surroundings constant so heat loss cancels upon subtraction.

items.stem: The diagram pairs a cubic gas-molecule collision model with a graph of pV / (nRT) against pressure p comparing an ideal gas to real argon gas.
items.workedSolution: elastic wall collision reverses velocity giving momentum change minus two m u, Newton second and third laws give wall force, and isotropic random motion gives the one-third factor in pV equals one-third N m c rms squared. Molecules rebounding elastically off a wall reverse velocity (+u to −u), producing momentum change −2mu over round-trip interval 2L/u; by Newton's second and third laws each exerts mean outward force mu²/L across area L² (p₁ = mu²/V). Summing over N molecules and using isotropic random motion (all x, y, z directions equally likely so ⟨u²⟩ = (1/3) c_rms²) yields pV = (1/3) N m c_rms². The model assumes negligible molecular volume, zero intermolecular forces except during elastic collisions, and negligible collision duration. Real gases deviate from pV/(nRT) = 1 at low temperatures and moderate pressures because intermolecular attractions pull molecules slightly inward, lowering wall impact force, and deviate upward at very high pressures because finite molecular volume occupies a significant fraction of V.

markScheme.criterion: L1a: Explains elastic wall collisions reverse velocity component giving Δp = −2mu and round-trip time t = 2L / u.
L1b: Uses Newton's second and third laws plus area L² to obtain pV = Nm⟨u²⟩ for N molecules.
L2a: Justifies the 1/3 factor via equal probability along x, y, z axes (⟨u²⟩ = ⟨v²⟩ = ⟨w²⟩ = (1/3) c_rms²) to obtain pV = (1/3) N m c_rms².
L2b: States core ideal-gas assumptions: negligible molecular volume, negligible intermolecular forces, elastic collisions, negligible collision duration.
L3a: Explains real-gas dip below ideal line at moderate pressure / low temperature due to intermolecular attractive forces reducing impact force on walls.
L3b: Explains steep upward deviation at very high pressure because finite molecular volume is no longer negligible compared with container volume.

parts.expectedAnswer: elastic wall collision reverses velocity giving momentum change minus two m u, Newton second and third laws give wall force, and isotropic random motion gives the one-third factor in pV equals one-third N m c rms squared. Molecules rebounding elastically off a wall reverse velocity (+u to −u), producing momentum change −2mu over round-trip interval 2L/u; by Newton's second and third laws each exerts mean outward force mu²/L across area L² (p₁ = mu²/V). Summing over N molecules and using isotropic random motion (all x, y, z directions equally likely so ⟨u²⟩ = (1/3) c_rms²) yields pV = (1/3) N m c_rms². The model assumes negligible molecular volume, zero intermolecular forces except during elastic collisions, and negligible collision duration. Real gases deviate from pV/(nRT) = 1 at low temperatures and moderate pressures because intermolecular attractions pull molecules slightly inward, lowering wall impact force, and deviate upward at very high pressures because finite molecular volume occupies a significant fraction of V.

items.stem: Inside a micro-electro-mechanical gas spring cavity, 0.6 mol of an ideal monatomic gas (γ = 5/3) performs a closed three-step cycle A → B → C → A: reversible adiabatic expansion from state A (6.5 × 10⁵ Pa, 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³) to volume 8.0 × 10⁻³ m³ at B, isobaric compression from B to volume 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ at C, and isochoric heating from C back to A. Taking work done by the gas as positive, what is the net work output W_net per cycle?
items.workedSolution: At B, P_B = P_A (V_A / V_B)^(5/3) = 6.449 × 10⁴ Pa. Adiabatic work W_AB = (3/2)(P_A V_A − P_B V_B) = 1.176 × 10³ J, and isobaric compression work W_BC = P_B(V_C − V_B) = -386.9 J (W_CA = 0). Thus W_net = W_AB + W_BC = 789 J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates the closed adiabatic heat-engine cycle to obtain 789 J (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes only the magnitude of the isobaric compression work P_B(V_B − V_C).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Computes only the adiabatic expansion work W_AB and forgets to subtract the isobaric compression work |W_BC|.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates total heat input Q_CA along the isochoric leg instead of net work W_net.

items.stem: A low-density plasma-free Xenon-131 (Xe) sample (M = 0.1313 kg mol⁻¹) is held in an atmospheric research dropsonde reference chamber at 260 K. Use molar gas constant R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Calculate the internal energy per mole of the gas.
items.workedSolution: For an ideal monatomic gas, molar internal energy U_m = (3/2) R T = 1.5 × 8.31 × 260 = 3.24 × 10³ J mol⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes T = 260 K into the monatomic kinetic-theory energy relation to obtain 3.24 × 10³ J mol⁻¹ (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Includes only one translational degree of freedom (1/2 R T) instead of three.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omits the 3/2 factor in monatomic molar internal energy U_m = (3/2) R T.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses molar enthalpy C_p T = (5/2) R T instead of molar internal energy (3/2) R T.

items.stem: Modelled as an ideal blackbody (emissivity = 1), an incandescent refractory-metal calibration sphere has surface area 3.6 × 10¹⁸ m², absolute surface temperature 5500 K, and is observed from a distance d = 6.8 × 10¹¹ m. Taking Wien's constant b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K, what is the peak emission wavelength λ_max in nanometres?
items.workedSolution: By Wien's displacement law, λ_max = b / T = (2.90 × 10⁻³) / 5500 = 5.273 × 10⁻⁷ m = 527 nm.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates the blackbody radiation law in SI units to obtain 527 nm (B).

options.label: A

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts 273.15 from the kelvin temperature before applying Wien's law.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies Wien's constant b by T instead of dividing b by T.

items.stem: Within a precision pneumatic actuator chamber sealed with a movable piston, 1 mol of monatomic working gas completes a four-stage Carnot engine loop between a hot reservoir at 836 K and a cold sink at 380 K, expanding from 1.5 × 10⁻³ m³ to 3.75 × 10⁻³ m³ while in contact with the hot source (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; net work output by the gas positive).

markScheme.criterion: Converts temperatures to kelvin and applies 1 − T_C / T_H.
Obtains 0.545.
Uses Q_H = nRT_H ln(V_B / V_A).
Obtains 6.37 × 10³ J.
Multiplies η by Q_H (or evaluates Q_H − Q_C).
Obtains 3.47 × 10³ J.

items.stem: Inside an ion-propulsion xenon feed manifold of internal volume 0.032 m³, 0.35 mol of ideal Helium-4 (He) gas (molar mass 4 g mol⁻¹) is maintained at 460 K. Taking R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, what is the mass density of the gas?

markScheme.criterion: Applies ρ = nM / V in SI units to obtain 0.0437 kg m⁻³ (B).

items.stem: Inside a thick-walled cork-lagged enthalpy cell, a copper calorimeter vessel of mass 0.16 kg (c_cup = 385 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) holds 0.55 kg of water (c_liq = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹), both initially at 294 K. A 0.28 kg iron block (c_s = 450 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 440 K is lowered into the bath; heat loss to the outside air is negligible.
items.workedSolution: (a) Solving the enthalpy balance yields T_eq = 301 K. (b) Heat released by the hot solid Q_lost = m_s c_s (T_s − T_eq) = 1.75 × 10⁴ J. (c) Heat gained by the water Q_liq = m_l c_liq (T_eq − T_l) = 1.70 × 10⁴ J.

markScheme.criterion: Sets up full calorimetry heat-balance equation.
Obtains 301 K.
Evaluates m_s c_s (T_s − T_eq).
Obtains 1.75 × 10⁴ J.
Evaluates m_l c_liq (T_eq − T_l).
Obtains 1.70 × 10⁴ J.

items.stem: A four-stroke petrol engine with 4 cylinders operates at 50.0 rev s⁻¹. The enclosed area of its $p$–$V$ indicator loop for one cylinder is 440 J. Calculate the indicated power of the engine.
items.workedSolution: A four-stroke cylinder executes $f_{\mathrm{cycle}} = \frac{50.0}{2} = 25.0\text{ cycles s}^{-1}$. Thus $P_{\mathrm{ind}} = \text{area} \times f_{\mathrm{cycle}} \times N_{\mathrm{cyl}} = 440 \times 25.0 \times 4 = 44\,000\text{ W} = 44.0 kW$.

markScheme.criterion: Indicated power equals 44.0 kW.

items.stem: Inside a sealed industrial distillation reboiler test cell, an electrical immersion heater of input power 1600 W and thermal transfer efficiency 0.8 supplies energy while a 0.4 kg sample of ethanol transitions from 121 K to 199 K as plotted on the temperature–time graph. Use melting point T_m = 159 K, c_solid = 1120 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, c_liquid = 2440 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, and L_f = 1.08 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) P_eff = η P = 1.28 × 10³ W. (b) Δt_f = m L_f / P_eff = 33.8 s. (c) Total energy Q_total = 9.926 × 10⁴ J, giving t_total = Q_total / P_eff = 77.5 s.

markScheme.criterion: Multiplies heater power P by efficiency η.
Obtains 1.28 × 10³ W.
Divides m L_f by P_eff.
Obtains 33.8 s.
Computes Q_total and divides by P_eff.
Obtains 77.5 s.

parts.prompt: Calculate the effective rate of thermal energy transfer P_eff to/from the ethanol sample.
Calculate the duration of the isothermal melting plateau at 159 K.
Determine the total time required for the temperature to change from 121 K to 199 K.
workingSteps: Q_total = m c_solid (159 − 121) + m L_f + m c_liquid (199 − 159) = 9.926 × 10⁴ J.

items.stem: The diagram illustrates a reversible rectangular heat-engine cycle A → B → C → D → A executed by 0.2 mol of monatomic ideal gas in a precision pneumatic actuator chamber sealed with a movable piston, operating between P_low = 1.2 × 10⁵ Pa and P_high = 3.6 × 10⁵ Pa and between V_min = 1.8 × 10⁻³ m³ and V_max = 4.5 × 10⁻³ m³. Take expansion work by the gas as positive.
items.workedSolution: (a) W_net = (P_high − P_low)(V_max − V_min) = 648 J. (b) Q_in = Q_DA + Q_AB = (3/2)(P_high − P_low)V_min + (5/2)P_high(V_max − V_min) = 3.08 × 10³ J. (c) η = W_net / Q_in = 0.211.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates enclosed loop area (P_high − P_low)(V_max − V_min).
Obtains 648 J.
Identifies heat input on both D → A (isochoric) and A → B (isobaric).
Uses monatomic factors (3/2) on D → A and (5/2) on A → B.
Obtains Q_in = 3.08 × 10³ J.
Divides W_net from (a) by Q_in from (b).
Obtains 0.211.

parts.prompt: Calculate the net mechanical work W_net done by the gas in one complete cycle.
Calculate the total thermal energy Q_in supplied to the monatomic gas during the heating stages D → A and A → B.
Determine the thermal efficiency η of this cycle.

items.stem: A thermal laboratory tests a solid block of low-melting tin-bismuth solder of mass 0.62 kg initially at 22 °C. The figure displays its temperature–time heating curve through its melting point of 104 °C. The solid has specific heat capacity 460 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and specific latent heat of fusion 5.40 × 10⁴ J kg⁻¹. An electrical immersion heater rated at 140 W transfers energy to the sample with thermal efficiency 86%. In a separate pressure-law check, a sealed nitrogen industrial sensor contains a fixed mass of ideal gas at pressure 126 kPa and temperature 22 °C, before being heated at constant volume to 136 °C (use T / K = θ / °C + 273.2).
items.workedSolution: (a)(i) Q₁ = m c Δθ = 0.62 × 460 × (104 − 22) = 2.339 × 10⁴ J ≈ 2.34 × 10⁴ J. (a)(ii) Q_melt = m L_f = 3.348 × 10⁴ J; Q_total = 5.687 × 10⁴ J; t = Q_total / (η P) = 472.3 s ≈ 472 s. (a)(iii) mean molecular kinetic energy stays constant while intermolecular potential energy changes to overcome or form intermolecular bonds. (a)(iv) thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings and absorbed by the container. (b)(i) T₁ = 295.2 K, T₂ = 409.2 K, so p₂ = 126 × (409.2 / 295.2) = 174.7 kPa ≈ 175 kPa. (b)(ii) faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Q = m c Δθ = 0.62 × 460 × 82.
Correctly computes 2.34 × 10⁴ J (4 s.f. 2.339 × 10⁴ J).
Computes Q_melt = 3.348 × 10⁴ J, Q_total = 5.687 × 10⁴ J, and substitutes t = Q_total / (η P).
Shows 4 s.f. value 472.3 s rounding cleanly to 472 s.
States that temperature and mean molecular kinetic energy remain constant along the plateau.
Explains that intermolecular potential energy changes as bonds are weakened, broken, or formed.
States accurately that thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings and absorbed by the container.
Converts both temperatures using T = θ + 273.2 (295.2 K and 409.2 K) and applies p₂ = p₁ T₂ / T₁.
Evaluates final gas pressure = 175 kPa (4 s.f. 174.7 kPa).

Explains via Newton second law that faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area (no credit for quoting pV = nRT alone).

parts.prompt: Calculate the thermal energy required to raise the temperature of the solid low-melting tin-bismuth solder from 22 °C to 104 °C. [2]
Show clearly that the actual time required for the 140 W heater operating at 86% efficiency to warm the solid from 22 °C and melt it completely at 104 °C is approximately 472 s. [2]
Referring to the horizontal phase-change plateau QR on the figure, explain in terms of molecular energies why the temperature stays constant while internal energy changes. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: During the plateau, mean molecular kinetic energy stays constant while intermolecular potential energy changes to overcome or form intermolecular bonds.
workingSteps: State that temperature measures mean random molecular kinetic energy which stays constant.
Explain that latent thermal energy changes intermolecular potential energy as bonds are broken or formed.

parts.prompt: State one physical reason why the measured heating time in the laboratory exceeds the ideal value calculated assuming perfect efficiency. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings and absorbed by the container.
workingSteps: Apply NCUK calorimetry observation: thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings and absorbed by the container.

parts.prompt: Calculate the new pressure of the ideal gas in the sealed nitrogen industrial sensor at 136 °C using T / K = θ / °C + 273.2. [2]
Explain in terms of kinetic theory and Newton's second law (without using the ideal gas equation) why heating the gas at constant volume increases its pressure. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Heating raises molecular speeds so faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area.
workingSteps: Link higher molecular speed to larger momentum change per collision, higher collision frequency, and larger force per unit area.

items.stem: The P–V graph shows an adiabatic path A → B for 0.75 mol of monatomic ideal gas (adiabatic exponent γ = 5/3) confined in a magnetically coupled piston calorimeter chamber. At state A, the pressure is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and the volume is 5.0 × 10⁻³ m³; at state B, the volume is 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³ (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).
items.workedSolution: (a) P_B = P_A (V_A / V_B)^(5/3) = 3.17 × 10⁵ Pa. (b) T_B = P_B V_B / (nR) = 127 K. (c) With Q = 0, W_on = ΔU = 441 J.

markScheme.criterion: Uses P_A V_A^(5/3) = P_B V_B^(5/3).
Obtains 3.17 × 10⁵ Pa.
Uses T_B = P_B V_B / (nR) or T_A (V_A / V_B)^(2/3).
Obtains 127 K.
Sets Q = 0 and evaluates |(3/2)(P_B V_B − P_A V_A)|.
Obtains 441 J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the final pressure P_B of the gas in state B.
Determine the absolute temperature T_B of the gas in state B.
Using the first law of thermodynamics, calculate the work done on the gas (taking work done on the gas as positive) during A → B.
workingSteps: W_on = ΔU = (3/2)(P_B V_B − P_A V_A) = 441 J.

items.stem: A sealed sample of dry air ($\gamma = 1.40$) at 480 kPa and $1.50 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3$ expands rapidly and adiabatically to $4.50 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3$. Calculate the final pressure of the gas.
items.workedSolution: For an adiabatic change, $p_2 = p_1\left(\frac{V_1}{V_2}\right)^{\gamma} = 480\left(\frac{1.50}{4.50}\right)^{1.40} = 103 kPa$.

markScheme.criterion: Final pressure equals 103 kPa.

options.distractorRationale: Applies the isothermal relation $p_1 V_1 = p_2 V_2$ instead of $p_1 V_1^{\gamma} = p_2 V_2^{\gamma}$.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the volume ratio, predicting pressure rises during expansion.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Raises the volume ratio to $1/\gamma$ instead of $\gamma$.

items.stem: As shown in the cutaway diagram, an open rectangular storage tank with horizontal base area 3.4 m² holds two immiscible liquids at rest: an upper layer of kerosene (ρ₁ = 810 kg m⁻³, depth h₁ = 0.8 m) resting above a lower layer of seawater (ρ₂ = 1025 kg m⁻³, depth h₂ = 1.6 m). Atmospheric pressure at the open top surface is 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa and g = 9.81 m s⁻². What is the total hydrostatic gauge pressure at point Y due to the two liquid layers combined?
items.workedSolution: Upper layer Δp₁ = 810 × 9.81 × 0.8 = 6357 Pa. Lower layer Δp₂ = 1025 × 9.81 × 1.6 = 1.609 × 10⁴ Pa. Total liquid gauge pressure Δp = 2.245 × 10⁴ Pa ≈ 2.24 × 10⁴ Pa. Absolute bottom pressure p_Y = 1.01 × 10⁵ + 2.245 × 10⁴ = 1.234 × 10⁵ Pa = 123.4 kPa ≈ 123 kPa.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 2.24 × 10⁴ Pa.

items.stem: A steam turbine plant operates between a superheated boiler source at 500 °C (773 K) and a condenser sink at 40 °C (313 K). Calculate the maximum theoretical thermal efficiency permitted by the Second Law of Thermodynamics.
items.workedSolution: Temperatures must be strictly in kelvin: $\eta_{\max} = \frac{T_{\mathrm{H}} - T_{\mathrm{C}}}{T_{\mathrm{H}}} = \frac{773 - 313}{773} = 59.5%$.

markScheme.criterion: Maximum Carnot efficiency equals 59.5%.

items.workedSolution: A gas is easily compressed because large empty spaces between widely separated molecules allow the gas volume to decrease easily under pressure.

parts.prompt: Using the particle model illustrated, explain why a gas is much more compressible than a liquid or solid.
parts.expectedAnswer: A gas is easily compressed because large empty spaces between widely separated molecules allow the gas volume to decrease easily under pressure.
workingSteps: State that gas molecules are widely separated with large empty spaces between them.
Explain that applied pressure pushes molecules closer together into this empty space, whereas solid and liquid particles are already closely packed.

items.stem: A student investigates microscopic particle motion by sealing a thin suspension of smoke in air beneath a microscope objective lens.
items.workedSolution: The speck moves erratically because of uneven rapid random collisions by much smaller invisible moving air molecules transferring momentum to the suspended speck.

markScheme.criterion: Collisions from much smaller invisible randomly moving fluid molecules.
Uneven/unbalanced bombardment transfers net momentum causing abrupt zig-zags.
