items.stem: Starting from state A (1.1 × 10⁵ Pa, 5.0 × 10⁻³ m³) in a cryocooler compression cylinder containing monatomic working gas, 1.2 mol of ideal gas expands isobarically to 0.011 m³ (state B) and is heated isochorically until the pressure reaches 2.64 × 10⁵ Pa (state C). Taking R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, find the temperature in state C.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates PV / (nR) at the target state to obtain 291 K (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Reports the final temperature converted to °C when the question and options specify kelvin.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes T_B after the isobaric stage and omits the isochoric pressure ratio P_C / P_A.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses the initial volume V_A instead of V_B = V_C when evaluating T_C = P_C V_C / (nR).

items.stem: Inside an atmospheric research dropsonde reference chamber of fixed volume 0.025 m³, 0.3 mol of ideal Krypton-84 (Kr) gas (M = 0.0838 kg mol⁻¹) is heated at constant volume from T₁ = 550 K to T₂ = 1238 K, producing the two speed distributions shown. Use R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (kinetic-theory pressure relation: pV = ⅓ N m v_rms²).

markScheme.criterion: Uses v_rms = √(3RT₁ / M) with M in kg mol⁻¹.
Obtains 405 m s⁻¹.
Applies p = nRT₁ / V.
Obtains 5.48 × 10⁴ Pa.
Scales v_rms by √(T₂ / T₁) or re-evaluates √(3RT₂ / M).
Obtains 607 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the root-mean-square speed v_rms of the Krypton-84 (Kr) atoms at T₁ = 550 K.
Calculate the gas pressure inside the vessel at T₁ = 550 K.
Determine the new root-mean-square speed of the atoms when heated to T₂ = 1238 K.

items.stem: In an infrared energy-balance investigation, a Martian mid-latitude rocky plain element of surface area 6.5 m² and greybody emissivity e = 0.95 has a uniform temperature of 326 K while exchanging radiation with an ambient environment at 268 K. Take b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.
items.workedSolution: (a) λ_max = b / T = 8.90 × 10⁻⁶ m. (b) Gross emitted power P_emitted = e σ A T⁴ = 3.95 × 10³ W. (c) Net radiative loss P_net = e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴) = 2.15 × 10³ W.

markScheme.criterion: Uses λ_max = (2.90 × 10⁻³) / T.
Obtains 8.90 × 10⁻⁶ m.
Uses P_emitted = e σ A T⁴.
Obtains 3.95 × 10³ W.
Evaluates e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴).
Obtains 2.15 × 10³ W.

parts.prompt: Calculate the peak infrared wavelength λ_max emitted by the surface.
Calculate the gross thermal power emitted by the greybody surface.
Determine the net rate of radiative thermal energy loss to the 268 K surroundings.
workingSteps: P_net = e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴) = 2.15 × 10³ W.

items.stem: Coupled thermally to a 350 K reservoir, 0.85 mol of ideal gas confined in a closed noble-gas power-conversion loop expands slowly from 5.0 × 10⁻³ m³ at A to 0.0175 m³ at B (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; define work done by the gas as positive).
items.workedSolution: (a) P_B = nRT / V_B = 1.41 × 10⁵ Pa. (b) W_by = nRT ln(V_B / V_A) = 3.10 × 10³ J. (c) Since ΔU = 0, Q = W_by and ΔS = Q / T = 8.85 J K⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses P_B = nRT / V_B.
Obtains 1.41 × 10⁵ Pa.
Evaluates nRT ln(V_B / V_A).
Obtains 3.10 × 10³ J.
Uses ΔS = Q / T with Q = W_by.
Obtains 8.85 J K⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the final pressure P_B of the gas in state B.
Calculate the work done by the gas during the reversible isothermal expansion A → B.
Determine the change in entropy ΔS of the gas during A → B.
workingSteps: Since ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas isotherm, Q = W_by.

items.stem: When 0.68 kg of warm water at 338.15 K in an expanded-polystyrene adiabatic quenching bath receives 0.035 kg of cold ice at 268.15 K, the ice warms to 273.15 K, melts completely (L_f = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹), and mixes adiabatically. Using 2100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ for solid ice and 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ for liquid water, find the final temperature.
items.workedSolution: Energy to warm and melt all ice at 273.15 K: Q_1+2 = 0.035 × 2100 × (273.15 − 268.15) + 0.035 × 3.34 × 10⁵ = 1.206 × 10⁴ J. Energy balance with warm water: m_w c_w (338.15 − T_eq) = Q_1+2 + m_ice c_w (T_eq − 273.15), giving T_eq = 331 K.

markScheme.criterion: Includes sub-zero ice warming, fusion latent heat, and meltwater warming to obtain 331 K (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Applies an extra factor of one-half from misremembering the degrees-of-freedom or geometric prefactor.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Introduces an extraneous integer factor when rearranging the governing thermal relation.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Introduces an extraneous integer factor when rearranging the governing thermal relation.

items.stem: A sample of 1.5 mol of an ideal monatomic gas in a cryocooler compression cylinder containing monatomic working gas expands isobarically at constant pressure 1.8 × 10⁵ Pa from volume 3.5 × 10⁻³ m³ (state A) to 6.3 × 10⁻³ m³ (state B). Using the first law ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW (thermal energy supplied to the gas and work done on the gas positive), how much thermal energy ΔQ is supplied to the gas during A → B?
items.workedSolution: Work done on the gas during expansion is ΔW = −P(V_B − V_A) = −1.8 × 10⁵ × (6.3 × 10⁻³ − 3.5 × 10⁻³) = -504.0 J. For a monatomic ideal gas, ΔU = (3/2) P ΔV = 756.0 J. By the first law ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW, thermal energy supplied is ΔQ = ΔU − ΔW = (5/2) P ΔV = 1.26 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates the first-law energy transfer with consistent work sign to obtain 1.26 × 10³ J (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates only the boundary work W = P ΔV during expansion and ignores the increase in internal energy ΔU.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates only the internal energy change ΔU = (3/2) P ΔV and omits the expansion work P ΔV.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the 3/2 factor in monatomic ΔU = (3/2) P ΔV, computing ΔU + W = P ΔV + P ΔV = 2 P ΔV instead of (5/2) P ΔV.

items.stem: Why is the internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas purely kinetic and directly proportional to its absolute thermodynamic temperature?
items.workedSolution: Since kinetic theory assumes negligible molecular volume compared with container volume, negligible intermolecular forces except during elastic collisions, and negligible collision duration, potential energy between molecules is zero. Therefore the correct statement is: Because kinetic theory assumes negligible molecular volume compared with container volume, negligible intermolecular forces except during elastic collisions, and negligible collision duration, so intermolecular potential energy is zero.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: negligible molecular volume compared with container volume, negligible intermolecular forces except during elastic collisions, and negligible collision duration.

options.label: A
options.text: Because kinetic theory assumes negligible molecular volume compared with container volume, negligible intermolecular forces except during elastic collisions, and negligible collision duration, so intermolecular potential energy is zero.

options.label: B
options.text: Because kinetic theory assumes strong long-range electrical attraction between molecules that stores constant potential energy.
options.distractorRationale: Strong attractions would create a volume-dependent potential energy term.

options.label: C
options.text: Because kinetic theory assumes molecules never collide with one another so kinetic energy cannot change.
options.distractorRationale: Molecules do collide elastically; zero potential energy follows from negligible intermolecular forces.

options.label: D
options.text: Because kinetic theory assumes every gas atom has zero rest mass and zero rotational inertia.
options.distractorRationale: Gas atoms have finite mass m.

items.stem: In Required Practical 8, dry air is trapped above an oil column attached to a Bourdon gauge with ungraduated dead volume $V_0 = 1.5$ cm³. At absolute pressure $p_1 = 112$ kPa, the graduated scale reads $V_1 = 36.0$ cm³. The pressure is then slowly raised to $p_2 = 210$ kPa at constant room temperature.
items.workedSolution: (a) $p(V+V_0) = 4.20e+3 kPa cm³$. (b) In SI: 4.20 J. (c) $V_2 = 18.5 cm³$. (d) change the pressure slowly and wait for thermal equilibrium so the trapped air temperature remains constant and isothermal boyle behaviour holds; plotting $1/p$ vs $V$ reveals $-V_0$ at $1/p = 0$.

markScheme.criterion: Adds dead volume $V_0$ to $V_1$ before multiplying by $p_1$.
$p(V+V_0) = 4.20e+3 kPa cm³$.
Applies $10^3 \times 10^{-6} = 10^{-3}$ unit conversion.
$pV_{\mathrm{total}} = 4.20 J$.
Divides constant by $p_2$ and subtracts $V_0$.
Scale reading $V_2 = 18.5 cm³$.
Rapid compression heats gas; pausing allows thermal equilibrium at constant $T$.
States isothermal condition $pV = \text{const}$ requires fixed temperature and fixed mass.
Plotting $1/p$ vs $V$ stays linear with x-intercept at $-V_0$.

parts.prompt: Calculate the isothermal constant $p(V + V_0)$ in kPa cm³.
Convert this product $pV_{\mathrm{total}}$ into SI base-derived units (J).
workingSteps: $1\text{ kPa cm}^3 = 10^3\text{ Pa}\times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^3 = 10^{-3}\text{ J}$, so $pV = 4.20 J$.

parts.prompt: Predict the graduated scale reading $V_2$ at $p_2 = 210$ kPa.
Explain why pressure must be changed slowly with pauses before reading, and how plotting $1/p$ against $V$ determines $V_0$ graphically.
parts.expectedAnswer: change the pressure slowly and wait for thermal equilibrium so the trapped air temperature remains constant and isothermal boyle behaviour holds; plotting 1/p against V produces a straight line whose negative horizontal intercept equals −V₀.
workingSteps: Work done compressing gas warms it; waiting lets heat transfer out to restore room temperature.
Rearranging p(V + V₀) = C gives 1/p = V/C + V₀/C, which cuts the V-axis at −V₀.

items.stem: A university thermodynamics lab measures the specific heat capacity of purified water using a steady continuous-flow electrical calorimeter. The water enters at 18.0 °C and exits at 26.0 °C in both steady trials. Run 1 uses ṁ₁ = 5.00 × 10⁻³ kg s⁻¹ with V₁ = 12.0 V and I₁ = 14.3 A. Run 2 uses ṁ₂ = 0.0100 kg s⁻¹ with V₂ = 16.0 V and I₂ = 21.2 A.
items.workedSolution: (a) P₁ = 172 W. (b) P₂ = 339 W; eliminating H gives c = (P₂ − P₁) / [(ṁ₂ − ṁ₁)Δθ] = 4.18e+3 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. (c) H = P₁ − ṁ₁cΔθ = 4.40 W. (d) identical inlet and outlet temperatures keep thermal energy loss rate to the surroundings constant so heat loss cancels upon subtraction.

markScheme.criterion: Uses electrical power P = V I for Run 1.
Correct Run 1 power P₁ = 172 W.
Calculates Run 2 power P₂ = 339 W and Δθ = 8.00 K.
Applies simultaneous elimination P₂ − P₁ = (ṁ₂ − ṁ₁) c Δθ.
Obtains specific heat capacity c = 4.18e+3 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Substitutes back to find H = 4.40 W.
States heat loss rate to surroundings depends on temperature difference above ambient.
Concludes identical inlet and outlet temperatures keep thermal energy loss rate to the surroundings constant so heat loss cancels upon subtraction.

items.stem: On the P–V diagram for a solar-thermal helium Brayton demonstrator cylinder, 0.25 mol of ideal monatomic gas (adiabatic index 5/3) undergoes adiabatic expansion A → B from (8.0 × 10⁵ Pa, 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³) to 7.5 × 10⁻³ m³, followed by isobaric compression B → C to 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³ and isochoric regeneration C → A. Adopt positive work for expansion by the gas.
items.workedSolution: (a) Adiabatic relation gives P_B = 1.28 × 10⁵ Pa. (b) Isochoric heat input Q_in = 2.52 × 10³ J. (c) By cyclic energy conservation ΔU_cycle = 0, W_net = Q_in − Q_out = 917 J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies P V^(5/3) = const along A → B.
Obtains 1.28 × 10⁵ Pa.
Uses Q_in = (3/2) ΔP V on the isochoric heating leg.
Obtains 2.52 × 10³ J.
Evaluates W_net = Q_in − Q_out (or sums leg works).
Obtains 917 J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the pressure P_B of the gas at state B.
Calculate the thermal energy Q_in absorbed by the gas during the isochoric heating leg.
workingSteps: On C → A (constant V = 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³, P_C = P_B), Q_in = ΔU_CA = (3/2)(P_A − P_B) V_A = 2.52 × 10³ J.

parts.prompt: Determine the net mechanical work W_net done by the gas per cycle.
workingSteps: Heat rejected on isobaric leg B → C is Q_out = (5/2) P_B (V_B − V_C) = 1.602 × 10³ J; W_net = Q_in − Q_out = 917 J.

items.stem: Within a laser-interferometer gas-cell enclosure, low-pressure monatomic Helium-4 (He) gas (M = 4.0 × 10⁻³ kg mol⁻¹) is held at 440 K. Data: k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹, 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) E_k,avg = (3/2) k_B T = 0 J. (b) Dividing by 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C gives 0.0569 eV. (c) v_rms = √(3RT / M) = 1.66 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Applies E_k = (3/2) k_B T in kelvin.
Obtains 0 J.
Divides energy in joules by elementary charge e.
Obtains 0.0569 eV.
Evaluates v_rms = √(3RT / M).
Obtains 1.66 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

items.stem: The heating curve shows how the temperature of a 0.45 kg sample of pure lead in an adiabatic micro-calorimeter ampoule varies with thermal energy supplied from 561 K (solid) to 646 K (liquid). Data for lead: melting point = 600.6 K, c_solid = 128 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, c_liquid = 147 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, and specific latent heat of fusion L_f = 2.3 × 10⁴ J kg⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) Q_sens = m c_solid ΔT₁ + m c_liquid ΔT₂ = 5.28 × 10³ J. (b) Plateau latent energy Q_lat = m L = 1.04 × 10⁴ J. (c) Total thermal energy Q_total = Q_sens + Q_lat = 1.56 × 10⁴ J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates m c₁ ΔT₁ + m c₂ ΔT₂.
Obtains 5.28 × 10³ J.
Evaluates m L on the phase-change plateau.
Obtains 1.04 × 10⁴ J.
Sums sensible and latent energies.
Obtains 1.56 × 10⁴ J.

items.stem: A bolometric sensor placed at d = 5 m in vacuum intercepts isotropic blackbody radiation (e = 1) from a K-dwarf stellar surface of area 3.2 × 10⁻³ m² and temperature 1200 K. Use Wien's constant 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K and Stefan–Boltzmann constant 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.
items.workedSolution: (a) λ_max = b / T = 2.42 × 10⁻⁶ m. (b) P = σ A T⁴ = 376 W. (c) I = P / (4π d²) = 1.20 W m⁻².

Obtains 2.42 × 10⁻⁶ m.
Applies P = σ A T⁴.
Obtains 376 W.
Divides P by 4π d².
Obtains 1.20 W m⁻².

items.stem: The diagram shows a reversible Carnot cycle A → B → C → D → A for 1 mol of monatomic ideal gas in a magnetically coupled piston calorimeter chamber coupled to a hot reservoir at 650 K and a cold sink at 260 K, with isothermal expansion from 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ to 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³. Taking R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, what magnitude of thermal energy Q_C is rejected to the cold sink per cycle?
items.workedSolution: During isothermal compression C → D at T_C = 260 K, V_C / V_D = V_B / V_A, so heat rejected to the cold sink is Q_C = nRT_C ln(V_B / V_A) = 1.50 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Carnot thermodynamics in kelvin to obtain 1.50 × 10³ J (B).

options.distractorRationale: Uses log₁₀(V_B / V_A) instead of ln(V_B / V_A) in Q_C = nRT_C ln(V_B / V_A).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Computes net work W_net = Q_H − Q_C instead of the rejected heat Q_C.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes the heat absorbed Q_H from the hot reservoir instead of the heat Q_C rejected to the cold sink.

items.workedSolution: (a) p = nRT / V = (2.2 × 8.31 × 360.15) / 0.016 = 4.12 × 10⁵ Pa. (b) Single-atom mass m = M / N_A = 0 kg. (c) Density ρ = nM / V = 2.78 kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes Kelvin temperature into p = nRT / V.
Obtains 4.12 × 10⁵ Pa.
Converts molar mass to kg mol⁻¹ and divides by Avogadro constant.
Obtains 0 kg.
Evaluates ρ = nM / V in SI units.
Obtains 2.78 kg m⁻³.

items.stem: In a calorimetry run using a closed-lid magnetic-stirrer calorimetry pot, a 0.85 kg cylinder of aluminium (c = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 410 K is quenched in 0.32 kg of mineral oil (c = 1960 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 285 K. During mixing, 1250 J of thermal energy escapes to the surroundings. What thermal energy does the cylinder give up?
items.workedSolution: Enthalpy balance: m_s c_s (T_s − T_eq) = m_l c_l (T_eq − T_l) + 1250, giving T_eq = 352.8 K. Heat released by the solid Q_lost = m_s c_s (T_s − T_eq) = 4.38 × 10⁴ J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies calorimetry energy balance to obtain 4.38 × 10⁴ J (B).

items.stem: In a precision constant-flux heating chamber, an electrical immersion heater of input power 750 W and thermal transfer efficiency 0.85 supplies energy as a 0.75 kg sample of ethanol goes from 141 K to 184 K across its 159 K fusion point (c_solid = 1120 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, c_liquid = 2440 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, L_f = 1.08 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹). What total time elapses for the complete temperature change?
items.workedSolution: Effective thermal power P_eff = η P = 0.85 × 750 = 637.5 W. Total energy Q_tot = m c_solid ΔT_s + m L_f + m c_liquid ΔT_l = 1.419 × 10⁵ J, giving t_total = Q_tot / P_eff = 223 s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses P_eff = η P and divides required thermal energy to obtain 223 s (D).

items.stem: In a frictionless piston-cylinder assembly on a thermodynamics test bench, 0.2 mol of a monatomic ideal gas executes a clockwise closed cycle A → B → C → D → A between pressures 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa and volumes 1.8 × 10⁻³ m³ and 4.5 × 10⁻³ m³ (A → B isobaric expansion at 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa, B → C isochoric cooling, C → D isobaric compression at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, D → An isochoric heating). What is the thermal efficiency η = W_net / Q_in of this rectangular monatomic-gas cycle?
items.workedSolution: W_net = (2.0 × 10⁵ − 1.0 × 10⁵)(4.5 × 10⁻³ − 1.8 × 10⁻³) = 270.0 J. Heat enters on D → A and A → B: Q_in = (3/2)(P_high − P_low)V_min + (5/2)P_high(V_max − V_min) = 1.620 × 10³ J. Efficiency η = W_net / Q_in = 0.167.

markScheme.criterion: Computes thermalEfficiency correctly for the closed rectangular cycle to obtain 0.167 (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides W_net by Q_AB alone, neglecting the heat input Q_DA on the isochoric leg D → A.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits internal energy gain ΔU_AB when computing total heat input Q_in.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes the Carnot efficiency 1 − T_min / T_max between extreme corner temperatures instead of the actual cycle efficiency W_net / Q_in.

items.stem: A calorimetry experiment records the cooling curve shown in the figure as 0.28 kg of molten purified lauric ester freezes at 52 °C and cools in solid form down to 19 °C. The solid has specific heat capacity 1740 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and specific latent heat of fusion 1.78 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. When previously melted from 19 °C using a 78 W immersion heater, the heating setup operated at 78% thermal efficiency. Separately, a constant-volume dry air sphere holds a fixed mass of ideal gas at 98 kPa and 19 °C before warming at constant volume to 88 °C (use T / K = θ / °C + 273.2).
items.workedSolution: (a)(i) Q₁ = m c Δθ = 0.28 × 1740 × (52 − 19) = 1.608 × 10⁴ J ≈ 1.61 × 10⁴ J. (a)(ii) Q_melt = m L_f = 4.984 × 10⁴ J; Q_total = 6.592 × 10⁴ J ≈ 6.59 × 10⁴ J. (a)(iii) mean molecular kinetic energy stays constant while intermolecular potential energy changes to overcome or form intermolecular bonds. (a)(iv) temperature remains constant along a horizontal plateau during freezing before falling smoothly toward ambient temperature. (b)(i) T₁ = 292.2 K, T₂ = 361.2 K, so p₂ = 98 × (361.2 / 292.2) = 121.1 kPa ≈ 121 kPa. (b)(ii) faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Q = m c Δθ = 0.28 × 1740 × 33.
Correctly computes 1.61 × 10⁴ J (4 s.f. 1.608 × 10⁴ J).
Computes latent energy Q_melt = 4.984 × 10⁴ J and sums Q_warm + Q_melt.
Shows 4 s.f. value 6.592 × 10⁴ J rounding cleanly to 6.59 × 10⁴ J.
States that temperature and mean molecular kinetic energy remain constant along the plateau.
Explains that intermolecular potential energy changes as bonds are weakened, broken, or formed.
States accurately that temperature remains constant along a horizontal plateau during freezing before falling smoothly toward ambient temperature.
Converts both temperatures using T = θ + 273.2 (292.2 K and 361.2 K) and applies p₂ = p₁ T₂ / T₁.
Evaluates final gas pressure = 121 kPa (4 s.f. 121.1 kPa).

Explains via Newton second law that faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area (no credit for quoting pV = nRT alone).

parts.prompt: Calculate the new pressure of the ideal gas in the constant-volume dry air sphere at 88 °C using T / K = θ / °C + 273.2. [2]
Explain in terms of kinetic theory and Newton's second law (without using the ideal gas equation) why heating the gas at constant volume increases its pressure. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Heating raises molecular speeds so faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area.
workingSteps: Link higher molecular speed to larger momentum change per collision, higher collision frequency, and larger force per unit area.

items.stem: A thermally isolated sample of 0.4 mol of monatomic ideal gas (γ = 5/3) in a solar-thermal helium Brayton demonstrator cylinder transitions adiabatically from state A (1.6 × 10⁵ Pa, 3.2 × 10⁻³ m³) to state B of volume 1.6 × 10⁻³ m³. Given R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, calculate the gas pressure at state B.
items.workedSolution: For a monatomic adiabatic process, P_B = P_A (V_A / V_B)^(5/3) = 1.6 × 10⁵ × (3.2 × 10⁻³ / 1.6 × 10⁻³)^(5/3) = 5.08 × 10⁵ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Applies P V^(5/3) = const to obtain 5.08 × 10⁵ Pa (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the adiabatic exponent, using 3/5 instead of γ = 5/3.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Treats the process as isothermal (P_A V_A = P_B V_B) rather than adiabatic (P_A V_A^(5/3) = P_B V_B^(5/3)).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses the diatomic adiabatic index γ = 7/5 instead of γ = 5/3 for a monatomic gas.

items.stem: A cylinder holds 0.300 mol of diatomic oxygen ($\gamma = 1.40$) initially at pressure 550 kPa and volume 1.60 × 10⁻³ m³. The gas undergoes an adiabatic change to a final volume of 4.00 × 10⁻³ m³. Take $R = 8.31\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$ and apply $Q = \Delta U + W$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $p_2 = 152 kPa$. (b) $T_2 = \frac{p_2 V_2}{nR} = 245 K$. (c) Work done by gas $W = 675 J$. (d) Change in internal energy $\Delta U = −675 J$.

markScheme.criterion: Applies the governing pressure-volume relation $p_1 V_1^{\gamma} = p_2 V_2^{\gamma}$.
Obtains $p_2 = 152 kPa$.
Applies $pV = nRT$ with $R = 8.31\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$.
Obtains $T_2 = 245 K$.
Evaluates mechanical work done by the gas with correct sign.
Obtains $W = 675 J$.
Applies $Q = \Delta U + W$ with $Q = 0$ for an adiabatic process.
Obtains $\Delta U = −675 J$.

parts.prompt: Calculate the final pressure of the gas in kPa.
Determine the final thermodynamic temperature of the gas in kelvin.
Calculate the work done BY the gas during the change, stating its sign clearly.
Hence calculate the change in internal energy $\Delta U$ of the gas.
workingSteps: For an adiabatic change $Q = 0$, so $\Delta U = -W = −675 J$.

items.stem: An open glass U-tube contains concentrated brine of known density ρ₂ = 1160 kg m⁻³ in its lower bend and right arm. An immiscible sample of vegetable oil of unknown density ρ₁ is poured into the left arm until equilibrium is reached as illustrated. Above the horizontal interface datum P–Q, the left oil column stands h₁ = 0.38 m tall while the right concentrated brine column stands h₂ = 0.258 m tall (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) pressures are equal at the same horizontal level within a continuous static liquid. (b) Δp = ρ₂gh₂ = 2936 Pa ≈ 2.94e+3 Pa. (c) ρ₁ = ρ₂(h₂/h₁) = 787.6 kg m⁻³ ≈ 788 kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: States equal pressure at the same horizontal level in a continuous static liquid.
Applies Δp = ρ₂gh₂.
Equates ρ₁gh₁ = ρ₂gh₂.
ρ₁ = 788 kg m⁻³.

items.stem: A large hospital currently buys electricity from a distant coal/gas power station and burns natural gas on-site in boilers for space heating. Engineers propose installing a local combined heat and power (CHP) station instead.
items.workedSolution: Standalone turbines must reject heat because $\eta_{\max} = (T_{\mathrm{H}} - T_{\mathrm{C}})/T_{\mathrm{H}} < 1$. Combined heat and power utilises rejected thermal energy for heating raising overall energy utilisation above a standalone power station and cuts transmission losses, traded against slightly higher $T_{\mathrm{C}}$ and siting near steady heat demand.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $\eta_{\max} = (T_{\mathrm{H}} - T_{\mathrm{C}})/T_{\mathrm{H}}$ in kelvin to explain why a power station must reject heat.
Explains that standalone power stations waste rejected condenser energy to the environment.
Explains that CHP captures rejected thermal energy for heating, boosting overall useful energy utilisation.
Notes reduced electrical grid transmission losses from local on-site generation.
Identifies the trade-off that rejecting heat at higher $T_{\mathrm{C}}$ for heating slightly reduces electrical turbine efficiency.
Identifies practical CHP deployment limits such as proximity to heat users, insulated piping costs, or seasonal demand mismatch.

parts.prompt: Explain using thermodynamic principles why a standalone power station wastes a large fraction of its fuel energy, how a CHP station improves overall energy utilisation, and the practical engineering limitations that govern CHP deployment.
parts.expectedAnswer: Any cyclic power-station turbine is governed by the Second Law limit $\eta_{\max} = (T_{\mathrm{H}} - T_{\mathrm{C}})/T_{\mathrm{H}}$ in kelvin; because the condenser cannot approach absolute zero and real irreversibilities occur, more than half of the fuel energy is rejected to cooling towers or rivers as low-grade heat. In contrast, combined heat and power utilises rejected thermal energy for heating raising overall energy utilisation above a standalone power station, while local generation also cuts high-voltage grid transmission losses. However, to supply useful district or hospital hot water, the CHP condenser must reject heat at a higher temperature $T_{\mathrm{C}}$, slightly lowering electrical Carnot efficiency, and the plant must be sited close to continuous heat demand to avoid insulated-pipe losses.
workingSteps: L1: State Carnot maximum efficiency $\eta_{\max} = (T_{\mathrm{H}} - T_{\mathrm{C}})/T_{\mathrm{H}}$ in kelvin and explain why $T_{\mathrm{C}} > 0\text{ K}$ forces heat rejection.
L1: Note that conventional stations dump this rejected condenser heat into rivers or cooling towers.
L2: Explain that a CHP plant captures rejected thermal energy for space heating or hot water, sharply raising total useful energy fraction.
L2: Note reduced electrical distribution losses because generation is close to the hospital load.
L3: Explain the thermodynamic trade-off: raising $T_{\mathrm{C}}$ so rejected water is hot enough for heating slightly reduces electrical efficiency.
L3: Identify siting/demand matching constraints (heat cannot be piped cheaply over long distances; seasonal heat-to-power mismatch).

items.stem: A thermodynamics textbook illustrates the contrast in intermolecular spacing across three phases of matter as shown. Which statement best characterizes the arrangement, motion, and intermolecular forces of the particles in the right-hand panel?
items.workedSolution: In the right-hand panel, particles are widely spaced and move rapidly and randomly in all directions with negligible intermolecular forces.

options.label: A
options.text: Particles oscillate back and forth about fixed points separated by tiny lattice gaps.
options.distractorRationale: Describes lattice vibration in a crystalline solid.

options.label: B
options.text: In the right-hand panel, particles are widely spaced and move rapidly and randomly in all directions with negligible intermolecular forces.

options.label: C
options.text: Particles move slowly in uniform parallel streams all pointing in the same direction.
options.distractorRationale: Thermal motion of gas molecules is rapid and isotropic (random in all directions).

options.label: D
options.text: Particles remain closely touching in small vibrating clusters held by strong rigid bonds.
options.distractorRationale: Confuses gas behaviour with condensed solid/liquid phases.

items.stem: During an AC3.1 matter practical, fine smoke particles suspended in still air inside a sealed glass chamber are observed under intense lateral illumination. What fundamental kinetic-theory conclusion is supported by this experiment?
items.workedSolution: This classic experiment provides direct experimental evidence that fluid molecules are in continuous random thermal motion.

markScheme.criterion: This classic experiment provides direct experimental evidence that fluid molecules are in continuous random thermal motion.

options.label: A
options.text: Proof that air molecules are larger than smoke particles and move only when illuminated.
options.distractorRationale: Air molecules are vastly smaller than smoke specks and move thermally even in total darkness.

options.label: B
options.text: Direct proof that solids melt whenever exposed to lateral visible light.
options.distractorRationale: Brownian motion demonstrates kinetic molecular agitation in fluids, not phase melting.

options.label: C
options.text: This classic experiment provides direct experimental evidence that fluid molecules are in continuous random thermal motion.

options.label: D
options.text: Evidence that gravity does not act on microscopic particles suspended inside sealed cells.
options.distractorRationale: Gravity still acts, but random molecular bombardment dominates the rapid lateral jiggling.

items.stem: An ideal gas sample (1.5 mol) confined in a solar-thermal helium Brayton demonstrator cylinder is taken from state A (1.6 × 10⁵ Pa, 6.0 × 10⁻³ m³) to state B (0.0132 m³) isobarically, and then from state B to state C (2.56 × 10⁵ Pa) isochorically, as illustrated on the pressure–volume (P–V) graph (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).
items.workedSolution: (a) T_A = P_A V_A / (nR) = 77.0 K. (b) Isobaric expansion gives T_B = T_A (V_B / V_A) = 169 K. (c) Isochoric heating gives T_C = T_B (P_C / P_A) = 271 K.

markScheme.criterion: Uses T_A = P_A V_A / (nR).
Obtains 77.0 K.
Applies V_B / T_B = V_A / T_A or P_A V_B / (nR).
Obtains 169 K.
Applies P_C / T_C = P_B / T_B or P_C V_B / (nR).
Obtains 271 K.

parts.prompt: Calculate the initial temperature T_A of the gas in state A.
Determine the temperature T_B at the end of the isobaric expansion A → B.
workingSteps: By Charles's law at constant pressure, T_B = T_A (V_B / V_A) = 169 K.

parts.prompt: Calculate the final temperature T_C in state C after the isochoric stage B → C.
workingSteps: At constant volume V_C = V_B, T_C = T_B (P_C / P_B) = (2.56 × 10⁵ × 0.0132) / (1.5 × 8.31) = 271 K.

items.stem: At 360 K, 2 mol of Argon-40 (Ar) with molar mass 0.04 kg mol⁻¹ fills an orbital satellite attitude-control propellant cylinder (capacity 0.04 m³). Using R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (kinetic-theory pressure relation: pV = ⅓ N m v_rms²), calculate the root-mean-square speed marked v_rms on the distribution.
items.workedSolution: Convert molar mass to SI units: M = 0.04 kg mol⁻¹. Using v_rms = √(3RT / M) at T = 360 K gives v_rms = √(3 × 8.31 × 360 / 0.04) = 474 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates √(3RT / M) with M in kg mol⁻¹ to obtain 474 m s⁻¹ (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes molar mass in g mol⁻¹ instead of kg mol⁻¹ into √(3RT / M), underestimating v_rms by a factor of √1000 ≈ 31.6.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 3 from the three translational degrees of freedom, evaluating √(RT / M).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses a factor of 2 instead of 3, computing the most probable speed v_p = √(2RT / M) rather than v_rms.

items.stem: An energy-budget sensor monitors a selectively coated solar-thermal collector plate (area 6.5 m², greybody emissivity 0.78) maintained at 343 K within a radiative environment at 268 K. Using σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, calculate P_net = e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴).
items.workedSolution: Net radiative power loss P_net = e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴) = 0.78 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 6.5 × ((343)⁴ − (268)⁴) = 2.50 × 10³ W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴) to obtain 2.50 × 10³ W (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Evaluates e σ A (T − T_amb)⁴ instead of e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴), a classic fourth-power algebra error.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the greybody emissivity factor e (< 1) from P_net = e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates gross emitted power e σ A T⁴ and ignores incoming radiation absorbed from the surroundings at T_amb.

items.stem: On the P–V diagram, 0.85 mol of an ideal gas in an insulated aerospace gas-accumulator cylinder undergoes a reversible isothermal expansion at 520 K from 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ to 6.0 × 10⁻³ m³. Take R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and expansion work by the gas as positive. Find W_AB.
items.workedSolution: At constant temperature T = 520 K, ΔU = 0 and W_by = Q = nRT ln(V_B / V_A) = 0.85 × 8.31 × 520 × ln(6.0 × 10⁻³ / 2.0 × 10⁻³) = 4.04 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates W = nRT ln(V_B / V_A) to obtain 4.04 × 10³ J (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes log₁₀(V_B / V_A) instead of ln(V_B / V_A).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Treats pressure as remaining constant at P_A, computing P_A(V_B − V_A) instead of ∫ P dV = nRT ln(V_B / V_A).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Adds U = (3/2)nRT to isothermal work, overlooking that ΔU = 0 at constant temperature.

items.stem: Neglecting container heat capacity in a thick-walled cork-lagged enthalpy cell, 0.045 kg of ice at 253.15 K warms across its 273.15 K fusion point (L_f = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹) when stirred into 0.48 kg of 348.15 K water (c_ice = 2100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, c_water = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹).
items.workedSolution: (a) Q_lat = m_ice L_f = 1.50 × 10⁴ J. (b) Full enthalpy balance yields T_eq = 334 K. (c) Heat released by warm water = 2.84 × 10⁴ J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates m_ice L_f.
Obtains 1.50 × 10⁴ J.
Balances ice warming, melting, and meltwater warming against warm water cooling.
Obtains 334 K.
Evaluates m_water c_water (T_water − T_eq).
Obtains 2.84 × 10⁴ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the latent thermal energy required solely to melt all the ice once it reaches 273.15 K.
Calculate the final thermal equilibrium temperature T_eq of the water.
workingSteps: m_water c_water (348.15 − T_eq) = m_ice c_ice (273.15 − 253.15) + Q_lat + m_ice c_water (T_eq − 273.15).

parts.prompt: Determine the total thermal energy released by the initially warm water.

items.stem: Inside a frictionless piston-cylinder assembly on a thermodynamics test bench, 0.25 mol of monatomic ideal gas undergoes two sequential processes plotted on the P–V graph: isochoric heating from A (2.4 × 10⁵ Pa, 1.5 × 10⁻³ m³) to B (3.6 × 10⁵ Pa, 1.5 × 10⁻³ m³), followed by isobaric expansion to C (3.6 × 10⁵ Pa, 3.9 × 10⁻³ m³). Use ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW with work done on the gas (ΔW) and heat transferred into the gas (ΔQ) taken as positive.
items.workedSolution: (a) Work is done only along B → C: ΔW = −P_B(V_C − V_B) = -864 J. (b) ΔU_AC = (3/2)(P_C V_C − P_A V_A) = 1.57 × 10³ J. (c) By ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW, total heat supplied ΔQ = ΔU_AC − ΔW = 2.43 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies ΔW_AB = 0 and computes ΔW = −P_B(V_C − V_B).
Obtains -864 J.
Applies ΔU = (3/2)(P_C V_C − P_A V_A).
Obtains 1.57 × 10³ J.
Applies ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW ⇒ ΔQ = ΔU_AC − ΔW to obtain total heat supplied.
Obtains 2.43 × 10³ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the total mechanical work done on the gas ΔW along path A → B → C (including its sign).
Calculate the total change in internal energy ΔU of the monatomic gas between state A and state C.
workingSteps: For a monatomic ideal gas, U = (3/2) PV, so ΔU_AC = (3/2)(P_C V_C − P_A V_A).

parts.prompt: Determine the total thermal energy ΔQ supplied to the gas over the complete path A → B → C.
workingSteps: By the first law of thermodynamics (ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW), ΔQ = ΔU_AC − ΔW = 1.566 × 10³ − (-864.0) = 2.43 × 10³ J.

items.stem: Water flows steadily through a continuous-flow calorimeter, rising from 18.0 °C to 26.0 °C in both trials. In Trial 1, ṁ₁ = 0.00500 kg s⁻¹ requires V₁ = 12.0 V and I₁ = 14.3 A. In Trial 2, ṁ₂ = 0.0100 kg s⁻¹ requires V₂ = 16.0 V and I₂ = 21.175 A. Calculate the specific heat capacity of water.

markScheme.criterion: Eliminates H via P₂ − P₁ = (ṁ₂ − ṁ₁)cΔθ to obtain c = 4.18e+3 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

items.stem: Nitrogen gas (molar mass M = 0.0280 kg mol⁻¹) is held at thermodynamic temperature T = 320 K inside a sealed container. Taking R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, calculate the root-mean-square speed c_rms of the nitrogen molecules.

options.label: A
options.text: Compressing rapidly prevents heat leaving the air so the process remains isothermal.
options.distractorRationale: Rapid compression heats the gas (adiabatic compression), causing pV to increase above the isothermal constant.

options.label: B
options.text: Change the pressure slowly and wait for thermal equilibrium so the trapped air temperature remains constant and isothermal boyle behaviour holds.

options.label: C
options.text: Pausing allows air to dissolve into the oil so total mass of gas stays constant.
options.distractorRationale: Fixed mass of gas requires no leakage or dissolution; pausing simply restores room temperature.

options.label: D
options.text: Slow compression ensures the oil meniscus turns flat, eliminating all parallax error.
options.distractorRationale: The oil meniscus curvature is due to surface tension; parallax is avoided by reading at eye level.

items.stem: In Required Practical 8 (Charles's law), a dry air sample trapped by a concentrated sulfuric acid bead inside a uniform vertical capillary tube is heated in a water bath. Two points on the best-fit straight line of air column length $L$ against temperature $\theta$ are $(15\ ^\circ\text{C}, 104.0\text{ mm})$ and $(85\ ^\circ\text{C}, 129.2\text{ mm})$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $m = 0.360 mm °C⁻¹$. (b) $L_0 = 98.6 mm$. (c) Absolute zero $= -274 °C$. (d) the concentrated sulfuric acid bead traps dry air at constant atmospheric pressure and absorbs water vapour while stirring the water bath keeps temperature uniform.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates $\Delta L / \Delta\theta$.
Gradient $m = 0.360 mm °C⁻¹$.
Substitutes into $L_0 = L_1 - m\theta_1$.
Length at 0 °C $= 98.6 mm$.
Sets $L = 0$ to solve $\theta = -L_0 / m$.
Extrapolated absolute zero $= -274 °C$.
Bead traps fixed mass of air at constant atmospheric pressure.
Concentrated sulfuric acid absorbs water vapour / keeps air dry.
Thorough stirring keeps water bath uniform so thermometer reads true air temperature.

Determine the air column length $L_0$ at $0\ ^\circ\text{C}$.
Hence extrapolate the experimental value of absolute zero in °C.
Explain the dual role of the concentrated sulfuric acid bead and why continuous stirring is essential.
parts.expectedAnswer: the concentrated sulfuric acid bead traps dry air at constant atmospheric pressure and absorbs water vapour while stirring the water bath keeps temperature uniform
workingSteps: Acid bead slides freely to keep trapped air at constant atmospheric pressure.
Concentrated H₂SO₄ dries the air by absorbing water vapour.
Stirring prevents thermal stratification so thermometer matches trapped air temperature.

items.stem: An automotive fluid laboratory tests synthetic mineral oil in an evacuated-jacket continuous-flow calorimeter across two steady flow rates. The mineral oil enters at 20.0 °C and exits at 32.0 °C in both steady trials. Run 1 uses ṁ₁ = 6.00 × 10⁻³ kg s⁻¹ with V₁ = 15.0 V and I₁ = 10.5 A. Run 2 uses ṁ₂ = 0.0120 kg s⁻¹ with V₂ = 20.0 V and I₂ = 15.4 A.
items.workedSolution: (a) P₁ = 157 W. (b) P₂ = 308 W; eliminating H gives c = (P₂ − P₁) / [(ṁ₂ − ṁ₁)Δθ] = 2.10e+3 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. (c) H = P₁ − ṁ₁cΔθ = 6.00 W. (d) identical inlet and outlet temperatures keep thermal energy loss rate to the surroundings constant so heat loss cancels upon subtraction.

markScheme.criterion: Uses electrical power P = V I for Run 1.
Correct Run 1 power P₁ = 157 W.
Calculates Run 2 power P₂ = 308 W and Δθ = 12.0 K.
Applies simultaneous elimination P₂ − P₁ = (ṁ₂ − ṁ₁) c Δθ.
Obtains specific heat capacity c = 2.10e+3 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Substitutes back to find H = 6.00 W.
States heat loss rate to surroundings depends on temperature difference above ambient.
Concludes identical inlet and outlet temperatures keep thermal energy loss rate to the surroundings constant so heat loss cancels upon subtraction.

parts.prompt: Calculate the electrical power P₁ supplied to the heating coil during Run 1.
Using data from both Run 1 and Run 2, calculate the specific heat capacity c of the mineral oil.
workingSteps: Subtract P₂ − P₁ = (ṁ₂ − ṁ₁) c Δθ with Δθ = 12.0 K

parts.prompt: Hence determine the steady rate of thermal energy loss H to the surroundings.
Explain why both experimental runs must maintain the exact same inlet and outlet temperatures.
parts.expectedAnswer: Maintaining identical inlet and outlet temperatures keep thermal energy loss rate to the surroundings constant so heat loss cancels upon subtraction.
workingSteps: Thermal energy loss rate H depends on temperature excess above room temperature.
Keeping identical inlet and outlet temperatures keep thermal energy loss rate to the surroundings constant so heat loss cancels upon subtraction.

items.stem: Three reversible stages A → B → C → A form a heat-engine cycle for 0.6 mol of monatomic gas (γ = 5/3) inside a laboratory heat-engine indicator rig with low-friction seals: adiabatic expansion from 6.5 × 10⁵ Pa and 1.5 × 10⁻³ m³ to 6.0 × 10⁻³ m³, constant-pressure compression to 1.5 × 10⁻³ m³, and constant-volume heating to A. What net mechanical work output does one cycle deliver?
items.workedSolution: At B, P_B = P_A (V_A / V_B)^(5/3) = 6.449 × 10⁴ Pa. Adiabatic work W_AB = (3/2)(P_A V_A − P_B V_B) = 882.1 J, and isobaric compression work W_BC = P_B(V_C − V_B) = -290.2 J (W_CA = 0). Thus W_net = W_AB + W_BC = 592 J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates the closed adiabatic heat-engine cycle to obtain 592 J (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes only the magnitude of the isobaric compression work P_B(V_B − V_C).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Computes only the adiabatic expansion work W_AB and forgets to subtract the isobaric compression work |W_BC|.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates total heat input Q_CA along the isochoric leg instead of net work W_net.

items.stem: Spectroscopic thermometry confirms that Neon-20 (Ne) atoms (molar mass 0.0202 kg mol⁻¹) in a rigid stainless-steel vacuum-calibration tank are equilibrated at 137 °C (take T(K) = θ(°C) + 273.15). Given R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, Determine the molar translational internal energy U_m.
items.workedSolution: T = 137 + 273.15 = 410.15 K. For an ideal monatomic gas, molar internal energy U_m = (3/2) R T = 1.5 × 8.31 × 410.15 = 5.11 × 10³ J mol⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes T = 410.15 K into the monatomic kinetic-theory energy relation to obtain 5.11 × 10³ J mol⁻¹ (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Includes only one translational degree of freedom (1/2 R T) instead of three.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omits the 3/2 factor in monatomic molar internal energy U_m = (3/2) R T.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Uses molar enthalpy C_p T = (5/2) R T instead of molar internal energy (3/2) R T.

items.stem: The phase-change graph plots temperature against thermal energy transferred for 0.65 kg of ethanol in a lagged laboratory phase-transition calorimeter warmed from 139 K to 244 K across its melting point at 159 K (c_solid = 1120 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, c_liquid = 2440 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, specific latent heat of fusion L_f = 1.08 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹). Calculate the total thermal energy required.
items.workedSolution: Sensible heating: Q_sens = 0.65 × 1120 × (159 − 139) + 0.65 × 2440 × (244 − 159) = 1.494 × 10⁵ J. Latent heat on plateau: Q_lat = mL = 0.65 × 1.08 × 10⁵ = 7.020 × 10⁴ J. Total Q = 2.20 × 10⁵ J.

markScheme.criterion: Sums sensible mcΔT stages and latent heat mL to obtain 2.20 × 10⁵ J (C).

items.stem: The Planck spectral curve shown corresponds to a vacuum-chamber blackbody radiometer target of radiating area 1.8 × 10¹⁸ m² and uniform blackbody temperature 5500 K, monitored by a radiometer 6.8 × 10¹¹ m away. Taking σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, what is the radiant intensity received at distance d (neglecting intervening absorption)?
items.workedSolution: Radiated luminosity L = σ A T⁴ = 9.339 × 10²⁵ W. Intensity at distance d is I = L / (4π d²) = 9.339 × 10²⁵ / (4π × (6.8 × 10¹¹)²) = 16.1 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates the blackbody radiation law in SI units to obtain 16.1 W m⁻² (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides radiated power by disc area π d² instead of spherical shell area 4π d².

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the geometric factor 4π for isotropic spherical spreading in I = L / (4π d²).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides by 4π d instead of 4π d², omitting the inverse-square exponent.

items.stem: Operating between a hot reservoir at 703 K and a cold sink at 380 K, 0.5 mol of ideal gas in a closed-cycle Stirling regenerator test cell executes an ideal Carnot power cycle whose high-temperature isothermal leg A → B expands from 1.2 × 10⁻³ m³ to 4.2 × 10⁻³ m³. Use R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and take work done by the gas as positive.

markScheme.criterion: Converts temperatures to kelvin and applies 1 − T_C / T_H.
Obtains 0.459.
Uses Q_H = nRT_H ln(V_B / V_A).
Obtains 3.66 × 10³ J.
Multiplies η by Q_H (or evaluates Q_H − Q_C).
Obtains 1.68 × 10³ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the thermal efficiency η of the Carnot cycle.
Calculate the thermal energy Q_H absorbed from the hot reservoir during the isothermal expansion A → B.
Determine the net mechanical work W_net done by the gas per cycle.

items.stem: Engineers charge a high-vacuum synchrotron beamline gas target (capacity 0.032 m³) with 0.65 mol of Argon-40 (Ar) of molar mass 40 g mol⁻¹ at an equilibrium temperature of 147 °C (take T(K) = θ(°C) + 273.15) (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹). Determine the density of the confined gas.
items.workedSolution: Total gas mass m = nM = 0.65 × 0.04 = 0.02600 kg. Density ρ = m / V = 0.02600 / 0.032 = 0.813 kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ρ = nM / V in SI units to obtain 0.813 kg m⁻³ (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies total gas mass nM by container volume V instead of dividing by V.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Computes molar concentration n / V (mol m⁻³) and omits multiplication by molar mass M.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Leaves molar mass in g mol⁻¹ instead of converting to kg mol⁻¹, overestimating density by a factor of 1000.

items.stem: Inside a thermally isolated materials-testing bath, a copper calorimeter vessel of mass 0.16 kg (c_cup = 385 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) holds 0.42 kg of water (c_liq = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹), both initially at 290 K. A 0.65 kg glass block (c_s = 840 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 410 K is lowered into the bath; heat loss to the outside air is negligible.
items.workedSolution: (a) Solving the enthalpy balance yields T_eq = 318 K. (b) Heat released by the hot solid Q_lost = m_s c_s (T_s − T_eq) = 5.04 × 10⁴ J. (c) Heat gained by the water Q_liq = m_l c_liq (T_eq − T_l) = 4.87 × 10⁴ J.

markScheme.criterion: Sets up full calorimetry heat-balance equation.
Obtains 318 K.
Evaluates m_s c_s (T_s − T_eq).
Obtains 5.04 × 10⁴ J.
Evaluates m_l c_liq (T_eq − T_l).
Obtains 4.87 × 10⁴ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the final thermal equilibrium temperature T_eq of the system.
workingSteps: m_s c_s (410 − T_eq) = (m_l c_liq + m_cup c_cup)(T_eq − 290).

parts.prompt: Calculate the thermal energy released by the glass block.
Determine the thermal energy absorbed specifically by the water.

items.stem: A four-stroke diesel engine delivers an output torque of 165 N m at 45.0 rev s⁻¹ while consuming fuel of calorific value $4.30 \times 10^7\text{ J kg}^{-1}$ at $3.40 \times 10^{-3}\text{ kg s}^{-1}$. Calculate the overall efficiency of the engine.
items.workedSolution: Overall efficiency $\eta_{\mathrm{ov}} = \eta_{\mathrm{th}} \times \eta_{\mathrm{mech}} = \frac{P_{\mathrm{ind}}}{P_{\mathrm{in}}} \times \frac{P_{\mathrm{brake}}}{P_{\mathrm{ind}}} = \frac{P_{\mathrm{brake}}}{P_{\mathrm{in}}}$. Here $P_{\mathrm{brake}} = 165 \times 2\pi(45.0) = 46.65\text{ kW}$ and $P_{\mathrm{in}} = 146.2\text{ kW}$, so $\eta_{\mathrm{ov}} = 31.9%$.

markScheme.criterion: Overall efficiency equals 31.9%.

items.stem: A 0.55 kg specimen of pure lead in an automated cryostat sample holder is driven from 583 K to 641 K as an electrical immersion heater of input power 600 W and thermal transfer efficiency 0.9 supplies energy. Material constants: fusion point 600.6 K, specific heats 128 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ (solid) and 147 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ (liquid), and specific latent heat of fusion 2.3 × 10⁴ J kg⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) P_eff = η P = 540 W. (b) Δt_f = m L_f / P_eff = 23.4 s. (c) Total energy Q_total = 1.716 × 10⁴ J, giving t_total = Q_total / P_eff = 31.8 s.

markScheme.criterion: Multiplies heater power P by efficiency η.
Obtains 540 W.
Divides m L_f by P_eff.
Obtains 23.4 s.
Computes Q_total and divides by P_eff.
Obtains 31.8 s.

parts.prompt: Calculate the effective rate of thermal energy transfer P_eff to/from the lead sample.
Calculate the duration of the isothermal melting plateau at 600.6 K.
Determine the total time required for the temperature to change from 583 K to 641 K.
workingSteps: Q_total = m c_solid (600.6 − 583) + m L_f + m c_liquid (641 − 600.6) = 1.716 × 10⁴ J.

items.stem: The diagram illustrates a reversible rectangular heat-engine cycle A → B → C → D → A executed by 0.2 mol of monatomic ideal gas in a frictionless piston-cylinder assembly on a thermodynamics test bench, operating between P_low = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and P_high = 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa and between V_min = 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³ and V_max = 0.012 m³. Take expansion work by the gas as positive.
items.workedSolution: (a) W_net = (P_high − P_low)(V_max − V_min) = 1.60 × 10³ J. (b) Q_in = Q_DA + Q_AB = (3/2)(P_high − P_low)V_min + (5/2)P_high(V_max − V_min) = 7.20 × 10³ J. (c) η = W_net / Q_in = 0.222.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates enclosed loop area (P_high − P_low)(V_max − V_min).
Obtains 1.60 × 10³ J.
Identifies heat input on both D → A (isochoric) and A → B (isobaric).
Uses monatomic factors (3/2) on D → A and (5/2) on A → B.
Obtains Q_in = 7.20 × 10³ J.
Divides W_net from (a) by Q_in from (b).
Obtains 0.222.

parts.prompt: Calculate the net mechanical work W_net done by the gas in one complete cycle.
Calculate the total thermal energy Q_in supplied to the monatomic gas during the heating stages D → A and A → B.
Determine the thermal efficiency η of this cycle.

items.stem: A thermal laboratory tests a solid block of filtered synthetic beeswax core of mass 0.34 kg initially at 19 °C. The figure displays its temperature–time heating curve through its melting point of 66 °C. The solid has specific heat capacity 2140 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and specific latent heat of fusion 1.68 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. An electrical immersion heater rated at 100 W transfers energy to the sample with thermal efficiency 80%. In a separate pressure-law check, a rigid dry-air reference flask contains a fixed mass of ideal gas at pressure 100 kPa and temperature 19 °C, before being heated at constant volume to 94 °C (use T / K = θ / °C + 273.2).
items.workedSolution: (a)(i) Q₁ = m c Δθ = 0.34 × 2140 × (66 − 19) = 3.420 × 10⁴ J ≈ 3.42 × 10⁴ J. (a)(ii) Q_melt = m L_f = 5.712 × 10⁴ J; Q_total = 9.132 × 10⁴ J; t = Q_total / (η P) = 1141 s ≈ 1.14e+3 s. (a)(iii) mean molecular kinetic energy stays constant while intermolecular potential energy changes to overcome or form intermolecular bonds. (a)(iv) thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings and absorbed by the container. (b)(i) T₁ = 292.2 K, T₂ = 367.2 K, so p₂ = 100 × (367.2 / 292.2) = 125.7 kPa ≈ 126 kPa. (b)(ii) faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Q = m c Δθ = 0.34 × 2140 × 47.
Correctly computes 3.42 × 10⁴ J (4 s.f. 3.420 × 10⁴ J).
Computes Q_melt = 5.712 × 10⁴ J, Q_total = 9.132 × 10⁴ J, and substitutes t = Q_total / (η P).
Shows 4 s.f. value 1141 s rounding cleanly to 1.14e+3 s.
States that temperature and mean molecular kinetic energy remain constant along the plateau.
Explains that intermolecular potential energy changes as bonds are weakened, broken, or formed.
States accurately that thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings and absorbed by the container.
Converts both temperatures using T = θ + 273.2 (292.2 K and 367.2 K) and applies p₂ = p₁ T₂ / T₁.
Evaluates final gas pressure = 126 kPa (4 s.f. 125.7 kPa).

Explains via Newton second law that faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area (no credit for quoting pV = nRT alone).

parts.prompt: Calculate the thermal energy required to raise the temperature of the solid filtered synthetic beeswax core from 19 °C to 66 °C. [2]
Show clearly that the actual time required for the 100 W heater operating at 80% efficiency to warm the solid from 19 °C and melt it completely at 66 °C is approximately 1.14e+3 s. [2]
Referring to the horizontal phase-change plateau QR on the figure, explain in terms of molecular energies why the temperature stays constant while internal energy changes. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: During the plateau, mean molecular kinetic energy stays constant while intermolecular potential energy changes to overcome or form intermolecular bonds.
workingSteps: State that temperature measures mean random molecular kinetic energy which stays constant.
Explain that latent thermal energy changes intermolecular potential energy as bonds are broken or formed.

parts.prompt: State one physical reason why the measured heating time in the laboratory exceeds the ideal value calculated assuming perfect efficiency. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings and absorbed by the container.
workingSteps: Apply NCUK calorimetry observation: thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings and absorbed by the container.

parts.prompt: Calculate the new pressure of the ideal gas in the rigid dry-air reference flask at 94 °C using T / K = θ / °C + 273.2. [2]
Explain in terms of kinetic theory and Newton's second law (without using the ideal gas equation) why heating the gas at constant volume increases its pressure. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Heating raises molecular speeds so faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area.
workingSteps: Link higher molecular speed to larger momentum change per collision, higher collision frequency, and larger force per unit area.

items.stem: The P–V graph shows an adiabatic path A → B for 0.4 mol of monatomic ideal gas (adiabatic exponent γ = 5/3) confined in a closed noble-gas power-conversion loop. At state A, the pressure is 1.4 × 10⁵ Pa and the volume is 4.2 × 10⁻³ m³; at state B, the volume is 1.2 × 10⁻³ m³ (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).

markScheme.criterion: Uses P_A V_A^(5/3) = P_B V_B^(5/3).
Obtains 1.13 × 10⁶ Pa.
Uses T_B = P_B V_B / (nR) or T_A (V_A / V_B)^(2/3).
Obtains 408 K.
Sets Q = 0 and evaluates |(3/2)(P_B V_B − P_A V_A)|.
Obtains 1.15 × 10³ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the final pressure P_B of the gas in state B.
Determine the absolute temperature T_B of the gas in state B.
Using the first law of thermodynamics, calculate the work done on the gas (taking work done on the gas as positive) during A → B.

items.stem: A sample of 0.250 mol of ideal gas ($\gamma = 1.40$, $R = 8.31\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$) starts at 105 kPa and $6.00 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3$ and is compressed adiabatically to $1.20 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3$. Calculate the maximum temperature reached by the gas.
items.workedSolution: Initial temperature $T_1 = \frac{p_1 V_1}{nR} = \frac{1.05 \times 10^5 \times 6.00 \times 10^{-3}}{0.250 \times 8.31} = 303 K$. Adiabatic final temperature $T_2 = T_1\left(\frac{V_1}{V_2}\right)^{\gamma - 1} = 303(5)^{0.40} = 577 K$.

markScheme.criterion: Final temperature equals 577 K.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses exponent $\gamma$ instead of $\gamma - 1$ in $T_2 = T_1 (V_1/V_2)^{\gamma - 1}$.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Assumes temperature stays constant as in an isothermal process.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Applies Charles's law linearly rather than adiabatic $T V^{\gamma - 1} = \text{const}$.

items.stem: An open glass U-tube contains glycerol of known density ρ₂ = 1260 kg m⁻³ in its lower bend and right arm. An immiscible sample of silicone oil of unknown density ρ₁ is poured into the left arm until equilibrium is reached as illustrated. Above the horizontal interface datum P–Q, the left oil column stands h₁ = 0.38 m tall while the right glycerol column stands h₂ = 0.258 m tall (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). What is the density ρ₁ of the unknown silicone oil?
items.workedSolution: Pressures at P and Q on the same horizontal datum are equal: p₀ + ρ₁ g h₁ = p₀ + ρ₂ g h₂ ⇒ ρ₁ = ρ₂ (h₂ / h₁) = 1260 × (0.258 / 0.38) = 855.5 kg m⁻³ ≈ 855 kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Correct unknown density ρ₁ = 855 kg m⁻³.

items.stem: During one operating interval, an air-source heat pump consumes 2400 J of electrical work and delivers 9600 J of thermal energy into a house. How much thermal energy is extracted from the cold outside air during this interval?
items.workedSolution: By conservation of energy $Q_{\mathrm{H}} = Q_{\mathrm{C}} + W$, so $Q_{\mathrm{C}} = Q_{\mathrm{H}} - W = 9600 - 2400 = 7.20e+3 J$.

markScheme.criterion: Thermal energy extracted from cold air equals 7.20e+3 J.

items.stem: 0.75 mol of ideal gas inside a closed-cycle Stirling regenerator test cell follows path A → B → C on the volume–temperature (V–T) plot: an isobaric expansion from (1.1 × 10⁵ Pa, 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³) to V_B = 0.01 m³, then an isochoric pressure increase to P_C = 2.2 × 10⁵ Pa. Using R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, determine T_C.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates PV / (nR) at the target state to obtain 353 K (D).

Take R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (kinetic-theory pressure relation: pV = ⅓ N m v_rms²).

markScheme.criterion: Uses v_rms = √(3RT₁ / M) with M in kg mol⁻¹.
Obtains 555 m s⁻¹.
Applies p = nRT₁ / V.
Obtains 1.25 × 10⁴ Pa.
Scales v_rms by √(T₂ / T₁) or re-evaluates √(3RT₂ / M).
Obtains 745 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Within an atmospheric/space radiative budget model, an orbital spacecraft thermal-control radiator panel covers 2.5 m² at 353 K with greybody emissivity 0.88 and faces a 278 K background radiation field (b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K; σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴).
items.workedSolution: (a) λ_max = b / T = 8.22 × 10⁻⁶ m. (b) Gross emitted power P_emitted = e σ A T⁴ = 1.94 × 10³ W. (c) Net radiative loss P_net = e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴) = 1.19 × 10³ W.

markScheme.criterion: Uses λ_max = (2.90 × 10⁻³) / T.
Obtains 8.22 × 10⁻⁶ m.
Uses P_emitted = e σ A T⁴.
Obtains 1.94 × 10³ W.
Evaluates e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴).
Obtains 1.19 × 10³ W.

parts.prompt: Calculate the peak infrared wavelength λ_max emitted by the surface.
Calculate the gross thermal power emitted by the greybody surface.
Determine the net rate of radiative thermal energy loss to the 278 K surroundings.
workingSteps: P_net = e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴) = 1.19 × 10³ W.

items.stem: The P–V diagram shows 2.2 mol of ideal gas in a laboratory heat-engine indicator rig with low-friction seals undergoing a quasi-static isothermal expansion at 280 K from initial volume 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³ (state A) to final volume 5.0 × 10⁻³ m³ (state B). Use R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and take work done by the gas as positive.
items.workedSolution: (a) P_B = nRT / V_B = 1.02 × 10⁶ Pa. (b) W_by = nRT ln(V_B / V_A) = 3.55 × 10³ J. (c) Since ΔU = 0, Q = W_by and ΔS = Q / T = 12.7 J K⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses P_B = nRT / V_B.
Obtains 1.02 × 10⁶ Pa.
Evaluates nRT ln(V_B / V_A).
Obtains 3.55 × 10³ J.
Uses ΔS = Q / T with Q = W_by.
Obtains 12.7 J K⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the final pressure P_B of the gas in state B.
Calculate the work done by the gas during the reversible isothermal expansion A → B.
Determine the change in entropy ΔS of the gas during A → B.
workingSteps: Since ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas isotherm, Q = W_by.

items.stem: Sub-freezing ice (0.045 kg at 263.15 K; c_ice = 2100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) is stirred into 0.48 kg of water (348.15 K; c_water = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) inside a lagged benchtop thermal-equilibrium chamber. Given T_m = 273.15 K and L_f = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹, determine the steady final temperature once melting finishes.
items.workedSolution: Energy to warm and melt all ice at 273.15 K: Q_1+2 = 0.045 × 2100 × (273.15 − 263.15) + 0.045 × 3.34 × 10⁵ = 1.598 × 10⁴ J. Energy balance with warm water: m_w c_w (348.15 − T_eq) = Q_1+2 + m_ice c_w (T_eq − 273.15), giving T_eq = 334 K.

markScheme.criterion: Includes sub-zero ice warming, fusion latent heat, and meltwater warming to obtain 334 K (B).

items.stem: A monatomic ideal gas (0.8 mol) in a closed-cycle Stirling regenerator test cell transitions from state A (1.5 × 10⁵ Pa, 1.5 × 10⁻³ m³) to state B (3.75 × 10⁵ Pa, 1.5 × 10⁻³ m³) and then to state C (3.75 × 10⁵ Pa, 4.8 × 10⁻³ m³). Defining work done on the gas as positive (ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW), calculate the total thermal energy ΔQ absorbed by the gas over A → B → C.
items.workedSolution: Along A → B → C, work done on the gas is ΔW = 0 − P_B(V_C − V_B) = -1.237 × 10³ J. Total internal energy change ΔU = (3/2)(P_C V_C − P_A V_A) = 2.362 × 10³ J. By the first law ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW, thermal energy supplied is ΔQ = ΔU − ΔW = 3.60 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates the first-law energy transfer with consistent work sign to obtain 3.60 × 10³ J (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Reverses the sign of expansion work ΔW in ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW, adding negative ΔW instead of evaluating ΔQ = ΔU − ΔW.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes only the total internal energy change ΔU_AC and omits the boundary work done during B → C.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the monatomic 3/2 factor in ΔU = (3/2)(P_C V_C − P_A V_A).

items.stem: Why does a continuous-flow calorimeter draw liquid from a constant-head reservoir rather than a draining beaker whose liquid level steadily falls?
items.workedSolution: A steady hydrostatic head keeps ṁ constant so the outlet temperature remains constant over time indicating thermal equilibrium before recording mass flow rate. Therefore the correct statement is: A constant pressure head keeps the flow rate steady so that the outlet temperature remains constant over time indicating thermal equilibrium before recording mass flow rate

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: outlet temperature remains constant over time indicating thermal equilibrium before recording mass flow rate.

options.label: D
options.text: A constant pressure head forces all heat loss to the surroundings to vanish completely.
options.distractorRationale: Heat loss H still exists and is removed by subtracting two runs.

items.stem: Which sequence of Newtonian mechanics steps correctly derives the kinetic theory equation for the pressure of an ideal gas in a cubic box?
items.workedSolution: An elastic wall collision reverses velocity giving momentum change minus two m u, Newton second and third laws give wall force, and isotropic random motion gives the one-third factor in pV equals one-third N m c rms squared. Therefore the correct statement is: An elastic wall collision reverses velocity giving momentum change minus two m u, Newton second and third laws give wall force, and isotropic random motion gives the one-third factor in pV equals one-third N m c rms squared

items.stem: In a Boyle's law experiment where a syringe connects to a pressure sensor via rubber tubing of unknown dead volume $V_0$, how does plotting $1/p$ against syringe volume $V$ reveal $V_0$ while maintaining isothermal conditions?
items.workedSolution: RP8 mark-scheme precision: The linear graph 1/p vs V intercepts the volume axis at −V₀; during measurements, students must change the pressure slowly and wait for thermal equilibrium so the trapped air temperature remains constant and isothermal boyle behaviour holds.

items.stem: A Carnot engine modelled in a micro-electro-mechanical gas spring cavity uses 0.3 mol of ideal gas operating between a hot reservoir at 327 °C and a cold sink at 87 °C (take T(K) = θ(°C) + 273.15). During the high-temperature isothermal stage A → B, the volume increases from 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³ to 7.5 × 10⁻³ m³. Taking net work done by the gas as positive (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹), what is the net work output W_net per cycle?
items.workedSolution: Q_H = nRT_H ln(V_B / V_A) = 1.644 × 10³ J and η = 1 − T_C / T_H = 0.3999. Net work output W_net = η Q_H = nR(T_H − T_C) ln(V_B / V_A) = 657 J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Carnot thermodynamics in kelvin to obtain 657 J (B).

items.stem: A heated brass block of mass 0.48 kg and specific heat capacity 380 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ at 410 K is plunged into 0.55 kg of water (c = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) initially at 298 K inside a lagged benchtop thermal-equilibrium chamber. During mixing, 950 J of thermal energy escapes to the surroundings. What is the final thermal equilibrium temperature T_eq?
items.workedSolution: Enthalpy balance: m_s c_s (T_s − T_eq) = m_l c_l (T_eq − T_l) + 950, giving T_eq = 305.8 K. Therefore T_eq = 306 K.

items.stem: The diagram contrasts the theoretical ideal Otto indicator loop with the actual measured $p$–$V$ loop of a real four-stroke petrol engine of identical swept volume.
items.workedSolution: The real indicator loop has rounded corners and a lower pumping loop reducing net enclosed work area due to finite combustion time, gradual valve timing, continuous heat loss to the coolant jacket, and gas-exchange pumping work, all of which directly reduce indicated power and thermal efficiency.

markScheme.criterion: Notes rounded corners and lower peak pressure compared with the sharp ideal Otto vertices.
Identifies the presence of the lower induction/exhaust pumping loop representing negative work.
Explains that fuel takes finite time to burn so heating is not instantaneous at constant volume.
Explains that valves open and close gradually before dead centres, reducing work extracted near the end of expansion.
Explains that thermal energy transfers to the cylinder walls/coolant so strokes are not truly adiabatic.
Concludes clearly that smaller net enclosed area directly lowers indicated power and thermal efficiency for the same fuel input.

parts.prompt: Explain in detail the physical causes of every major difference between the actual indicator diagram and the ideal Otto cycle, and explain how these differences reduce both indicated power and thermal efficiency.
parts.expectedAnswer: Unlike the theoretical air-standard Otto cycle, the real indicator loop has rounded corners and a lower pumping loop reducing net enclosed work area. First, fuel combustion takes finite time rather than occurring instantaneously at constant volume, so the spark is fired slightly before top dead centre and peak pressure is lower and rounded. Second, exhaust and inlet valves open and close gradually before dead centres to clear exhaust gas, rounding the bottom-right corner and lowering expansion work. Third, significant thermal energy transfers continuously through the cylinder walls into the coolant so compression and expansion are not strictly adiabatic. Fourth, drawing fresh charge in below atmospheric pressure and expelling exhaust above atmospheric pressure creates a negative-work pumping loop that must be subtracted from the positive power loop, reducing both net work per cycle (indicated power) and thermal efficiency.
workingSteps: L1: Identify two visible differences: rounded corners with lower peak pressure and a negative bottom pumping loop.
L1: State that net work per cycle equals the positive power-loop area minus the pumping-loop area.
L2: Explain finite combustion duration and pre-ignition spark timing preventing constant-volume vertical pressure rise.
L2: Explain finite valve-opening times rounding the expansion-exhaust corner and reducing expansion work.
L3: Explain continuous heat loss to the cooling jacket making compression/expansion non-adiabatic and lowering peak temperature/pressure.
L3: Explain pumping work during induction/exhaust and connect smaller net enclosed area directly to lower indicated power and thermal efficiency.

items.stem: A 0.3 kg charge of ethanol starts at 121 K and finishes at 219 K inside a lagged laboratory phase-transition calorimeter while an electrical immersion heater of input power 320 W and thermal transfer efficiency 0.75 supplies energy. Using fusion temperature 159 K, specific heats 1120 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ (solid) and 2440 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ (liquid), and latent heat 1.08 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹, find the overall elapsed time.
items.workedSolution: Effective thermal power P_eff = η P = 0.75 × 320 = 240.0 W. Total energy Q_tot = m c_solid ΔT_s + m L_f + m c_liquid ΔT_l = 8.909 × 10⁴ J, giving t_total = Q_tot / P_eff = 371 s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses P_eff = η P and divides required thermal energy to obtain 371 s (D).

items.stem: The diagram shows a closed four-leg cycle A → B → C → D → A for 0.5 mol of monatomic ideal gas in a laboratory heat-engine indicator rig with low-friction seals, bounded by P_low = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, P_high = 2.5 × 10⁵ Pa, V_min = 1.8 × 10⁻³ m³, and V_max = 4.5 × 10⁻³ m³. What is the thermal efficiency η = W_net / Q_in of this rectangular monatomic-gas cycle?
items.workedSolution: W_net = (2.5 × 10⁵ − 1.0 × 10⁵)(4.5 × 10⁻³ − 1.8 × 10⁻³) = 405.0 J. Heat enters on D → A and A → B: Q_in = (3/2)(P_high − P_low)V_min + (5/2)P_high(V_max − V_min) = 2.092 × 10³ J. Efficiency η = W_net / Q_in = 0.194.

markScheme.criterion: Computes thermalEfficiency correctly for the closed rectangular cycle to obtain 0.194 (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides W_net by Q_AB alone, neglecting the heat input Q_DA on the isochoric leg D → A.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits internal energy gain ΔU_AB when computing total heat input Q_in.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes the Carnot efficiency 1 − T_min / T_max between extreme corner temperatures instead of the actual cycle efficiency W_net / Q_in.

items.stem: A thermal laboratory tests a solid block of synthetic stearic wax of mass 0.36 kg initially at 21 °C. The figure displays its temperature–time heating curve through its melting point of 69 °C. The solid has specific heat capacity 1920 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and specific latent heat of fusion 1.96 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. An electrical immersion heater rated at 110 W transfers energy to the sample with thermal efficiency 84%. In a separate pressure-law check, a sealed neon calibration cylinder contains a fixed mass of ideal gas at pressure 116 kPa and temperature 21 °C, before being heated at constant volume to 115 °C (use T / K = θ / °C + 273.2).
items.workedSolution: (a)(i) Q₁ = m c Δθ = 0.36 × 1920 × (69 − 21) = 3.318 × 10⁴ J ≈ 3.32 × 10⁴ J. (a)(ii) Q_melt = m L_f = 7.056 × 10⁴ J; Q_total = 1.037 × 10⁵ J; t = Q_total / (η P) = 1123 s ≈ 1.12e+3 s. (a)(iii) mean molecular kinetic energy stays constant while intermolecular potential energy changes to overcome or form intermolecular bonds. (a)(iv) thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings and absorbed by the container. (b)(i) T₁ = 294.2 K, T₂ = 388.2 K, so p₂ = 116 × (388.2 / 294.2) = 153.1 kPa ≈ 153 kPa. (b)(ii) faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Q = m c Δθ = 0.36 × 1920 × 48.
Correctly computes 3.32 × 10⁴ J (4 s.f. 3.318 × 10⁴ J).
Computes Q_melt = 7.056 × 10⁴ J, Q_total = 1.037 × 10⁵ J, and substitutes t = Q_total / (η P).
Shows 4 s.f. value 1123 s rounding cleanly to 1.12e+3 s.
States that temperature and mean molecular kinetic energy remain constant along the plateau.
Explains that intermolecular potential energy changes as bonds are weakened, broken, or formed.
States accurately that thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings and absorbed by the container.
Converts both temperatures using T = θ + 273.2 (294.2 K and 388.2 K) and applies p₂ = p₁ T₂ / T₁.
Evaluates final gas pressure = 153 kPa (4 s.f. 153.1 kPa).

Explains via Newton second law that faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area (no credit for quoting pV = nRT alone).

parts.prompt: Calculate the thermal energy required to raise the temperature of the solid synthetic stearic wax from 21 °C to 69 °C. [2]
Show clearly that the actual time required for the 110 W heater operating at 84% efficiency to warm the solid from 21 °C and melt it completely at 69 °C is approximately 1.12e+3 s. [2]
Referring to the horizontal phase-change plateau QR on the figure, explain in terms of molecular energies why the temperature stays constant while internal energy changes. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: During the plateau, mean molecular kinetic energy stays constant while intermolecular potential energy changes to overcome or form intermolecular bonds.
workingSteps: State that temperature measures mean random molecular kinetic energy which stays constant.
Explain that latent thermal energy changes intermolecular potential energy as bonds are broken or formed.

parts.prompt: State one physical reason why the measured heating time in the laboratory exceeds the ideal value calculated assuming perfect efficiency. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings and absorbed by the container.
workingSteps: Apply NCUK calorimetry observation: thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings and absorbed by the container.

parts.prompt: Calculate the new pressure of the ideal gas in the sealed neon calibration cylinder at 115 °C using T / K = θ / °C + 273.2. [2]
Explain in terms of kinetic theory and Newton's second law (without using the ideal gas equation) why heating the gas at constant volume increases its pressure. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Heating raises molecular speeds so faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area.
workingSteps: Link higher molecular speed to larger momentum change per collision, higher collision frequency, and larger force per unit area.

items.stem: Inside a variable-volume optical pressure cell, 0.5 mol of an ideal monatomic gas (adiabatic index γ = 5/3) initially at P_A = 4.8 × 10⁵ Pa and V_A = 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³ is reversibly and adiabatically expanded to V_B = 7.5 × 10⁻³ m³. Take R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Taking work done by the gas as positive, how much mechanical work is done by the gas during A → B?
items.workedSolution: First find P_B = P_A (V_A / V_B)^(5/3) = 1.042 × 10⁵ Pa. Since Q = 0 in an adiabatic process, W_by = −ΔU = (3/2)(P_A V_A − P_B V_B) = 987 J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies P V^(5/3) = const and Q = 0 to obtain 987 J (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Omits the 3/2 factor in |ΔU| = (3/2)|P_B V_B − P_A V_A| when applying Q = 0 => |W| = |ΔU|.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses the isothermal work formula P_A V_A |ln(V_B / V_A)| instead of adiabatic work.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Treats pressure as constant at P_A, computing P_A |V_B − V_A| instead of adiabatic work.

items.stem: A cylinder holds 0.150 mol of nitrogen gas ($\gamma = 1.40$) initially at pressure 300 kPa and volume 1.50 × 10⁻³ m³. The gas undergoes an isobaric change to a final volume of 3.50 × 10⁻³ m³. Take $R = 8.31\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$ and apply $Q = \Delta U + W$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $T_1 = 361 K$. (b) $T_2 = 842 K$. (c) Work done by gas $W = p\Delta V = 600 J$. (d) With $\Delta U = 1.50e+3 J$, $Q = \Delta U + W = 2.10e+3 J$.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $p_1 V_1 = n R T_1$ with $R = 8.31\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$.
Obtains $T_1 = 361 K$.
Applies constant-pressure $T_2 = T_1(V_2/V_1)$.
Obtains $T_2 = 842 K$.
Applies $W = p(V_2 - V_1)$.
Obtains $W = 600 J$.
Computes $\Delta U = W/(\gamma - 1)$ and adds $Q = \Delta U + W$.
Obtains $Q = 2.10e+3 J$.

parts.prompt: Calculate the initial thermodynamic temperature $T_1$ of the gas in kelvin.
Determine the final thermodynamic temperature $T_2$ of the gas in kelvin.
Calculate the work done BY the gas during this isobaric expansion.
Given that $\Delta U = \frac{W}{\gamma - 1}$ for an isobaric ideal-gas change, calculate the total thermal energy $Q$ supplied to the gas.
workingSteps: By AQA First Law $Q = \Delta U + W = 2.10e+3 J$.

items.stem: An open glass U-tube contains saline water of known density ρ₂ = 1050 kg m⁻³ in its lower bend and right arm. An immiscible sample of turpentine of unknown density ρ₁ is poured into the left arm until equilibrium is reached as illustrated. Above the horizontal interface datum P–Q, the left oil column stands h₁ = 0.44 m tall while the right saline water column stands h₂ = 0.334 m tall (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) pressures are equal at the same horizontal level within a continuous static liquid. (b) Δp = ρ₂gh₂ = 3440 Pa ≈ 3.44e+3 Pa. (c) ρ₁ = ρ₂(h₂/h₁) = 797.0 kg m⁻³ ≈ 797 kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: States equal pressure at the same horizontal level in a continuous static liquid.
Applies Δp = ρ₂gh₂.
Equates ρ₁gh₁ = ρ₂gh₂.
ρ₁ = 797 kg m⁻³.

items.stem: A gas-turbine heat engine operates between a hot reservoir at 820 K and a cold sink at 308 K. In each cycle it absorbs 6000 J from the hot reservoir and produces 2400 J of useful mechanical work.
items.workedSolution: (a) $\eta_{\max} = 62.4%$. (b) $\eta_{\mathrm{actual}} = 40.0%$. (c) Rejected heat $Q_{\mathrm{C}} = 3.60e+3 J$.

markScheme.criterion: Applies $\eta_{\max} = (T_{\mathrm{H}} - T_{\mathrm{C}})/T_{\mathrm{H}}$ in kelvin.
Obtains 62.4%.
Applies $\eta = W/Q_{\mathrm{H}}$.
Obtains 40.0%.
Applies $Q_{\mathrm{C}} = Q_{\mathrm{H}} - W$.
Obtains 3.60e+3 J.

items.stem: A materials-science student inspects the schematic particle models of three distinct states of matter shown in the figure. Why can the state depicted in the right-hand panel be compressed into a much smaller volume far more easily than either of the other two states?
items.workedSolution: The right-hand gaseous state is readily compressed because large empty spaces between widely separated molecules allow the gas volume to decrease easily under pressure.

markScheme.criterion: The right-hand gaseous state is readily compressed because large empty spaces between widely separated molecules allow the gas volume to decrease easily under pressure.
