options.label: A
options.text: Gas molecules are arranged in collapsible hollow crystal layers that fold under pressure.
options.distractorRationale: Gases possess no crystal structure or layered lattice.

options.label: B
options.text: The gas molecules themselves shrink dramatically in physical diameter whenever external pressure rises.
options.distractorRationale: Compression reduces inter-molecular spacing, not the intrinsic size of individual molecules.

options.label: C
options.text: The right-hand gaseous state is readily compressed because large empty spaces between widely separated molecules allow the gas volume to decrease easily under pressure.

options.label: D
options.text: Attractive intermolecular forces pull the gas molecules together whenever the piston moves inward.
options.distractorRationale: Intermolecular attractions in a dilute gas are negligible compared with thermal kinetic energy.

items.stem: Consider the illuminated Brownian-motion cell and magnified eyepiece trace depicted in the schematic diagram. How does the observed motion of the illuminated specks change if the fluid inside the sealed cell is warmed uniformly to a higher temperature?
items.workedSolution: If the sealed cell is warmed uniformly to a higher steady temperature, higher temperature increases average molecular speed so collisions become more frequent and vigorous and the erratic motion becomes faster.

markScheme.criterion: If the sealed cell is warmed uniformly to a higher steady temperature, higher temperature increases average molecular speed so collisions become more frequent and vigorous and the erratic motion becomes faster.

options.text: The erratic motion slows down and stops because warmer fluid molecules expand and lock together.
options.distractorRationale: Higher temperature raises molecular kinetic energy and speeds up Brownian agitation.

options.label: B
options.text: If the sealed cell is warmed uniformly to a higher steady temperature, higher temperature increases average molecular speed so collisions become more frequent and vigorous and the erratic motion becomes faster.

options.label: C
options.text: All specks begin moving together in a single straight line away from the microscope lens.
options.distractorRationale: Uniform warming intensifies random isotropic motion rather than creating a single-direction beam.

options.label: D
options.text: The motion remains completely unchanged because temperature does not affect molecular speeds.

items.stem: Inside an insulated aerospace gas-accumulator cylinder, 0.35 mol of ideal gas starts in state A (2.2 × 10⁵ Pa, 6.0 × 10⁻³ m³). As plotted on the volume–temperature (V–T) axes, the gas first expands at constant pressure to V_B = 9.0 × 10⁻³ m³ (state B) and is then heated at constant volume to P_C = 3.52 × 10⁵ Pa (state C). Use R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) T_A = P_A V_A / (nR) = 454 K. (b) Isobaric expansion gives T_B = T_A (V_B / V_A) = 681 K. (c) Isochoric heating gives T_C = T_B (P_C / P_A) = 1.09 × 10³ K.

markScheme.criterion: Uses T_A = P_A V_A / (nR).
Obtains 454 K.
Applies V_B / T_B = V_A / T_A or P_A V_B / (nR).
Obtains 681 K.
Applies P_C / T_C = P_B / T_B or P_C V_B / (nR).
Obtains 1.09 × 10³ K.

parts.prompt: Calculate the initial temperature T_A of the gas in state A.
Determine the temperature T_B at the end of the isobaric expansion A → B.
workingSteps: By Charles's law at constant pressure, T_B = T_A (V_B / V_A) = 681 K.

parts.prompt: Calculate the final temperature T_C in state C after the isochoric stage B → C.

items.stem: In a semiconductor lithography purge canister (volume 0.08 m³), 0.8 mol of monatomic Xenon-131 (Xe) of molar mass 0.1313 kg mol⁻¹ is warmed from T₁ = 410 K to T₂ = 1025 K, shifting the Maxwell–Boltzmann speed curve as plotted. Given R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (kinetic-theory pressure relation: pV = ⅓ N m v_rms²), determine v_rms at the higher temperature T₂.
items.workedSolution: Convert molar mass to SI units: M = 0.1313 kg mol⁻¹. Using v_rms = √(3RT / M) at T = 1025 K gives v_rms = √(3 × 8.31 × 1025 / 0.1313) = 441 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates √(3RT / M) with M in kg mol⁻¹ to obtain 441 m s⁻¹ (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes molar mass in g mol⁻¹ instead of kg mol⁻¹ into √(3RT / M), underestimating v_rms by a factor of √1000 ≈ 31.6.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 3 from the three translational degrees of freedom, evaluating √(RT / M).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses a factor of 2 instead of 3, computing the most probable speed v_p = √(2RT / M) rather than v_rms.

items.stem: An energy-budget sensor monitors an orbital spacecraft thermal-control radiator panel (area 4 m², greybody emissivity 0.72) maintained at 336 K within a radiative environment at 278 K. Using σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, calculate P_net = e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴).
items.workedSolution: Net radiative power loss P_net = e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴) = 0.72 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 4 × ((336)⁴ − (278)⁴) = 1.11 × 10³ W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴) to obtain 1.11 × 10³ W (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Evaluates e σ A (T − T_amb)⁴ instead of e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴), a classic fourth-power algebra error.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the greybody emissivity factor e (< 1) from P_net = e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates gross emitted power e σ A T⁴ and ignores incoming radiation absorbed from the surroundings at T_amb.

items.stem: In a solar-thermal helium Brayton demonstrator cylinder coupled to a thermal reservoir at 280 K, 0.6 mol of an ideal gas expands reversibly and isothermally from V_A = 1.5 × 10⁻³ m³ to V_B = 3.6 × 10⁻³ m³. Take R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the change in entropy ΔS of the gas?
items.workedSolution: For a reversible isothermal expansion, ΔU = 0 so Q = W_by = nRT ln(V_B / V_A). Therefore ΔS = Q / T = nR ln(V_B / V_A) = 0.6 × 8.31 × ln(3.6 × 10⁻³ / 1.5 × 10⁻³) = 4.37 J K⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔS = nR ln(V_B / V_A) to obtain 4.37 J K⁻¹ (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses base-10 logarithm log₁₀(V_B / V_A) instead of the natural logarithm ln(V_B / V_A).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Replaces ln(V_B / V_A) with the linear fractional change (V_B − V_A) / V_A.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes isothermal heat Q = nRT ln(V_B / V_A) without dividing by T to obtain ΔS = Q / T.

items.stem: Zero heat enters a sealed foam-insulated metallurgical quench tank while 0.28 kg of water initially at 301.15 K equilibrates against 0.42 kg of 273.15 K ice (4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ for liquid water; L_f = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹).
items.workedSolution: (a) Q_water = m_water c_water (301.15 − 273.15) = 3.28 × 10⁴ J, which is below m_ice L_f. (b) Melted mass Δm = Q_water / L_f = 0.0981 kg. (c) Melted fraction f = Δm / m_ice = 0.234.

markScheme.criterion: Computes m_water c_water (T_water − 273.15).
Obtains 3.28 × 10⁴ J.
Divides Q_water by L_f.
Obtains 0.0981 kg.
Divides Δm by initial ice mass m_ice.
Obtains 0.234.

workingSteps: Q_water = m_water c_water (301.15 − 273.15) = 3.28 × 10⁴ J (< m_ice L_f = 1.40 × 10⁵ J).

parts.prompt: Calculate the mass of ice that melts by the time thermal equilibrium is reached.
Determine the fraction of the initial ice sample that has melted at equilibrium.

items.stem: A sealed sample of 0.25 mol of monatomic ideal gas in an insulated aerospace gas-accumulator cylinder follows path A → B → C on the P–V diagram: state A is at (1.5 × 10⁵ Pa, 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³), state B is at (3.0 × 10⁵ Pa, 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³), and state C is at (3.0 × 10⁵ Pa, 8.0 × 10⁻³ m³). Use the sign convention ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW where work done on the gas is positive.
items.workedSolution: (a) Work is done only along B → C: ΔW = −P_B(V_C − V_B) = -1.65 × 10³ J. (b) ΔU_AC = (3/2)(P_C V_C − P_A V_A) = 3.04 × 10³ J. (c) By ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW, total heat supplied ΔQ = ΔU_AC − ΔW = 4.69 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies ΔW_AB = 0 and computes ΔW = −P_B(V_C − V_B).
Obtains -1.65 × 10³ J.
Applies ΔU = (3/2)(P_C V_C − P_A V_A).
Obtains 3.04 × 10³ J.
Applies ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW ⇒ ΔQ = ΔU_AC − ΔW to obtain total heat supplied.
Obtains 4.69 × 10³ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the total mechanical work done on the gas ΔW along path A → B → C (including its sign).
Calculate the total change in internal energy ΔU of the monatomic gas between state A and state C.
workingSteps: For a monatomic ideal gas, U = (3/2) PV, so ΔU_AC = (3/2)(P_C V_C − P_A V_A).

parts.prompt: Determine the total thermal energy ΔQ supplied to the gas over the complete path A → B → C.
workingSteps: By the first law of thermodynamics (ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW), ΔQ = ΔU_AC − ΔW = 3.038 × 10³ − (-1.650 × 10³) = 4.69 × 10³ J.

items.stem: In a continuous-flow test (18.0 °C to 26.0 °C), Run 1 has ṁ₁ = 0.00500 kg s⁻¹, V₁ = 12.0 V, I₁ = 14.3 A, and Run 2 has ṁ₂ = 0.0100 kg s⁻¹, V₂ = 16.0 V, I₂ = 21.175 A. Calculate the steady rate of thermal energy loss H to the surroundings.
items.workedSolution: Since ṁ₂ = 2ṁ₁, P₁ = ṁ₁cΔθ + H = 171.6 W and P₂ = 2ṁ₁cΔθ + H = 338.8 W. Thus H = 2P₁ − P₂ = 343.2 − 338.8 = 4.40 W.

markScheme.criterion: Finds thermal loss rate H = 4.40 W.

items.stem: In the kinetic theory derivation of pV = (1/3) N m c_rms², what physical justification introduces the factor of one-third?
items.workedSolution: Since c² = u² + v² + w² and all three orthogonal directions are equally likely giving one-third of mean square speed, ⟨u²⟩ = (1/3) c_rms². Therefore the correct statement is: Because random motion means all three orthogonal directions are equally likely giving one-third of mean square speed

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: all three orthogonal directions are equally likely giving one-third of mean square speed.

items.stem: During a Boyle's law investigation (RP8), trapped dry air sits in a graduated column of reading 42.0 cm³ plus an ungraduated Bourdon-tube dead volume of 2.0 cm³ at absolute pressure 104 kPa. Calculate the isothermal constant $pV_{\mathrm{total}}$ in joules.
items.workedSolution: Total initial volume $V_{\mathrm{total}} = 42 + 2 = 44.0$ cm³. Thus $pV = 104\times 10^3 \times 44.0\times 10^{-6} = 4.58 J$, and at 182 kPa the tube reads $V_2 = 23.1 cm³$.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly evaluates pVConstJ $= 4.58 J$.

items.stem: In the Charles's law water-bath capillary experiment (RP8), what dual physical purpose does the drop of concentrated sulfuric acid ($\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$) serve, and why is the water bath stirred continuously?
items.workedSolution: RP8 mark-scheme precision: The concentrated sulfuric acid bead traps dry air at constant atmospheric pressure and absorbs water vapour while stirring the water bath keeps temperature uniform.

markScheme.criterion: The concentrated sulfuric acid bead traps dry air at constant atmospheric pressure and absorbs water vapour while stirring the water bath keeps temperature uniform.

options.text: The sulfuric acid heats the trapped air chemically so a Bunsen burner is unnecessary.
options.distractorRationale: Concentrated H₂SO₄ is a hygroscopic drying agent and movable constant-pressure index seal, not a heat source.

options.label: B
options.text: The acid bead keeps the air volume constant while pressure rises with temperature.
options.distractorRationale: The bead slides freely inside the open-topped capillary tube, maintaining constant atmospheric pressure as volume changes.

options.label: C
options.text: Stirring is unnecessary because water is a rapid thermal conductor with zero convection stratification.
options.distractorRationale: Water is a poor conductor and stratifies strongly; thorough stirring ensures the thermometer matches the capillary air temperature.

options.label: D
options.text: The concentrated sulfuric acid bead traps dry air at constant atmospheric pressure and absorbs water vapour while stirring the water bath keeps temperature uniform.

items.stem: Starting at state A (1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, 3.6 × 10⁻³ m³), 0.8 mol of monatomic gas (γ = 5/3) in a magnetically coupled piston calorimeter chamber is compressed adiabatically to 1.2 × 10⁻³ m³, heated at constant volume to 1.623 × 10⁶ Pa, expanded adiabatically to 3.6 × 10⁻³ m³, and cooled at constant volume back to A. Find η.
items.workedSolution: For an ideal monatomic Otto cycle (γ = 5/3), η = 1 − (V_min / V_max)^(γ − 1) = 1 − (1.2 × 10⁻³ / 3.6 × 10⁻³)^(2/3) = 0.519 (equivalently W_net / Q_in = 933.2 / 1.797 × 10³ = 0.519).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates the closed adiabatic heat-engine cycle to obtain 0.519 (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Applies an extra factor of one-half from misremembering the degrees-of-freedom or geometric prefactor.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses exponent 1 instead of γ − 1 = 2/3 in the Otto efficiency relation η = 1 − (V_min / V_max)^(γ − 1).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Raises V_min / V_max to γ = 5/3 rather than γ − 1 = 2/3.

items.stem: Thermalised Xenon-131 (Xe) vapour of molar mass 0.1313 kg mol⁻¹ fills a high-vacuum synchrotron beamline gas target at a uniform temperature of 680 K. Take k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ and e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the mean translational kinetic energy per atom in electronvolts?

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes T = 680 K into the monatomic kinetic-theory energy relation to obtain 0.0880 eV (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Evaluates (1/2) k_B T / e for a single degree of freedom instead of three.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes k_B T / e and omits the 3/2 translational factor.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Doubles the 3/2 factor to 3 k_B T / e by omitting the 1/2 in kinetic energy.

items.stem: A 0.25 kg specimen of pure aluminium inside a guarded electrical immersion-heating vessel is heated from 904 K (solid) to 1019 K (liquid). Take melting point = 933.5 K, c_solid = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, c_liquid = 1180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, and specific latent heat of fusion L_f = 3.97 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. Find the total heat transferred to the specimen.

markScheme.criterion: Sums sensible mcΔT stages and latent heat mL to obtain 1.31 × 10⁵ J (D).

items.stem: The Planck spectral curve shown corresponds to an exoplanet host star in radiative equilibrium of radiating area 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m² and uniform blackbody temperature 1500 K, monitored by a radiometer 1.5 m away. Taking σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, what is the total electromagnetic power radiated?
items.workedSolution: By the Stefan–Boltzmann law for a blackbody (e = 1), P = σ A T⁴ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ × (1500)⁴ = 71.8 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates the blackbody radiation law in SI units to obtain 71.8 W (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses T² instead of T⁴ in the Stefan–Boltzmann law P = σ A T⁴.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses Celsius-shifted temperature (T − 273.15)⁴ instead of absolute kelvin temperature T⁴.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes surface exitance σ T⁴ (W m⁻²) and omits multiplication by surface area A.

items.stem: Operating between a hot reservoir at 416 K and a cold sink at 260 K, 1 mol of ideal gas in a cryocooler compression cylinder containing monatomic working gas executes an ideal Carnot power cycle whose high-temperature isothermal leg A → B expands from 1.2 × 10⁻³ m³ to 3.6 × 10⁻³ m³. Use R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and take work done by the gas as positive.

markScheme.criterion: Converts temperatures to kelvin and applies 1 − T_C / T_H.
Obtains 0.375.
Uses Q_H = nRT_H ln(V_B / V_A).
Obtains 3.80 × 10³ J.
Multiplies η by Q_H (or evaluates Q_H − Q_C).
Obtains 1.42 × 10³ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the thermal efficiency η of the Carnot cycle.
Calculate the thermal energy Q_H absorbed from the hot reservoir during the isothermal expansion A → B.
Determine the net mechanical work W_net done by the gas per cycle.

items.stem: In a rigid stainless-steel vacuum-calibration tank of volume 8.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 1.2 mol of Helium-4 (He) (molar mass 4.0 × 10⁻³ kg mol⁻¹) is held in thermal equilibrium at 380 K. Taking R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, what pressure does the gas exert on the walls?
items.workedSolution: From the ideal gas equation p = nRT / V = (1.2 × 8.31 × 380) / 8.0 × 10⁻³ = 4.74 × 10⁵ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Applies p = nRT / V in SI units to obtain 4.74 × 10⁵ Pa (D).

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the amount of substance n in p = nRT / V, solving for 1 mol instead of the given molar amount.

items.stem: A 0.36 kg iron specimen (c = 450 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) heated to 510 K is immersed in 0.72 kg of mineral oil (c = 1960 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) initially at 285 K inside a precision isothermal-jacket mixing cup. While reaching thermal equilibrium, 1250 J of thermal energy is lost to the surroundings.
items.workedSolution: (a) Solving the enthalpy balance yields T_eq = 307 K. (b) Heat released by the hot solid Q_lost = m_s c_s (T_s − T_eq) = 3.28 × 10⁴ J. (c) Heat gained by the mineral oil Q_liq = m_l c_liq (T_eq − T_l) = 3.16 × 10⁴ J.

markScheme.criterion: Sets up full calorimetry heat-balance equation.
Obtains 307 K.
Evaluates m_s c_s (T_s − T_eq).
Obtains 3.28 × 10⁴ J.
Evaluates m_l c_liq (T_eq − T_l).
Obtains 3.16 × 10⁴ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the final thermal equilibrium temperature T_eq of the system.
Calculate the thermal energy released by the iron block.
Determine the thermal energy absorbed specifically by the mineral oil.

items.stem: A four-stroke engine with 4 cylinders running at 60.0 rev s⁻¹ has indicator loop area 510 J per cylinder and burns fuel of calorific value $4.50 \times 10^7\text{ J kg}^{-1}$ at a mass flow rate of $3.60 \times 10^{-3}\text{ kg s}^{-1}$. Calculate the thermal efficiency of the engine.
items.workedSolution: Explicit definition: $\eta_{\mathrm{th}} = \frac{P_{\mathrm{ind}}}{P_{\mathrm{in}}}$. Here $P_{\mathrm{ind}} = 510 \times 30.0 \times 4 = 61.2\text{ kW}$ and $P_{\mathrm{in}} = (4.50 \times 10^7)(3.60 \times 10^{-3}) = 162\text{ kW}$, giving $\eta_{\mathrm{th}} = \frac{61.2}{162} = 37.8%$.

markScheme.criterion: Thermal efficiency equals 37.8%.

Calculate the duration of the isothermal melting plateau at 933.5 K.
Determine the total time required for the temperature to change from 906 K to 959 K.

items.stem: A closed-loop test cylinder (a closed noble-gas power-conversion loop) carries 0.2 mol of monatomic ideal gas clockwise around cycle A → B → C → D → A between volume limits 1.2 × 10⁻³ m³ and 4.8 × 10⁻³ m³ and pressure limits 1.8 × 10⁵ Pa and 3.6 × 10⁵ Pa (with A at 3.6 × 10⁵ Pa, 1.2 × 10⁻³ m³ and B at 3.6 × 10⁵ Pa, 4.8 × 10⁻³ m³). Define work done by the gas as positive.
items.workedSolution: (a) W_net = (P_high − P_low)(V_max − V_min) = 648 J. (b) Q_in = Q_DA + Q_AB = (3/2)(P_high − P_low)V_min + (5/2)P_high(V_max − V_min) = 3.56 × 10³ J. (c) η = W_net / Q_in = 0.182.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates enclosed loop area (P_high − P_low)(V_max − V_min).
Obtains 648 J.
Identifies heat input on both D → A (isochoric) and A → B (isobaric).
Uses monatomic factors (3/2) on D → A and (5/2) on A → B.
Obtains Q_in = 3.56 × 10³ J.
Divides W_net from (a) by Q_in from (b).
Obtains 0.182.

parts.prompt: Calculate the net mechanical work W_net done by the gas in one complete cycle.
Calculate the total thermal energy Q_in supplied to the monatomic gas during the heating stages D → A and A → B.
Determine the thermal efficiency η of this cycle.

items.stem: A calorimetry experiment records the cooling curve shown in the figure as 0.30 kg of molten thermal-storage resin wax freezes at 74 °C and cools in solid form down to 24 °C. The solid has specific heat capacity 2050 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and specific latent heat of fusion 1.54 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. When previously melted from 24 °C using a 105 W immersion heater, the heating setup operated at 81% thermal efficiency. Separately, a constant-volume krypton gas vessel holds a fixed mass of ideal gas at 122 kPa and 24 °C before warming at constant volume to 122 °C (use T / K = θ / °C + 273.2).
items.workedSolution: (a)(i) Q₁ = m c Δθ = 0.30 × 2050 × (74 − 24) = 3.075 × 10⁴ J ≈ 3.08 × 10⁴ J. (a)(ii) Q_melt = m L_f = 4.620 × 10⁴ J; Q_total = 7.695 × 10⁴ J ≈ 7.70 × 10⁴ J. (a)(iii) mean molecular kinetic energy stays constant while intermolecular potential energy changes to overcome or form intermolecular bonds. (a)(iv) temperature remains constant along a horizontal plateau during freezing before falling smoothly toward ambient temperature. (b)(i) T₁ = 297.2 K, T₂ = 395.2 K, so p₂ = 122 × (395.2 / 297.2) = 162.2 kPa ≈ 162 kPa. (b)(ii) faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Q = m c Δθ = 0.30 × 2050 × 50.
Correctly computes 3.08 × 10⁴ J (4 s.f. 3.075 × 10⁴ J).
Computes latent energy Q_melt = 4.620 × 10⁴ J and sums Q_warm + Q_melt.
Shows 4 s.f. value 7.695 × 10⁴ J rounding cleanly to 7.70 × 10⁴ J.
States that temperature and mean molecular kinetic energy remain constant along the plateau.
Explains that intermolecular potential energy changes as bonds are weakened, broken, or formed.
States accurately that temperature remains constant along a horizontal plateau during freezing before falling smoothly toward ambient temperature.
Converts both temperatures using T = θ + 273.2 (297.2 K and 395.2 K) and applies p₂ = p₁ T₂ / T₁.
Evaluates final gas pressure = 162 kPa (4 s.f. 162.2 kPa).

Explains via Newton second law that faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area (no credit for quoting pV = nRT alone).

parts.prompt: Calculate the thermal energy released as the solidified thermal-storage resin wax cools from 74 °C down to 24 °C. [2]
Show clearly that the total thermal energy required to warm the solid from 24 °C to 74 °C and melt it completely is approximately 7.70 × 10⁴ J. [2]
Referring to the horizontal phase-change plateau QR on the figure, explain in terms of molecular energies why the temperature stays constant while internal energy changes. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: During the plateau, mean molecular kinetic energy stays constant while intermolecular potential energy changes to overcome or form intermolecular bonds.
workingSteps: State that temperature measures mean random molecular kinetic energy which stays constant.
Explain that latent thermal energy changes intermolecular potential energy as bonds are broken or formed.

parts.prompt: Describe the shape of the cooling curve along QR and RS as the substance freezes and cools to ambient temperature. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: temperature remains constant along a horizontal plateau during freezing before falling smoothly toward ambient temperature.
workingSteps: Apply NCUK calorimetry observation: temperature remains constant along a horizontal plateau during freezing before falling smoothly toward ambient temperature.

parts.prompt: Calculate the new pressure of the ideal gas in the constant-volume krypton gas vessel at 122 °C using T / K = θ / °C + 273.2. [2]
Explain in terms of kinetic theory and Newton's second law (without using the ideal gas equation) why heating the gas at constant volume increases its pressure. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Heating raises molecular speeds so faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area.
workingSteps: Link higher molecular speed to larger momentum change per collision, higher collision frequency, and larger force per unit area.

items.stem: During a fast insulated stroke in a closed noble-gas power-conversion loop, 0.5 mol of ideal monatomic gas (γ = 5/3) changes volume adiabatically from 4.8 × 10⁻³ m³ at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa (state A) to 1.2 × 10⁻³ m³ (state B). Use R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses P_A V_A^(5/3) = P_B V_B^(5/3).
Obtains 1.01 × 10⁶ Pa.
Uses T_B = P_B V_B / (nR) or T_A (V_A / V_B)^(2/3).
Obtains 291 K.
Sets Q = 0 and evaluates |(3/2)(P_B V_B − P_A V_A)|.
Obtains 1.09 × 10³ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the final pressure P_B of the gas in state B.
Determine the absolute temperature T_B of the gas in state B.
Using the first law of thermodynamics, calculate the work done on the gas (taking work done on the gas as positive) during A → B.

items.stem: An ideal diatomic gas ($\gamma = 1.40$) at 120 kPa and $4.00 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3$ is compressed adiabatically to $1.00 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3$. Applying the AQA First Law $Q = \Delta U + W$ (where $W$ is work done by the gas), calculate the change in internal energy $\Delta U$ of the gas.
items.workedSolution: Final pressure $p_2 = 120(4)^{1.40} = 836 kPa$. Work done by gas $W = \frac{p_1 V_1 - p_2 V_2}{\gamma - 1} = −889 J$ (negative on compression). Since $Q = 0$, $Q = \Delta U + W \Rightarrow \Delta U = -W = 889 J$.

markScheme.criterion: Change in internal energy equals 889 J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Reverses the sign of $\Delta U$, forgetting that work done BY the gas is negative on compression so $\Delta U = -W > 0$.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes isobaric $p_1 \Delta V$ instead of adiabatic work.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Introduces an erroneous factor of one-half during rearrangement.

items.stem: As shown in the cutaway diagram, an open rectangular storage tank with horizontal base area 1.2 m² holds two immiscible liquids at rest: an upper layer of turpentine (ρ₁ = 870 kg m⁻³, depth h₁ = 1.2 m) resting above a lower layer of saline water (ρ₂ = 1050 kg m⁻³, depth h₂ = 2.2 m). Atmospheric pressure at the open top surface is 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa and g = 9.81 m s⁻². What is the total absolute pressure at point Y on the tank base in kPa?
items.workedSolution: Upper layer Δp₁ = 870 × 9.81 × 1.2 = 1.024 × 10⁴ Pa. Lower layer Δp₂ = 1050 × 9.81 × 2.2 = 2.266 × 10⁴ Pa. Total liquid gauge pressure Δp = 3.290 × 10⁴ Pa ≈ 3.29 × 10⁴ Pa. Absolute bottom pressure p_Y = 1.01 × 10⁵ + 3.290 × 10⁴ = 1.339 × 10⁵ Pa = 133.9 kPa ≈ 134 kPa.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 134 kPa.

items.stem: A ground-source heat pump maintains a school hall at 25 °C (298 K) while extracting thermal energy from soil at 0 °C (273 K). Calculate the maximum theoretical coefficient of performance $\mathrm{COP}_{\mathrm{hp}}$ of this heat pump.
items.workedSolution: Using kelvin temperatures: $\mathrm{COP}_{\mathrm{hp,max}} = \frac{T_{\mathrm{H}}}{T_{\mathrm{H}} - T_{\mathrm{C}}} = \frac{298}{298 - 273} = 11.9$ (a dimensionless ratio greater than unity, never a percentage efficiency).

markScheme.criterion: Maximum heat-pump COP equals 11.9.

parts.prompt: Using the particle model illustrated, explain why a gas is much more compressible than a liquid or solid.
parts.expectedAnswer: A gas is easily compressed because large empty spaces between widely separated molecules allow the gas volume to decrease easily under pressure.
workingSteps: State that gas molecules are widely separated with large empty spaces between them.
Explain that applied pressure pushes molecules closer together into this empty space, whereas solid and liquid particles are already closely packed.

items.stem: At 310 K, a high-altitude alpine glacier surface zone (surface area 12 m², emissivity e = 0.84) emits and absorbs thermal radiation in an environment at 268 K. Adopt Wien constant 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K and Stefan–Boltzmann constant 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.
items.workedSolution: (a) λ_max = b / T = 9.35 × 10⁻⁶ m. (b) Gross emitted power P_emitted = e σ A T⁴ = 5.28 × 10³ W. (c) Net radiative loss P_net = e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴) = 2.33 × 10³ W.

markScheme.criterion: Uses λ_max = (2.90 × 10⁻³) / T.
Obtains 9.35 × 10⁻⁶ m.
Uses P_emitted = e σ A T⁴.
Obtains 5.28 × 10³ W.
Evaluates e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴).
Obtains 2.33 × 10³ W.

Calculate the gross thermal power emitted by the greybody surface.

items.stem: Inside a laboratory heat-engine indicator rig with low-friction seals immersed in a constant-temperature bath at 310 K, 0.45 mol of an ideal monatomic gas expands reversibly along isotherm A → B from V_A = 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³ to V_B = 5.0 × 10⁻³ m³. Take R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and expansion work done by the gas as positive.
items.workedSolution: (a) P_B = nRT / V_B = 2.32 × 10⁵ Pa. (b) W_by = nRT ln(V_B / V_A) = 804 J. (c) Since ΔU = 0, Q = W_by and ΔS = Q / T = 2.59 J K⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses P_B = nRT / V_B.
Obtains 2.32 × 10⁵ Pa.
Evaluates nRT ln(V_B / V_A).
Obtains 804 J.
Uses ΔS = Q / T with Q = W_by.
Obtains 2.59 J K⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the final pressure P_B of the gas in state B.
Calculate the work done by the gas during the reversible isothermal expansion A → B.
Determine the change in entropy ΔS of the gas during A → B.
workingSteps: Since ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas isotherm, Q = W_by.

items.stem: Inside a sealed foam-insulated metallurgical quench tank, a 0.3 kg block of melting ice at 273.15 K is placed into 0.28 kg of water initially at 289.15 K (c_water = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, L_f = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹). Because the ice mass is large, the mixture reaches phase-coexistence equilibrium at 273.15 K. What mass of ice melts?
items.workedSolution: Maximum heat released by water cooling to 273.15 K is Q = 0.28 × 4180 × (289.15 − 273.15) = 1.873 × 10⁴ J, which is less than m_ice L_f = 1.002 × 10⁵ J. Mass melted Δm = Q / L_f = 0.0561 kg.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Δm = m_water c_water (T_water − 273.15) / L_f to obtain 0.0561 kg (B).

items.stem: A sample of 0.4 mol of an ideal monatomic gas in a closed noble-gas power-conversion loop expands isobarically at constant pressure 4.5 × 10⁵ Pa from volume 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ (state A) to 4.4 × 10⁻³ m³ (state B). Using the first law ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW (thermal energy supplied to the gas and work done on the gas positive), how much thermal energy ΔQ is supplied to the gas during A → B?
items.workedSolution: Work done on the gas during expansion is ΔW = −P(V_B − V_A) = −4.5 × 10⁵ × (4.4 × 10⁻³ − 2.0 × 10⁻³) = -1.080 × 10³ J. For a monatomic ideal gas, ΔU = (3/2) P ΔV = 1.620 × 10³ J. By the first law ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW, thermal energy supplied is ΔQ = ΔU − ΔW = (5/2) P ΔV = 2.70 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates the first-law energy transfer with consistent work sign to obtain 2.70 × 10³ J (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates only the boundary work W = P ΔV during expansion and ignores the increase in internal energy ΔU.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates only the internal energy change ΔU = (3/2) P ΔV and omits the expansion work P ΔV.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the 3/2 factor in monatomic ΔU = (3/2) P ΔV, computing ΔU + W = P ΔV + P ΔV = 2 P ΔV instead of (5/2) P ΔV.

items.stem: During the second trial of a continuous-flow experiment, the liquid mass flow rate is doubled. Why must the electrical heater power be adjusted carefully until the outlet thermometer returns to its exact first-trial reading?
items.workedSolution: Matching the outlet reading ensures identical inlet and outlet temperatures keep thermal energy loss rate to the surroundings constant so heat loss cancels upon subtraction. Therefore the correct statement is: So that identical inlet and outlet temperatures keep thermal energy loss rate to the surroundings constant so heat loss cancels upon subtraction

items.stem: Under what macroscopic conditions does a real gas deviate most strongly from the ideal gas equation pV = nRT, and why?
items.workedSolution: Close packing and low kinetic energy mean ideal gas behaviour breaks down at high pressure and low temperature because finite molecular volume and intermolecular attractive forces become significant. Therefore the correct statement is: The ideal gas behaviour breaks down at high pressure and low temperature because finite molecular volume and intermolecular attractive forces become significant

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: ideal gas behaviour breaks down at high pressure and low temperature because finite molecular volume and intermolecular attractive forces become significant.

options.text: The ideal gas behaviour breaks down at very low pressure and high temperature because molecules move too fast to collide with walls.

options.text: The ideal gas behaviour breaks down at low pressure and low density because intermolecular forces grow infinite at large separation.
options.distractorRationale: Intermolecular forces vanish rapidly as molecular separation increases.

options.distractorRationale: Thermal speeds at laboratory temperatures are non-relativistic.

items.stem: Within a cryocooler compression cylinder containing monatomic working gas, 1 mol of monatomic working gas (adiabatic exponent γ = 5/3) traverses clockwise Otto loop A → B → C → D → A: insulated compression from 6.0 × 10⁻³ m³ at 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa to 1.5 × 10⁻³ m³, constant-volume heat addition to 3.326 × 10⁶ Pa, insulated expansion back to 6.0 × 10⁻³ m³, and constant-volume heat rejection to state A (work done by the gas positive).
items.workedSolution: (a) Adiabatic relation gives P_B = 1.51 × 10⁶ Pa. (b) Isochoric heat input Q_in = 4.08 × 10³ J. (c) By cyclic energy conservation ΔU_cycle = 0, W_net = Q_in − Q_out = 2.46 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies P V^(5/3) = const along A → B.
Obtains 1.51 × 10⁶ Pa.
Uses Q_in = (3/2) ΔP V on the isochoric heating leg.
Obtains 4.08 × 10³ J.
Evaluates W_net = Q_in − Q_out (or sums leg works).
Obtains 2.46 × 10³ J.

Obtains 3.92 × 10⁻⁷ m.

items.stem: A Carnot engine modelled in a micro-electro-mechanical gas spring cavity uses 0.3 mol of ideal gas operating between a hot reservoir at 527 °C and a cold sink at 87 °C (take T(K) = θ(°C) + 273.15). During the high-temperature isothermal stage A → B, the volume increases from 1.2 × 10⁻³ m³ to 2.4 × 10⁻³ m³. Taking net work done by the gas as positive (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹), what is the net work output W_net per cycle?
items.workedSolution: Q_H = nRT_H ln(V_B / V_A) = 1.383 × 10³ J and η = 1 − T_C / T_H = 0.5499. Net work output W_net = η Q_H = nR(T_H − T_C) ln(V_B / V_A) = 760 J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Carnot thermodynamics in kelvin to obtain 760 J (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses base-10 log₁₀(V_B / V_A) instead of natural logarithm ln(V_B / V_A).

options.label: B

items.stem: A sample of 0.45 mol of monatomic Neon-20 (Ne) gas (molar mass 20.2 g mol⁻¹) is sealed inside a semiconductor lithography purge canister of constant volume 0.024 m³ at 310 K. Take R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) p = nRT / V = (0.45 × 8.31 × 310) / 0.024 = 4.83 × 10⁴ Pa. (b) Single-atom mass m = M / N_A = 0 kg. (c) Density ρ = nM / V = 0.379 kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes Kelvin temperature into p = nRT / V.
Obtains 4.83 × 10⁴ Pa.
Converts molar mass to kg mol⁻¹ and divides by Avogadro constant.
Obtains 0 kg.
Evaluates ρ = nM / V in SI units.
Obtains 0.379 kg m⁻³.

Determine the mass of a single Neon-20 (Ne) atom in kilograms.

items.stem: A heated copper block of mass 0.36 kg and specific heat capacity 385 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ at 380 K is plunged into 0.55 kg of water (c = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) initially at 285 K inside a well-insulated copper-lined laboratory calorimeter. Thermal energy exchange with the surroundings and container is negligible. What is the final thermal equilibrium temperature T_eq?
items.workedSolution: Enthalpy balance: m_s c_s (T_s − T_eq) = m_l c_l (T_eq − T_l), giving T_eq = 290.4 K. Therefore T_eq = 290 K.

markScheme.criterion: Applies calorimetry energy balance to obtain 290 K (B).

items.stem: An automotive laboratory mounts a four-stroke petrol engine on a testbed to separate thermodynamic combustion losses from mechanical friction losses.
items.workedSolution: Measure fuel flow rate, crankshaft speed $f$, dynamometer torque $T$, and cylinder $p$–$V$ area. Dynamometer torque and angular speed give brake power while indicator loop area times firing frequency gives indicated power ($P_{\mathrm{ind}} = A(f/2)N_{\mathrm{cyl}}$, $P_{\mathrm{brake}} = 2\pi f T$, $P_{\mathrm{in}} = \text{CV}\cdot\dot{m}$). Computing $\eta_{\mathrm{th}} = P_{\mathrm{ind}}/P_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $\eta_{\mathrm{mech}} = P_{\mathrm{brake}}/P_{\mathrm{ind}}$ lets engineers distinguish combustion/cooling losses from mechanical friction losses.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies measurements of fuel flow rate, crankshaft rotational speed, dynamometer torque, and cylinder $p$–$V$ loop.
Correctly links fuel calorific value times flow rate to input power $P_{\mathrm{in}}$.
Correctly states $P_{\mathrm{ind}} = \text{area} \times (f/2) \times N_{\mathrm{cyl}}$ explicitly using one power stroke per two revolutions.
Correctly states $P_{\mathrm{brake}} = 2\pi f T$ and links difference $P_{\mathrm{ind}} - P_{\mathrm{brake}}$ to friction power.

Correctly defines $\eta_{\mathrm{th}} = P_{\mathrm{ind}}/P_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $\eta_{\mathrm{mech}} = P_{\mathrm{brake}}/P_{\mathrm{ind}}$ (with overall $\eta_{\mathrm{ov}} = \eta_{\mathrm{th}}\eta_{\mathrm{mech}}$).
Explains diagnostic distinction: thermal efficiency isolates combustion/heat-loss issues while mechanical efficiency isolates sliding/bearing friction.

parts.prompt: Describe the experimental measurements taken on the engine testbed, explain how input power, indicated power, brake power, thermal efficiency, and mechanical efficiency are calculated from them, and discuss why separating thermal and mechanical efficiencies helps engineers diagnose poor performance.
parts.expectedAnswer: Engineers measure fuel mass flow rate and fuel calorific value to determine input power, record a cylinder pressure against volume indicator diagram alongside crankshaft speed, and measure output shaft torque on a brake dynamometer. In data analysis, dynamometer torque and angular speed give brake power while indicator loop area times firing frequency gives indicated power (with firing frequency equal to half the crankshaft revolutions per second multiplied by the number of cylinders). Dividing indicated power by input power yields thermal efficiency, while dividing brake power by indicated power gives mechanical efficiency; separating the two immediately reveals whether poor overall efficiency arises from incomplete combustion and cooling heat losses (low thermal efficiency) or from excessive bearing, piston-ring, and auxiliary friction (low mechanical efficiency).
workingSteps: L1: List key measurements: fuel flow rate (plus calorific value), crankshaft speed, output torque on dynamometer, and cylinder $p$–$V$ pressure transducer trace.
L1: State input power $P_{\mathrm{in}} = \text{CV} \times \text{fuel flow rate}$.
L2: State $P_{\mathrm{ind}} = \text{net loop area} \times \frac{f}{2} \times N_{\mathrm{cyl}}$ noting four-stroke firing once per two revolutions.
L2: State $P_{\mathrm{brake}} = T\omega = 2\pi f T$ and friction power $P_{\mathrm{fric}} = P_{\mathrm{ind}} - P_{\mathrm{brake}}$.
L3: Explain diagnostic value: low $\eta_{\mathrm{th}}$ points to combustion/cooling/timing defects, whereas low $\eta_{\mathrm{mech}}$ points to lubrication or bearing friction losses.

items.stem: The temperature–time curve shows 0.2 kg of aluminium inside a guarded electrical immersion-heating vessel (heated between 916 K and 994 K; T_m = 933.5 K, c_solid = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, c_liquid = 1180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, L_f = 3.97 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹) while an electrical immersion heater of input power 320 W and thermal transfer efficiency 0.9 supplies energy. Calculate the total duration of the process.
items.workedSolution: Effective thermal power P_eff = η P = 0.9 × 320 = 288.0 W. Total energy Q_tot = m c_solid ΔT_s + m L_f + m c_liquid ΔT_l = 9.683 × 10⁴ J, giving t_total = Q_tot / P_eff = 336 s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses P_eff = η P and divides required thermal energy to obtain 336 s (D).

items.stem: In a frictionless piston-cylinder assembly on a thermodynamics test bench, 0.5 mol of a monatomic ideal gas executes a clockwise closed cycle A → B → C → D → A between pressures 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa and 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa and volumes 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³ and 0.012 m³ (A → B isobaric expansion at 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa, B → C isochoric cooling, C → D isobaric compression at 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa, D → An isochoric heating). What is the thermal efficiency η = W_net / Q_in of this rectangular monatomic-gas cycle?
items.workedSolution: W_net = (3.0 × 10⁵ − 1.5 × 10⁵)(0.012 − 4.0 × 10⁻³) = 1.200 × 10³ J. Heat enters on D → A and A → B: Q_in = (3/2)(P_high − P_low)V_min + (5/2)P_high(V_max − V_min) = 6.900 × 10³ J. Efficiency η = W_net / Q_in = 0.174.

markScheme.criterion: Computes thermalEfficiency correctly for the closed rectangular cycle to obtain 0.174 (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides W_net by Q_AB alone, neglecting the heat input Q_DA on the isochoric leg D → A.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits internal energy gain ΔU_AB when computing total heat input Q_in.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes the Carnot efficiency 1 − T_min / T_max between extreme corner temperatures instead of the actual cycle efficiency W_net / Q_in.

items.stem: A thermal laboratory tests a solid block of synthetic gallium-indium compound of mass 0.48 kg initially at 16 °C. The figure displays its temperature–time heating curve through its melting point of 48 °C. The solid has specific heat capacity 390 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and specific latent heat of fusion 7.60 × 10⁴ J kg⁻¹. An electrical immersion heater rated at 64 W transfers energy to the sample with thermal efficiency 88%. In a separate pressure-law check, a sealed dry-helium manometer flask contains a fixed mass of ideal gas at pressure 94 kPa and temperature 16 °C, before being heated at constant volume to 84 °C (use T / K = θ / °C + 273.2).
items.workedSolution: (a)(i) Q₁ = m c Δθ = 0.48 × 390 × (48 − 16) = 5990 J ≈ 5.99e+3 J. (a)(ii) Q_melt = m L_f = 3.648 × 10⁴ J; Q_total = 4.247 × 10⁴ J; t = Q_total / (η P) = 754.1 s ≈ 754 s. (a)(iii) mean molecular kinetic energy stays constant while intermolecular potential energy changes to overcome or form intermolecular bonds. (a)(iv) thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings and absorbed by the container. (b)(i) T₁ = 289.2 K, T₂ = 357.2 K, so p₂ = 94 × (357.2 / 289.2) = 116.1 kPa ≈ 116 kPa. (b)(ii) faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Q = m c Δθ = 0.48 × 390 × 32.
Correctly computes 5.99e+3 J (4 s.f. 5990 J).
Computes Q_melt = 3.648 × 10⁴ J, Q_total = 4.247 × 10⁴ J, and substitutes t = Q_total / (η P).
Shows 4 s.f. value 754.1 s rounding cleanly to 754 s.
States that temperature and mean molecular kinetic energy remain constant along the plateau.
Explains that intermolecular potential energy changes as bonds are weakened, broken, or formed.
States accurately that thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings and absorbed by the container.
Converts both temperatures using T = θ + 273.2 (289.2 K and 357.2 K) and applies p₂ = p₁ T₂ / T₁.
Evaluates final gas pressure = 116 kPa (4 s.f. 116.1 kPa).

Explains via Newton second law that faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area (no credit for quoting pV = nRT alone).

parts.prompt: Calculate the thermal energy required to raise the temperature of the solid synthetic gallium-indium compound from 16 °C to 48 °C. [2]
Show clearly that the actual time required for the 64 W heater operating at 88% efficiency to warm the solid from 16 °C and melt it completely at 48 °C is approximately 754 s. [2]
Referring to the horizontal phase-change plateau QR on the figure, explain in terms of molecular energies why the temperature stays constant while internal energy changes. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: During the plateau, mean molecular kinetic energy stays constant while intermolecular potential energy changes to overcome or form intermolecular bonds.
workingSteps: State that temperature measures mean random molecular kinetic energy which stays constant.
Explain that latent thermal energy changes intermolecular potential energy as bonds are broken or formed.

parts.prompt: State one physical reason why the measured heating time in the laboratory exceeds the ideal value calculated assuming perfect efficiency. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings and absorbed by the container.
workingSteps: Apply NCUK calorimetry observation: thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings and absorbed by the container.

parts.prompt: Calculate the new pressure of the ideal gas in the sealed dry-helium manometer flask at 84 °C using T / K = θ / °C + 273.2. [2]
Explain in terms of kinetic theory and Newton's second law (without using the ideal gas equation) why heating the gas at constant volume increases its pressure. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Heating raises molecular speeds so faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area.
workingSteps: Link higher molecular speed to larger momentum change per collision, higher collision frequency, and larger force per unit area.

items.stem: The P–V diagram shows a rapid thermally insulated (adiabatic) expansion A → B of 0.75 mol of monatomic ideal gas (γ = 5/3) in an insulated aerospace gas-accumulator cylinder from (6.0 × 10⁵ Pa, 1.2 × 10⁻³ m³) to final volume 3.6 × 10⁻³ m³ (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹). Taking work done by the gas as positive, how much mechanical work is done by the gas during A → B?
items.workedSolution: First find P_B = P_A (V_A / V_B)^(5/3) = 9.615 × 10⁴ Pa. Since Q = 0 in an adiabatic process, W_by = −ΔU = (3/2)(P_A V_A − P_B V_B) = 561 J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies P V^(5/3) = const and Q = 0 to obtain 561 J (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Omits the 3/2 factor in |ΔU| = (3/2)|P_B V_B − P_A V_A| when applying Q = 0 => |W| = |ΔU|.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses the isothermal work formula P_A V_A |ln(V_B / V_A)| instead of adiabatic work.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Treats pressure as constant at P_A, computing P_A |V_B − V_A| instead of adiabatic work.

items.stem: A cylinder holds 0.220 mol of monatomic argon ($\gamma = 1.67$) initially at pressure 110 kPa and volume 5.00 × 10⁻³ m³. The gas undergoes an adiabatic change to a final volume of 1.00 × 10⁻³ m³. Take $R = 8.31\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$ and apply $Q = \Delta U + W$.
items.workedSolution: (a) $p_2 = 1.62e+3 kPa$. (b) $T_2 = \frac{p_2 V_2}{nR} = 884 K$. (c) Work done by gas $W = −1.59e+3 J$. (d) Change in internal energy $\Delta U = 1.59e+3 J$.

markScheme.criterion: Applies the governing pressure-volume relation $p_1 V_1^{\gamma} = p_2 V_2^{\gamma}$.
Obtains $p_2 = 1.62e+3 kPa$.
Applies $pV = nRT$ with $R = 8.31\text{ J mol}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$.
Obtains $T_2 = 884 K$.
Evaluates mechanical work done by the gas with correct sign.
Obtains $W = −1.59e+3 J$.
Applies $Q = \Delta U + W$ with $Q = 0$ for an adiabatic process.
Obtains $\Delta U = 1.59e+3 J$.

parts.prompt: Calculate the final pressure of the gas in kPa.
Determine the final thermodynamic temperature of the gas in kelvin.
Calculate the work done BY the gas during the change, stating its sign clearly.
Hence calculate the change in internal energy $\Delta U$ of the gas.
workingSteps: For an adiabatic change $Q = 0$, so $\Delta U = -W = 1.59e+3 J$.

items.stem: An open glass U-tube contains seawater of known density ρ₂ = 1025 kg m⁻³ in its lower bend and right arm. An immiscible sample of kerosene of unknown density ρ₁ is poured into the left arm until equilibrium is reached as illustrated. Above the horizontal interface datum P–Q, the left oil column stands h₁ = 0.34 m tall while the right seawater column stands h₂ = 0.245 m tall (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²).
items.workedSolution: (a) pressures are equal at the same horizontal level within a continuous static liquid. (b) Δp = ρ₂gh₂ = 2464 Pa ≈ 2.46e+3 Pa. (c) ρ₁ = ρ₂(h₂/h₁) = 738.6 kg m⁻³ ≈ 739 kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: States equal pressure at the same horizontal level in a continuous static liquid.
Applies Δp = ρ₂gh₂.
Equates ρ₁gh₁ = ρ₂gh₂.
ρ₁ = 739 kg m⁻³.

options.text: Particles are locked into a rigid repeating crystal lattice and can only vibrate in place.
options.distractorRationale: Describes a solid lattice; liquids lack fixed lattice positions.

options.label: B
options.text: Particles are widely spaced with negligible intermolecular forces so the substance easily compresses.
options.distractorRationale: Describes a gas; liquid particles stay almost touching and are nearly incompressible.

options.label: C
options.text: In the middle panel representing a liquid, particles are closely packed in an irregular arrangement and can slide past one another.

options.label: D
options.text: Particles expand to occupy the entire empty upper volume of the sealed container uniformly.
options.distractorRationale: Liquids keep a definite volume and form a free surface under gravity.

items.stem: A laboratory microscope focuses on microscopic pollen grains suspended in still water inside a sealed observation cell, revealing the jagged path shown. What is the correct physical explanation for the erratic zig-zag path traced by the illuminated speck?
items.workedSolution: The abrupt changes in direction occur because of uneven rapid random collisions by much smaller invisible moving water molecules transferring momentum to the suspended speck.

markScheme.criterion: The abrupt changes in direction occur because of uneven rapid random collisions by much smaller invisible moving water molecules transferring momentum to the suspended speck.

options.label: A
options.text: The visible specks themselves are living organisms or electrically charged dust repelling one another.
options.distractorRationale: Inert smoke or pollen specks move passively due to bombardment by invisible fluid molecules.

options.label: B
options.text: The abrupt changes in direction occur because of uneven rapid random collisions by much smaller invisible moving water molecules transferring momentum to the suspended speck.

options.label: C
options.text: Photons in the side light beam push the smoke specks erratically sideways whenever they scatter light.
options.distractorRationale: Radiation pressure from a lab lamp is far too weak and uniform to produce random isotropic zig-zags.

options.label: D
options.text: Warm convection currents generated by the lamp continuously sweep all specks in smooth circular loops.
options.distractorRationale: Convection produces smooth bulk drift in one direction, not independent erratic zig-zag jumps.

items.stem: Inside a micro-electro-mechanical gas spring cavity, 1.2 mol of ideal gas starts in state A (1.1 × 10⁵ Pa, 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³). As plotted on the volume–temperature (V–T) axes, the gas first expands at constant pressure to V_B = 7.5 × 10⁻³ m³ (state B) and is then heated at constant volume to P_C = 1.54 × 10⁵ Pa (state C). Use R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) T_A = P_A V_A / (nR) = 33.1 K. (b) Isobaric expansion gives T_B = T_A (V_B / V_A) = 82.7 K. (c) Isochoric heating gives T_C = T_B (P_C / P_A) = 116 K.

markScheme.criterion: Uses T_A = P_A V_A / (nR).
Obtains 33.1 K.
Applies V_B / T_B = V_A / T_A or P_A V_B / (nR).
Obtains 82.7 K.
Applies P_C / T_C = P_B / T_B or P_C V_B / (nR).
Obtains 116 K.

parts.prompt: Calculate the initial temperature T_A of the gas in state A.
Determine the temperature T_B at the end of the isobaric expansion A → B.
workingSteps: By Charles's law at constant pressure, T_B = T_A (V_B / V_A) = 82.7 K.

parts.prompt: Calculate the final temperature T_C in state C after the isochoric stage B → C.
workingSteps: At constant volume V_C = V_B, T_C = T_B (P_C / P_B) = (1.54 × 10⁵ × 7.5 × 10⁻³) / (1.2 × 8.31) = 116 K.

items.stem: An experiment records the molecular speed distribution of 1.2 mol of Argon-40 (Ar) gas (molar mass 40 g mol⁻¹) occupying 0.025 m³ in a sealed borosilicate acoustic-thermometry sphere at 480 K (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (kinetic-theory pressure relation: pV = ⅓ N m v_rms²)). Which value equals the rms speed of the atoms?
items.workedSolution: Convert molar mass to SI units: M = 0.04 kg mol⁻¹. Using v_rms = √(3RT / M) at T = 480 K gives v_rms = √(3 × 8.31 × 480 / 0.04) = 547 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates √(3RT / M) with M in kg mol⁻¹ to obtain 547 m s⁻¹ (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes molar mass in g mol⁻¹ instead of kg mol⁻¹ into √(3RT / M), underestimating v_rms by a factor of √1000 ≈ 31.6.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 3 from the three translational degrees of freedom, evaluating √(RT / M).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses a factor of 2 instead of 3, computing the most probable speed v_p = √(2RT / M) rather than v_rms.

items.stem: In a climate radiative-transfer model, a dark oceanic mixed-layer surface patch of area 4 m² and surface emissivity e = 0.88 is at 350 K while exchanging thermal infrared radiation with an effective surrounding environment at 255 K. Taking σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, what is the net rate of radiative energy loss P_net from the surface?
items.workedSolution: Net radiative power loss P_net = e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴) = 0.88 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 4 × ((350)⁴ − (255)⁴) = 2.15 × 10³ W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴) to obtain 2.15 × 10³ W (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Evaluates e σ A (T − T_amb)⁴ instead of e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴), a classic fourth-power algebra error.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the greybody emissivity factor e (< 1) from P_net = e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates gross emitted power e σ A T⁴ and ignores incoming radiation absorbed from the surroundings at T_amb.

items.stem: The P–V curve shows a reversible isothermal expansion at 280 K of 1.6 mol of ideal gas inside a frictionless piston-cylinder assembly on a thermodynamics test bench from volume 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ to 7.0 × 10⁻³ m³ (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹). Calculate the entropy increase ΔS of the gas.
items.workedSolution: For a reversible isothermal expansion, ΔU = 0 so Q = W_by = nRT ln(V_B / V_A). Therefore ΔS = Q / T = nR ln(V_B / V_A) = 1.6 × 8.31 × ln(7.0 × 10⁻³ / 2.0 × 10⁻³) = 16.7 J K⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔS = nR ln(V_B / V_A) to obtain 16.7 J K⁻¹ (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses base-10 logarithm log₁₀(V_B / V_A) instead of the natural logarithm ln(V_B / V_A).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Replaces ln(V_B / V_A) with the linear fractional change (V_B − V_A) / V_A.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes isothermal heat Q = nRT ln(V_B / V_A) without dividing by T to obtain ΔS = Q / T.

items.stem: Zero heat enters a precision isothermal-jacket mixing cup while 0.24 kg of water initially at 301.15 K equilibrates against 0.18 kg of 273.15 K ice (4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ for liquid water; L_f = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹).
items.workedSolution: (a) Q_water = m_water c_water (301.15 − 273.15) = 2.81 × 10⁴ J, which is below m_ice L_f. (b) Melted mass Δm = Q_water / L_f = 0.0841 kg. (c) Melted fraction f = Δm / m_ice = 0.467.

markScheme.criterion: Computes m_water c_water (T_water − 273.15).
Obtains 2.81 × 10⁴ J.
Divides Q_water by L_f.
Obtains 0.0841 kg.
Divides Δm by initial ice mass m_ice.
Obtains 0.467.

workingSteps: Q_water = m_water c_water (301.15 − 273.15) = 2.81 × 10⁴ J (< m_ice L_f = 6.01 × 10⁴ J).

parts.prompt: Calculate the mass of ice that melts by the time thermal equilibrium is reached.
Determine the fraction of the initial ice sample that has melted at equilibrium.

items.stem: The P–V diagram shows 0.4 mol of an ideal monatomic gas in a solar-thermal helium Brayton demonstrator cylinder taken from state A (1.5 × 10⁵ Pa, 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³) to state B (2.25 × 10⁵ Pa, 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³) at constant volume, and then from state B to state C (2.25 × 10⁵ Pa, 6.4 × 10⁻³ m³) at constant pressure. Throughout this question, use the first law ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW where thermal energy supplied to the gas (ΔQ) and work done on the gas (ΔW) are positive.
items.workedSolution: (a) Work is done only along B → C: ΔW = −P_B(V_C − V_B) = -990 J. (b) ΔU_AC = (3/2)(P_C V_C − P_A V_A) = 1.71 × 10³ J. (c) By ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW, total heat supplied ΔQ = ΔU_AC − ΔW = 2.70 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies ΔW_AB = 0 and computes ΔW = −P_B(V_C − V_B).
Obtains -990 J.
Applies ΔU = (3/2)(P_C V_C − P_A V_A).
Obtains 1.71 × 10³ J.
Applies ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW ⇒ ΔQ = ΔU_AC − ΔW to obtain total heat supplied.
Obtains 2.70 × 10³ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the total mechanical work done on the gas ΔW along path A → B → C (including its sign).
Calculate the total change in internal energy ΔU of the monatomic gas between state A and state C.
workingSteps: For a monatomic ideal gas, U = (3/2) PV, so ΔU_AC = (3/2)(P_C V_C − P_A V_A).

parts.prompt: Determine the total thermal energy ΔQ supplied to the gas over the complete path A → B → C.
workingSteps: By the first law of thermodynamics (ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW), ΔQ = ΔU_AC − ΔW = 1.710 × 10³ − (-990.0) = 2.70 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates steady heat loss rate H = 6.00 W.

items.stem: In the kinetic theory cube model, an oxygen molecule bounces elastically back and forth perpendicularly between opposite walls of a cube of side L = 0.200 m at x-velocity u = 450 m s⁻¹. Calculate the time interval t between consecutive collisions with the same wall.
items.workedSolution: The molecule travels distance 2L before returning to the same face: t = 2L / u = (2 × 0.200) / 450 = 8.89 × 10⁻⁴ s.

markScheme.criterion: Applies round-trip interval t = 2L / u = 8.89 × 10⁻⁴ s.

items.stem: A closed heat engine (a micro-electro-mechanical gas spring cavity) takes 0.8 mol of monatomic ideal gas (γ = 5/3) from A (5.5 × 10⁵ Pa, 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³) adiabatically to V_B = 6.25 × 10⁻³ m³, compresses it at constant pressure back to V_C = 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³, and heats it isochorically back to A. Find the net work done by the gas per cycle (work by gas positive).
items.workedSolution: At B, P_B = P_A (V_A / V_B)^(5/3) = 1.194 × 10⁵ Pa. Adiabatic work W_AB = (3/2)(P_A V_A − P_B V_B) = 942.8 J, and isobaric compression work W_BC = P_B(V_C − V_B) = -447.9 J (W_CA = 0). Thus W_net = W_AB + W_BC = 495 J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates the closed adiabatic heat-engine cycle to obtain 495 J (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes only the magnitude of the isobaric compression work P_B(V_B − V_C).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Computes only the adiabatic expansion work W_AB and forgets to subtract the isobaric compression work |W_BC|.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates total heat input Q_CA along the isochoric leg instead of net work W_net.

items.stem: Inside a high-vacuum synchrotron beamline gas target, an ideal monatomic sample of Argon-40 (Ar) (M = 0.04 kg mol⁻¹) is in thermal equilibrium at 820 K. Use Boltzmann constant 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ and elementary charge 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Find the average translational kinetic energy of a single atom in eV.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes T = 820 K into the monatomic kinetic-theory energy relation to obtain 0.106 eV (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Evaluates (1/2) k_B T / e for a single degree of freedom instead of three.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes k_B T / e and omits the 3/2 translational factor.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Doubles the 3/2 factor to 3 k_B T / e by omitting the 1/2 in kinetic energy.

Calculate the total thermal energy required.

markScheme.criterion: Sums sensible mcΔT stages and latent heat mL to obtain 4.41 × 10⁵ J (D).

items.stem: Radiometric observations characterise a nearby solar-type star modelled as an ideal spherical radiator (ideal blackbody, area 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ m², surface temperature 2600 K) from a separation d = 2.4 m. Taking Wien's constant b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K, what is the peak emission wavelength λ_max in nanometres?
items.workedSolution: By Wien's displacement law, λ_max = b / T = (2.90 × 10⁻³) / 2600 = 1.115 × 10⁻⁶ m = 1.12 × 10³ nm.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates the blackbody radiation law in SI units to obtain 1.12 × 10³ nm (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Inverts Wien's displacement law by dividing T by b instead of b by T.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts 273.15 from the kelvin temperature before applying Wien's law.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies Wien's constant b by T instead of dividing b by T.

items.stem: Within a closed noble-gas power-conversion loop, 1.4 mol of monatomic working gas completes a four-stage Carnot engine loop between a hot reservoir at 527 °C and a cold sink at 67 °C (take T(K) = θ(°C) + 273.15), expanding from 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³ to 5.0 × 10⁻³ m³ while in contact with the hot source (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; net work output by the gas positive).

markScheme.criterion: Converts temperatures to kelvin and applies 1 − T_C / T_H.
Obtains 0.575.
Uses Q_H = nRT_H ln(V_B / V_A).
Obtains 6.45 × 10³ J.
Multiplies η by Q_H (or evaluates Q_H − Q_C).
Obtains 3.71 × 10³ J.

items.stem: 0.45 mol of monatomic Krypton-84 (Kr) (molar mass 83.8 g mol⁻¹) fills a sealed quartz spectroscopy cell of volume 0.075 m³ at a steady temperature of 177 °C (take T(K) = θ(°C) + 273.15). Take R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Find the gas pressure.
items.workedSolution: Convert temperature to kelvin: T = 177 + 273.15 = 450.15 K. From the ideal gas equation p = nRT / V = (0.45 × 8.31 × 450.15) / 0.075 = 2.24 × 10⁴ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Applies p = nRT / V in SI units to obtain 2.24 × 10⁴ Pa (C).

options.distractorRationale: Multiplies nRT by volume V instead of dividing nRT by V.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes Celsius temperature θ directly into pV = nRT without converting to absolute temperature in kelvin.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the amount of substance n in p = nRT / V, solving for 1 mol instead of the given molar amount.

items.stem: With negligible heat loss to the surroundings, 0.65 kg of hot glass at 475 K (c = 840 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) is placed into 0.42 kg of ethanol (c = 2440 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) held in a 0.16 kg copper liner (c = 385 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 285 K within a lagged benchtop thermal-equilibrium chamber.
items.workedSolution: (a) Solving the enthalpy balance yields T_eq = 349 K. (b) Heat released by the hot solid Q_lost = m_s c_s (T_s − T_eq) = 6.90 × 10⁴ J. (c) Heat gained by the ethanol Q_liq = m_l c_liq (T_eq − T_l) = 6.51 × 10⁴ J.

markScheme.criterion: Sets up full calorimetry heat-balance equation.
Obtains 349 K.
Evaluates m_s c_s (T_s − T_eq).
Obtains 6.90 × 10⁴ J.
Evaluates m_l c_liq (T_eq − T_l).
Obtains 6.51 × 10⁴ J.

items.stem: How does combustion initiation in an ideal four-stroke diesel cycle fundamentally differ from that in an ideal four-stroke Otto petrol cycle?
items.workedSolution: Because air alone is compressed without risk of premature detonation, a diesel engine compresses air alone to a higher compression ratio so injected fuel self-ignites at constant pressure.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that diesel engine compresses air alone to a higher compression ratio so injected fuel self-ignites at constant pressure.

items.stem: In an automated cryostat sample holder, a Peltier extraction module rated at 1200 W with coupling efficiency 0.8 removes thermal energy as a 0.55 kg sample of water goes from 313 K to 235 K across its 273.15 K fusion point (c_solid = 2100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, c_liquid = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, L_f = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹). How long does the isothermal freezing plateau last?
items.workedSolution: Effective thermal power P_eff = η P = 0.8 × 1200 = 960.0 W. Plateau latent energy Q_f = m L_f = 1.837 × 10⁵ J, giving Δt_plateau = Q_f / P_eff = 191 s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses P_eff = η P and divides required thermal energy to obtain 191 s (C).

items.stem: In a high-efficiency reciprocating research engine cylinder, 0.5 mol of an ideal monatomic gas undergoes the clockwise closed heat-engine cycle A → B → C → D → A: isobaric expansion A → B at 3.6 × 10⁵ Pa from 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³ to 0.012 m³, isochoric cooling B → C to 1.8 × 10⁵ Pa, isobaric compression C → D at 1.8 × 10⁵ Pa back to 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³, and isochoric heating D → A to 3.6 × 10⁵ Pa. Take work done by the gas as positive.
items.workedSolution: (a) W_net = (P_high − P_low)(V_max − V_min) = 1.44 × 10³ J. (b) Q_in = Q_DA + Q_AB = (3/2)(P_high − P_low)V_min + (5/2)P_high(V_max − V_min) = 8.28 × 10³ J. (c) η = W_net / Q_in = 0.174.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates enclosed loop area (P_high − P_low)(V_max − V_min).
Obtains 1.44 × 10³ J.
Identifies heat input on both D → A (isochoric) and A → B (isobaric).
Uses monatomic factors (3/2) on D → A and (5/2) on A → B.
Obtains Q_in = 8.28 × 10³ J.
Divides W_net from (a) by Q_in from (b).
Obtains 0.174.

Calculate the total thermal energy Q_in supplied to the monatomic gas during the heating stages D → A and A → B.
Determine the thermal efficiency η of this cycle.

items.stem: A calorimetry experiment records the cooling curve shown in the figure as 0.32 kg of molten crystalline octadecanol wax freezes at 58 °C and cools in solid form down to 22 °C. The solid has specific heat capacity 1620 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and specific latent heat of fusion 1.65 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. When previously melted from 22 °C using a 95 W immersion heater, the heating setup operated at 80% thermal efficiency. Separately, a rigid nitrogen gas canister holds a fixed mass of ideal gas at 108 kPa and 22 °C before warming at constant volume to 105 °C (use T / K = θ / °C + 273.2).
items.workedSolution: (a)(i) Q₁ = m c Δθ = 0.32 × 1620 × (58 − 22) = 1.866 × 10⁴ J ≈ 1.87 × 10⁴ J. (a)(ii) Q_melt = m L_f = 5.280 × 10⁴ J; Q_total = 7.146 × 10⁴ J ≈ 7.15 × 10⁴ J. (a)(iii) mean molecular kinetic energy stays constant while intermolecular potential energy changes to overcome or form intermolecular bonds. (a)(iv) temperature remains constant along a horizontal plateau during freezing before falling smoothly toward ambient temperature. (b)(i) T₁ = 295.2 K, T₂ = 378.2 K, so p₂ = 108 × (378.2 / 295.2) = 138.4 kPa ≈ 138 kPa. (b)(ii) faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Q = m c Δθ = 0.32 × 1620 × 36.
Correctly computes 1.87 × 10⁴ J (4 s.f. 1.866 × 10⁴ J).
Computes latent energy Q_melt = 5.280 × 10⁴ J and sums Q_warm + Q_melt.
Shows 4 s.f. value 7.146 × 10⁴ J rounding cleanly to 7.15 × 10⁴ J.
States that temperature and mean molecular kinetic energy remain constant along the plateau.
Explains that intermolecular potential energy changes as bonds are weakened, broken, or formed.
States accurately that temperature remains constant along a horizontal plateau during freezing before falling smoothly toward ambient temperature.
Converts both temperatures using T = θ + 273.2 (295.2 K and 378.2 K) and applies p₂ = p₁ T₂ / T₁.
Evaluates final gas pressure = 138 kPa (4 s.f. 138.4 kPa).

Explains via Newton second law that faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area (no credit for quoting pV = nRT alone).

parts.prompt: Calculate the thermal energy released as the solidified crystalline octadecanol wax cools from 58 °C down to 22 °C. [2]
Show clearly that the total thermal energy required to warm the solid from 22 °C to 58 °C and melt it completely is approximately 7.15 × 10⁴ J. [2]
Referring to the horizontal phase-change plateau QR on the figure, explain in terms of molecular energies why the temperature stays constant while internal energy changes. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: During the plateau, mean molecular kinetic energy stays constant while intermolecular potential energy changes to overcome or form intermolecular bonds.
workingSteps: State that temperature measures mean random molecular kinetic energy which stays constant.
Explain that latent thermal energy changes intermolecular potential energy as bonds are broken or formed.

parts.prompt: Describe the shape of the cooling curve along QR and RS as the substance freezes and cools to ambient temperature. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: temperature remains constant along a horizontal plateau during freezing before falling smoothly toward ambient temperature.
workingSteps: Apply NCUK calorimetry observation: temperature remains constant along a horizontal plateau during freezing before falling smoothly toward ambient temperature.

parts.prompt: Calculate the new pressure of the ideal gas in the rigid nitrogen gas canister at 105 °C using T / K = θ / °C + 273.2. [2]
Explain in terms of kinetic theory and Newton's second law (without using the ideal gas equation) why heating the gas at constant volume increases its pressure. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Heating raises molecular speeds so faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area.
workingSteps: Link higher molecular speed to larger momentum change per collision, higher collision frequency, and larger force per unit area.

items.stem: The P–V graph shows an adiabatic path A → B for 1.5 mol of monatomic ideal gas (adiabatic exponent γ = 5/3) confined in a closed-cycle Stirling regenerator test cell. At state A, the pressure is 7.5 × 10⁵ Pa and the volume is 1.2 × 10⁻³ m³; at state B, the volume is 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³ (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).

markScheme.criterion: Uses P_A V_A^(5/3) = P_B V_B^(5/3).
Obtains 1.63 × 10⁵ Pa.
Uses T_B = P_B V_B / (nR) or T_A (V_A / V_B)^(2/3).
Obtains 39.2 K.
Sets Q = 0 and evaluates |(3/2)(P_B V_B − P_A V_A)|.
Obtains 617 J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the final pressure P_B of the gas in state B.
Determine the absolute temperature T_B of the gas in state B.
Using the first law of thermodynamics, calculate the work done by the gas (taking work done by the gas as positive) during A → B.

items.stem: A cylinder of nitrogen ($\gamma = 1.40$) expands isobarically at 250 kPa from $2.00 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3$ to $3.40 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3$, causing its internal energy to rise by 875 J. Using $Q = \Delta U + W$, calculate the thermal energy $Q$ supplied to the gas.
items.workedSolution: Work done by gas $W = p\Delta V = 2.50 \times 10^5 (3.40 - 2.00) \times 10^{-3} = 350 J$. By $Q = \Delta U + W$, $Q = 875 + 350 = 1.23e+3 J$.

markScheme.criterion: Thermal energy supplied equals 1.23e+3 J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts $W$ from $\Delta U$ instead of adding work done BY the gas in $Q = \Delta U + W$.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Reports only the mechanical work $p\Delta V$ and omits $\Delta U$.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses $p V_2$ rather than $p(V_2 - V_1)$ for isobaric work.

items.stem: An open glass U-tube contains freshwater of known density ρ₂ = 1000 kg m⁻³ in its lower bend and right arm. An immiscible sample of diesel fuel of unknown density ρ₁ is poured into the left arm until equilibrium is reached as illustrated. Above the horizontal interface datum P–Q, the left oil column stands h₁ = 0.4 m tall while the right freshwater column stands h₂ = 0.288 m tall (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). What is the density ρ₁ of the unknown diesel fuel?
items.workedSolution: Pressures at P and Q on the same horizontal datum are equal: p₀ + ρ₁ g h₁ = p₀ + ρ₂ g h₂ ⇒ ρ₁ = ρ₂ (h₂ / h₁) = 1000 × (0.288 / 0.4) = 720.0 kg m⁻³ ≈ 720 kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Correct unknown density ρ₁ = 720 kg m⁻³.

items.stem: Why can a combined heat and power (CHP) station achieve overall energy utilisation exceeding 75% even though its electrical turbine generator is still bounded by Carnot efficiency?
items.workedSolution: Although electrical generation remains limited by $(T_{\mathrm{H}} - T_{\mathrm{C}})/T_{\mathrm{H}}$, combined heat and power utilises rejected thermal energy for heating raising overall energy utilisation above a standalone power station.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that combined heat and power utilises rejected thermal energy for heating raising overall energy utilisation above a standalone power station.

Widely spaced with negligible intermolecular forces.
Rapid random motion in all directions.

As shown on the pressure–temperature (P–T) diagram, the gas expands isobarically from A to state B of volume 4.5 × 10⁻³ m³, before undergoing isochoric heating from B to state C at 3.52 × 10⁵ Pa. Take R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the temperature T_B at state B?

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates PV / (nR) at the target state to obtain 159 K (C).

options.label: B

Obtains 628 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: In an infrared energy-balance investigation, a dark oceanic mixed-layer surface patch of surface area 2.5 m² and greybody emissivity e = 0.78 has a uniform temperature of 343 K while exchanging radiation with an ambient environment at 268 K. Take b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.
items.workedSolution: (a) λ_max = b / T = 8.45 × 10⁻⁶ m. (b) Gross emitted power P_emitted = e σ A T⁴ = 1.53 × 10³ W. (c) Net radiative loss P_net = e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴) = 960 W.

markScheme.criterion: Uses λ_max = (2.90 × 10⁻³) / T.
Obtains 8.45 × 10⁻⁶ m.
Uses P_emitted = e σ A T⁴.
Obtains 1.53 × 10³ W.
Evaluates e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴).
Obtains 960 W.

items.stem: Inside a closed-cycle Stirling regenerator test cell immersed in a constant-temperature bath at 450 K, 1.6 mol of an ideal monatomic gas expands reversibly along isotherm A → B from V_A = 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³ to V_B = 5.0 × 10⁻³ m³. Take R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and expansion work done by the gas as positive.
items.workedSolution: (a) P_B = nRT / V_B = 1.20 × 10⁶ Pa. (b) W_by = nRT ln(V_B / V_A) = 4.15 × 10³ J. (c) Since ΔU = 0, Q = W_by and ΔS = Q / T = 9.22 J K⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Uses P_B = nRT / V_B.
Obtains 1.20 × 10⁶ Pa.
Evaluates nRT ln(V_B / V_A).
Obtains 4.15 × 10³ J.
Uses ΔS = Q / T with Q = W_by.
Obtains 9.22 J K⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the final pressure P_B of the gas in state B.
Calculate the work done by the gas during the reversible isothermal expansion A → B.
Determine the change in entropy ΔS of the gas during A → B.
workingSteps: Since ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas isotherm, Q = W_by.

items.stem: A 0.28 kg bath of liquid water at 301.15 K in a closed-lid magnetic-stirrer calorimetry pot is stirred with 0.18 kg of ice already at its melting point of 273.15 K. Take c_water = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and L_f = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. How many kilograms of ice melt by the time thermal equilibrium is established?
items.workedSolution: Maximum heat released by water cooling to 273.15 K is Q = 0.28 × 4180 × (301.15 − 273.15) = 3.277 × 10⁴ J, which is less than m_ice L_f = 6.012 × 10⁴ J. Mass melted Δm = Q / L_f = 0.0981 kg.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Δm = m_water c_water (T_water − 273.15) / L_f to obtain 0.0981 kg (C).

items.stem: A sample of 0.8 mol of an ideal monatomic gas in a closed noble-gas power-conversion loop expands isobarically at constant pressure 6.0 × 10⁵ Pa from volume 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ (state A) to 6.4 × 10⁻³ m³ (state B). Using the first law ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW (thermal energy supplied to the gas and work done on the gas positive), how much thermal energy ΔQ is supplied to the gas during A → B?
items.workedSolution: Work done on the gas during expansion is ΔW = −P(V_B − V_A) = −6.0 × 10⁵ × (6.4 × 10⁻³ − 2.0 × 10⁻³) = -2.640 × 10³ J. For a monatomic ideal gas, ΔU = (3/2) P ΔV = 3.960 × 10³ J. By the first law ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW, thermal energy supplied is ΔQ = ΔU − ΔW = (5/2) P ΔV = 6.60 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates the first-law energy transfer with consistent work sign to obtain 6.60 × 10³ J (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Calculates only the boundary work W = P ΔV during expansion and ignores the increase in internal energy ΔU.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates only the internal energy change ΔU = (3/2) P ΔV and omits the expansion work P ΔV.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the 3/2 factor in monatomic ΔU = (3/2) P ΔV, computing ΔU + W = P ΔV + P ΔV = 2 P ΔV instead of (5/2) P ΔV.

items.stem: In a continuous-flow electrical calorimeter experiment to measure the specific heat capacity of a liquid, two different flow rates are tested. Why must the inlet and outlet temperatures be kept identical in both runs?
items.workedSolution: At steady state P = ṁcΔθ + H. Keeping identical inlet and outlet temperatures keep thermal energy loss rate to the surroundings constant so heat loss cancels upon subtraction. Therefore the correct statement is: Maintaining identical inlet and outlet temperatures keep thermal energy loss rate to the surroundings constant so heat loss cancels upon subtraction

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: identical inlet and outlet temperatures keep thermal energy loss rate to the surroundings constant so heat loss cancels upon subtraction.

options.label: A
options.text: Maintaining identical inlet and outlet temperatures ensures zero heat is lost to the surroundings in either run.
options.distractorRationale: Wrongly claims heat loss H becomes zero rather than remaining constant and cancelling.

options.label: B
options.text: Maintaining identical inlet and outlet temperatures keep thermal energy loss rate to the surroundings constant so heat loss cancels upon subtraction

options.label: C
options.text: Maintaining identical inlet and outlet temperatures guarantees the heater current stays constant across both flow rates.
options.distractorRationale: Power must actually be increased at the higher flow rate to keep Δθ identical.

options.label: D
options.text: Maintaining identical inlet and outlet temperatures prevents the specific heat capacity of the glass tube from changing.
options.distractorRationale: In steady state the glass tube temperature is constant anyway and does not absorb net energy.

items.stem: A student views illuminated smoke trapped in a glass cell under a microscope and observes bright specks jittering unpredictably. What does Brownian motion demonstrate?
items.workedSolution: Brownian motion is the random zigzag motion of larger visible smoke particles caused by uneven random collisions with much smaller fast-moving air molecules. Therefore the correct statement is: It shows the random zigzag motion of larger visible smoke particles caused by uneven random collisions with much smaller fast-moving air molecules

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: random zigzag motion of larger visible smoke particles caused by uneven random collisions with much smaller fast-moving air molecules.
