options.label: A
options.text: It shows individual air molecules directly under visible light bouncing off the glass microscope slide.
options.distractorRationale: Air molecules are far too small to resolve optically; we see smoke specks, not molecules.

options.label: B
options.text: It shows the random zigzag motion of larger visible smoke particles caused by uneven random collisions with much smaller fast-moving air molecules

options.label: C
options.text: It shows convection currents lifting all smoke particles uniformly upward at constant velocity.
options.distractorRationale: Convection produces smooth bulk drift rather than erratic random changes in direction.

options.label: D
options.text: It shows electrostatic repulsion between identically charged smoke grains pushing them into circular orbits.
options.distractorRationale: Smoke motion is random and driven by molecular thermal bombardment, not circular orbits.

items.stem: Inside a high-efficiency reciprocating research engine cylinder, 1 mol of monatomic ideal gas (γ = 5/3) completes the three-step cycle A → B → C → A shown on the P–V diagram: reversible adiabatic expansion from A (8.0 × 10⁵ Pa, 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³) to V_B = 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³ at B, isobaric compression at P_B back to V_C = 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ at C, and isochoric heating from C back to A. Take work done by the gas as positive.
items.workedSolution: (a) Adiabatic relation gives P_B = 2.52 × 10⁵ Pa. (b) Isochoric heat input Q_in = 1.64 × 10³ J. (c) By cyclic energy conservation ΔU_cycle = 0, W_net = Q_in − Q_out = 384 J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies P V^(5/3) = const along A → B.
Obtains 2.52 × 10⁵ Pa.
Uses Q_in = (3/2) ΔP V on the isochoric heating leg.
Obtains 1.64 × 10³ J.
Evaluates W_net = Q_in − Q_out (or sums leg works).
Obtains 384 J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the pressure P_B of the gas at state B.
Calculate the thermal energy Q_in absorbed by the gas during the isochoric heating leg.
workingSteps: On C → A (constant V = 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³, P_C = P_B), Q_in = ΔU_CA = (3/2)(P_A − P_B) V_A = 1.64 × 10³ J.

parts.prompt: Determine the net mechanical work W_net done by the gas per cycle.
workingSteps: Heat rejected on isobaric leg B → C is Q_out = (5/2) P_B (V_B − V_C) = 1.260 × 10³ J; W_net = Q_in − Q_out = 384 J.

items.stem: Thermal analysis of 1.25 kg of lead in an automated cryostat sample holder records the three-segment temperature–energy profile from 561 K to 686 K (melting point 600.6 K; c_solid = 128 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; c_liquid = 147 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; specific latent heat of fusion L_f = 2.3 × 10⁴ J kg⁻¹).
items.workedSolution: (a) Q_sens = m c_solid ΔT₁ + m c_liquid ΔT₂ = 2.20 × 10⁴ J. (b) Plateau latent energy Q_lat = m L = 2.88 × 10⁴ J. (c) Total thermal energy Q_total = Q_sens + Q_lat = 5.08 × 10⁴ J.

Obtains 2.20 × 10⁴ J.
Evaluates m L on the phase-change plateau.
Obtains 2.88 × 10⁴ J.

Obtains 5.08 × 10⁴ J.

items.stem: A bolometric sensor placed at d = 3.5 m in vacuum intercepts isotropic blackbody radiation (e = 1) from an isothermal silicon-carbide calibration cavity of area 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m² and temperature 2200 K. Use Wien's constant 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K and Stefan–Boltzmann constant 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.
items.workedSolution: (a) λ_max = b / T = 1.32 × 10⁻⁶ m. (b) P = σ A T⁴ = 332 W. (c) I = P / (4π d²) = 2.16 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Applies λ_max = (2.90 × 10⁻³) / T.
Obtains 1.32 × 10⁻⁶ m.
Applies P = σ A T⁴.
Obtains 332 W.
Divides P by 4π d².
Obtains 2.16 W m⁻².

items.stem: The diagram shows a reversible Carnot cycle A → B → C → D → A for 1.4 mol of monatomic ideal gas in a solar-thermal helium Brayton demonstrator cylinder coupled to a hot reservoir at 277 °C and a cold sink at 27 °C (take T(K) = θ(°C) + 273.15), with isothermal expansion from 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ to 6.0 × 10⁻³ m³. Taking R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, what magnitude of thermal energy Q_C is rejected to the cold sink per cycle?
items.workedSolution: During isothermal compression C → D at T_C = 300.15 K, V_C / V_D = V_B / V_A, so heat rejected to the cold sink is Q_C = nRT_C ln(V_B / V_A) = 3.84 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Carnot thermodynamics in kelvin to obtain 3.84 × 10³ J (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses log₁₀(V_B / V_A) instead of ln(V_B / V_A) in Q_C = nRT_C ln(V_B / V_A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes net work W_net = Q_H − Q_C instead of the rejected heat Q_C.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes the heat absorbed Q_H from the hot reservoir instead of the heat Q_C rejected to the cold sink.

items.stem: During a calibration experiment, a sealed borosilicate acoustic-thermometry sphere of internal volume 0.075 m³ is filled with 2.8 mol of ideal Xenon-131 (Xe) gas of molar mass 0.1313 kg mol⁻¹ and stabilised at 67 °C (take T(K) = θ(°C) + 273.15). Use R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) p = nRT / V = (2.8 × 8.31 × 340.15) / 0.075 = 1.06 × 10⁵ Pa. (b) Single-atom mass m = M / N_A = 0 kg. (c) Density ρ = nM / V = 4.90 kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes Kelvin temperature into p = nRT / V.
Obtains 1.06 × 10⁵ Pa.
Converts molar mass to kg mol⁻¹ and divides by Avogadro constant.
Obtains 0 kg.
Evaluates ρ = nM / V in SI units.
Obtains 4.90 kg m⁻³.

items.stem: In a calorimetry run using a closed-lid magnetic-stirrer calorimetry pot, a 0.18 kg cylinder of aluminium (c = 900 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 410 K is quenched in 0.55 kg of mineral oil (c = 1960 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 294 K. During mixing, 1250 J of thermal energy escapes to the surroundings. What thermal energy does the cylinder give up?
items.workedSolution: Enthalpy balance: m_s c_s (T_s − T_eq) = m_l c_l (T_eq − T_l) + 1250, giving T_eq = 308.1 K. Heat released by the solid Q_lost = m_s c_s (T_s − T_eq) = 1.65 × 10⁴ J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies calorimetry energy balance to obtain 1.65 × 10⁴ J (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Assumes the final equilibrium temperature is the unweighted midpoint (T_solid + T_liquid) / 2.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes only the heat gained by the liquid bath without adding the heat lost to the surroundings.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Assumes the solid cools all the way down to the initial bath temperature T_liquid instead of T_eq.

items.stem: During a testbed trial of a dynamometer-mounted four-cylinder hatchback engine (4 cylinders) running at 64.0 rev s⁻¹, each cylinder indicator loop encloses 520 J. The dynamometer records a brake torque of 135 N m while fuel of calorific value 4.50 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹ enters at 3.90 × 10⁻³ kg s⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) $P_{\mathrm{ind}} = 66.6 kW$. (b) $P_{\mathrm{brake}} = 54.3 kW$. (c) $\eta_{\mathrm{th}} = \frac{P_{\mathrm{ind}}}{P_{\mathrm{in}}} = 37.9%$. (d) $\eta_{\mathrm{mech}} = \frac{P_{\mathrm{brake}}}{P_{\mathrm{ind}}} = 81.6%$ (overall $\eta_{\mathrm{ov}} = \eta_{\mathrm{th}} \eta_{\mathrm{mech}} = 30.9%$).

markScheme.criterion: Applies four-stroke firing frequency $f/2$ times loop area times cylinder count.
Obtains $P_{\mathrm{ind}} = 66.6 kW$.
Applies $P_{\mathrm{brake}} = T(2\pi f)$.
Obtains $P_{\mathrm{brake}} = 54.3 kW$.
Computes $P_{\mathrm{in}} = \text{CV} \times \dot{m}$ and writes $\eta_{\mathrm{th}} = P_{\mathrm{ind}}/P_{\mathrm{in}}$.
Obtains $\eta_{\mathrm{th}} = 37.9%$.
Uses $\eta_{\mathrm{mech}} = P_{\mathrm{brake}}/P_{\mathrm{ind}}$.
Obtains $\eta_{\mathrm{mech}} = 81.6%$.

items.stem: In an adiabatic micro-calorimeter ampoule, a Peltier extraction module rated at 1200 W with coupling efficiency 0.9 removes thermal energy as a 0.55 kg sample of water goes from 333 K to 245 K across its 273.15 K fusion point (c_solid = 2100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, c_liquid = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, L_f = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹). How long does the isothermal freezing plateau last?
items.workedSolution: Effective thermal power P_eff = η P = 0.9 × 1200 = 1.080 × 10³ W. Plateau latent energy Q_f = m L_f = 1.837 × 10⁵ J, giving Δt_plateau = Q_f / P_eff = 170 s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses P_eff = η P and divides required thermal energy to obtain 170 s (C).

items.stem: A heat-engine test rig (a variable-volume optical pressure cell) drives 0.2 mol of ideal monatomic gas around a rectangular cycle with upper pressure 3.5 × 10⁵ Pa, lower pressure 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, minimum volume 1.2 × 10⁻³ m³, and maximum volume 4.8 × 10⁻³ m³. What is the thermal efficiency η = W_net / Q_in of this rectangular monatomic-gas cycle?
items.workedSolution: W_net = (3.5 × 10⁵ − 1.0 × 10⁵)(4.8 × 10⁻³ − 1.2 × 10⁻³) = 900.0 J. Heat enters on D → A and A → B: Q_in = (3/2)(P_high − P_low)V_min + (5/2)P_high(V_max − V_min) = 3.600 × 10³ J. Efficiency η = W_net / Q_in = 0.250.

markScheme.criterion: Computes thermalEfficiency correctly for the closed rectangular cycle to obtain 0.250 (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides W_net by Q_AB alone, neglecting the heat input Q_DA on the isochoric leg D → A.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits internal energy gain ΔU_AB when computing total heat input Q_in.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes the Carnot efficiency 1 − T_min / T_max between extreme corner temperatures instead of the actual cycle efficiency W_net / Q_in.

items.stem: A calorimetry experiment records the cooling curve shown in the figure as 0.22 kg of molten synthetic organic sugar-alcohol wax freezes at 88 °C and cools in solid form down to 25 °C. The solid has specific heat capacity 1520 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and specific latent heat of fusion 2.40 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. When previously melted from 25 °C using a 125 W immersion heater, the heating setup operated at 77% thermal efficiency. Separately, a sealed helium constant-volume probe holds a fixed mass of ideal gas at 110 kPa and 25 °C before warming at constant volume to 130 °C (use T / K = θ / °C + 273.2).
items.workedSolution: (a)(i) Q₁ = m c Δθ = 0.22 × 1520 × (88 − 25) = 2.107 × 10⁴ J ≈ 2.11 × 10⁴ J. (a)(ii) Q_melt = m L_f = 5.280 × 10⁴ J; Q_total = 7.387 × 10⁴ J ≈ 7.39 × 10⁴ J. (a)(iii) mean molecular kinetic energy stays constant while intermolecular potential energy changes to overcome or form intermolecular bonds. (a)(iv) temperature remains constant along a horizontal plateau during freezing before falling smoothly toward ambient temperature. (b)(i) T₁ = 298.2 K, T₂ = 403.2 K, so p₂ = 110 × (403.2 / 298.2) = 148.7 kPa ≈ 149 kPa. (b)(ii) faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Q = m c Δθ = 0.22 × 1520 × 63.
Correctly computes 2.11 × 10⁴ J (4 s.f. 2.107 × 10⁴ J).
Computes latent energy Q_melt = 5.280 × 10⁴ J and sums Q_warm + Q_melt.
Shows 4 s.f. value 7.387 × 10⁴ J rounding cleanly to 7.39 × 10⁴ J.
States that temperature and mean molecular kinetic energy remain constant along the plateau.
Explains that intermolecular potential energy changes as bonds are weakened, broken, or formed.
States accurately that temperature remains constant along a horizontal plateau during freezing before falling smoothly toward ambient temperature.
Converts both temperatures using T = θ + 273.2 (298.2 K and 403.2 K) and applies p₂ = p₁ T₂ / T₁.
Evaluates final gas pressure = 149 kPa (4 s.f. 148.7 kPa).

Explains via Newton second law that faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area (no credit for quoting pV = nRT alone).

items.stem: A thermally isolated sample of 0.75 mol of monatomic ideal gas (γ = 5/3) in a solar-thermal helium Brayton demonstrator cylinder transitions adiabatically from state A (1.2 × 10⁵ Pa, 5.6 × 10⁻³ m³) to state B of volume 1.6 × 10⁻³ m³. Given R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, calculate the gas pressure at state B.
items.workedSolution: For a monatomic adiabatic process, P_B = P_A (V_A / V_B)^(5/3) = 1.2 × 10⁵ × (5.6 × 10⁻³ / 1.6 × 10⁻³)^(5/3) = 9.68 × 10⁵ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Applies P V^(5/3) = const to obtain 9.68 × 10⁵ Pa (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the adiabatic exponent, using 3/5 instead of γ = 5/3.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Treats the process as isothermal (P_A V_A = P_B V_B) rather than adiabatic (P_A V_A^(5/3) = P_B V_B^(5/3)).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses the diatomic adiabatic index γ = 7/5 instead of γ = 5/3 for a monatomic gas.

items.stem: A fixed mass of ideal gas at 360 kPa and $1.80 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3$ expands slowly and isothermally to $5.40 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^3$. Given $W = p_1 V_1 \ln(V_2/V_1)$, calculate the thermal energy absorbed from the constant-temperature bath.
items.workedSolution: For an ideal gas at constant temperature, $\Delta U = 0$, so $Q = W = p_1 V_1 \ln(V_2/V_1) = (3.60 \times 10^5)(1.80 \times 10^{-3})\ln 3 = 712 J$.

markScheme.criterion: Thermal energy absorbed equals 712 J.

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses constant-pressure $p_1 \Delta V$ instead of isothermal work $p_1 V_1 \ln(V_2/V_1)$.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses base-10 logarithm instead of natural logarithm $\ln$.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the $\ln(V_2/V_1)$ factor.

items.stem: A university campus is choosing between direct electric resistive heaters and an air-source heat pump to warm a lecture building during winter.
items.workedSolution: Resistive heating gives $Q = W$, whereas a heat pump delivers more thermal energy than electrical work supplied because work moves additional heat from the cold reservoir ($Q_{\mathrm{H}} = Q_{\mathrm{C}} + W$, so $\mathrm{COP}_{\mathrm{hp}} = Q_{\mathrm{H}}/W > 1$ as a ratio, not percentage efficiency). Since $\mathrm{COP}_{\mathrm{hp,max}} = T_{\mathrm{H}}/(T_{\mathrm{H}} - T_{\mathrm{C}})$ in K, colder exterior temperatures widen $T_{\mathrm{H}} - T_{\mathrm{C}}$ and reduce COP.

markScheme.criterion: States that an electric resistive heater delivers heat equal to electrical work input (1:1 conversion).
Writes and explains $Q_{\mathrm{H}} = Q_{\mathrm{C}} + W$ for the heat pump cycle.
Explains that the heat pump delivers more heat than electrical work supplied because it transfers additional heat from the cold reservoir.
Clarifies explicitly that $\mathrm{COP}_{\mathrm{hp}} > 1$ is a performance ratio, not a percentage efficiency violating energy conservation.
Applies $\mathrm{COP}_{\mathrm{hp,max}} = T_{\mathrm{H}}/(T_{\mathrm{H}} - T_{\mathrm{C}})$ in kelvin to deduce that falling outside temperature lowers COP.
Includes a balanced engineering consideration such as higher installation cost or reduced winter margin versus lower operating energy.

parts.prompt: Analyse both heating options using the First and Second Laws of Thermodynamics, explaining why a heat pump outperforms resistive heating in energy terms, why its COP is not an efficiency, and how colder outside temperatures affect its performance.
parts.expectedAnswer: A direct resistive heater converts electrical work directly into thermal energy at a one-to-one ratio, whereas a heat pump delivers more thermal energy than electrical work supplied because work moves additional heat from the cold reservoir ($Q_{\mathrm{H}} = Q_{\mathrm{C}} + W$). Consequently $\mathrm{COP}_{\mathrm{hp}} = Q_{\mathrm{H}}/W$ is strictly greater than unity; it is a ratio of useful heat delivered to work input rather than a percentage efficiency, so energy conservation is fully obeyed. By the Second Law, $\mathrm{COP}_{\mathrm{hp,max}} = T_{\mathrm{H}}/(T_{\mathrm{H}} - T_{\mathrm{C}})$ in kelvin, meaning that when outside winter temperature $T_{\mathrm{C}}$ drops, the temperature difference $T_{\mathrm{H}} - T_{\mathrm{C}}$ widens and the achievable COP falls, requiring more electrical input (and higher capital/maintenance cost) on the coldest days.
workingSteps: L1: State that resistive heating converts $1\text{ J}$ of electrical work into at most $1\text{ J}$ of heat.
L1: State energy balance $Q_{\mathrm{H}} = Q_{\mathrm{C}} + W$ for the heat pump.
L2: Explain that $\mathrm{COP}_{\mathrm{hp}} = Q_{\mathrm{H}}/W > 1$ because outdoor thermal energy $Q_{\mathrm{C}}$ is transferred alongside work $W$.
L2: Clarify that COP is a dimensionless ratio and not an efficiency exceeding 100%.
L3: Use $\mathrm{COP}_{\mathrm{hp,max}} = T_{\mathrm{H}}/(T_{\mathrm{H}} - T_{\mathrm{C}})$ (in K) to explain why performance drops in severe frost when $T_{\mathrm{C}}$ falls.
L3: Weigh practical engineering trade-offs (capital cost, defrosting, noise vs lower running energy and carbon footprint).

items.stem: A foundation physics student prepares a classic side-lit glass smoke cell beneath an upright microscope and sketches the trajectory of a single illuminated speck. What is directly seen when looking into the microscope eyepiece?
items.workedSolution: Looking through the microscope eyepiece, the student observes bright specks move continuously along erratic irregular jagged random paths.

markScheme.criterion: Looking through the microscope eyepiece, the student observes bright specks move continuously along erratic irregular jagged random paths.

options.label: A
options.text: Looking through the microscope eyepiece, the student observes bright specks move continuously along erratic irregular jagged random paths.

options.label: B
options.text: Bright specks falling smoothly downwards at constant terminal speed in straight vertical lines.
options.distractorRationale: Ignores the characteristic continuous random jiggling caused by unbalanced molecular impacts.

options.label: C
options.text: Individual transparent air molecules bouncing off one another along smooth curved orbits.
options.distractorRationale: Fluid molecules are far too small to resolve with an optical microscope; only the much larger specks are seen.

options.label: D
options.text: A stationary regular crystal grid of glowing specks vibrating in phase with the light beam.
options.distractorRationale: Suspended particles in a fluid do not form a fixed crystal lattice.

items.stem: On the pressure–temperature (P–T) diagram, 0.5 mol of an ideal gas in a precision pneumatic actuator chamber sealed with a movable piston starts at state A (1.1 × 10⁵ Pa, 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³), expands at constant pressure to 8.8 × 10⁻³ m³ at state B, and is then heated at constant volume to a final pressure of 1.54 × 10⁵ Pa at state C. Take R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the final temperature T_C at state C?

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates PV / (nR) at the target state to obtain 326 K (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Reports the final temperature converted to °C when the question and options specify kelvin.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses the initial volume V_A instead of V_B = V_C when evaluating T_C = P_C V_C / (nR).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Computes T_B after the isobaric stage and omits the isochoric pressure ratio P_C / P_A.

items.stem: An experiment records the molecular speed distribution of 1.2 mol of Xenon-131 (Xe) gas (molar mass 131.3 g mol⁻¹) occupying 0.04 m³ in a sealed borosilicate acoustic-thermometry sphere at 360 K (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (kinetic-theory pressure relation: pV = ⅓ N m v_rms²)). Which value equals the rms speed of the atoms?
items.workedSolution: Convert molar mass to SI units: M = 0.1313 kg mol⁻¹. Using v_rms = √(3RT / M) at T = 360 K gives v_rms = √(3 × 8.31 × 360 / 0.1313) = 261 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates √(3RT / M) with M in kg mol⁻¹ to obtain 261 m s⁻¹ (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes molar mass in g mol⁻¹ instead of kg mol⁻¹ into √(3RT / M), underestimating v_rms by a factor of √1000 ≈ 31.6.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 3 from the three translational degrees of freedom, evaluating √(RT / M).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses a factor of 2 instead of 3, computing the most probable speed v_p = √(2RT / M) rather than v_rms.

items.stem: In a climate radiative-transfer model, an arid continental land-surface test plot of area 18 m² and surface emissivity e = 0.92 is at 296 K while exchanging thermal infrared radiation with an effective surrounding environment at 268 K. Taking σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, what is the net rate of radiative energy loss P_net from the surface?
items.workedSolution: Net radiative power loss P_net = e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴) = 0.92 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 18 × ((296)⁴ − (268)⁴) = 2.36 × 10³ W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴) to obtain 2.36 × 10³ W (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Evaluates e σ A (T − T_amb)⁴ instead of e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴), a classic fourth-power algebra error.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the greybody emissivity factor e (< 1) from P_net = e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates gross emitted power e σ A T⁴ and ignores incoming radiation absorbed from the surroundings at T_amb.

items.stem: In a closed noble-gas power-conversion loop coupled to a thermal reservoir at 310 K, 1.6 mol of an ideal gas expands reversibly and isothermally from V_A = 3.5 × 10⁻³ m³ to V_B = 8.4 × 10⁻³ m³. Take R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the change in entropy ΔS of the gas?
items.workedSolution: For a reversible isothermal expansion, ΔU = 0 so Q = W_by = nRT ln(V_B / V_A). Therefore ΔS = Q / T = nR ln(V_B / V_A) = 1.6 × 8.31 × ln(8.4 × 10⁻³ / 3.5 × 10⁻³) = 11.6 J K⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔS = nR ln(V_B / V_A) to obtain 11.6 J K⁻¹ (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses base-10 logarithm log₁₀(V_B / V_A) instead of the natural logarithm ln(V_B / V_A).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Replaces ln(V_B / V_A) with the linear fractional change (V_B − V_A) / V_A.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes isothermal heat Q = nRT ln(V_B / V_A) without dividing by T to obtain ΔS = Q / T.

items.stem: An insulated run in a thermally isolated materials-testing bath combines 0.3 kg of pure ice at 273.15 K with 0.18 kg of tepid water at 289.15 K. Adopt c_w = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and fusion enthalpy L_f = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) Q_water = m_water c_water (289.15 − 273.15) = 1.20 × 10⁴ J, which is below m_ice L_f. (b) Melted mass Δm = Q_water / L_f = 0.0360 kg. (c) Melted fraction f = Δm / m_ice = 0.120.

markScheme.criterion: Computes m_water c_water (T_water − 273.15).
Obtains 1.20 × 10⁴ J.
Divides Q_water by L_f.
Obtains 0.0360 kg.
Divides Δm by initial ice mass m_ice.
Obtains 0.120.

parts.prompt: Show that not all the ice melts by calculating the thermal energy released when the warm water cools to 273.15 K.
workingSteps: Q_water = m_water c_water (289.15 − 273.15) = 1.20 × 10⁴ J (< m_ice L_f = 1.00 × 10⁵ J).

parts.prompt: Calculate the mass of ice that melts by the time thermal equilibrium is reached.
Determine the fraction of the initial ice sample that has melted at equilibrium.

items.stem: The P–V diagram shows 0.6 mol of an ideal monatomic gas in a solar-thermal helium Brayton demonstrator cylinder taken from state A (2.4 × 10⁵ Pa, 3.5 × 10⁻³ m³) to state B (7.2 × 10⁵ Pa, 3.5 × 10⁻³ m³) at constant volume, and then from state B to state C (7.2 × 10⁵ Pa, 9.1 × 10⁻³ m³) at constant pressure. Throughout this question, use the first law ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW where thermal energy supplied to the gas (ΔQ) and work done on the gas (ΔW) are positive.
items.workedSolution: (a) Work is done only along B → C: ΔW = −P_B(V_C − V_B) = -4.03 × 10³ J. (b) ΔU_AC = (3/2)(P_C V_C − P_A V_A) = 8.57 × 10³ J. (c) By ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW, total heat supplied ΔQ = ΔU_AC − ΔW = 1.26 × 10⁴ J.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies ΔW_AB = 0 and computes ΔW = −P_B(V_C − V_B).
Obtains -4.03 × 10³ J.
Applies ΔU = (3/2)(P_C V_C − P_A V_A).
Obtains 8.57 × 10³ J.
Applies ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW ⇒ ΔQ = ΔU_AC − ΔW to obtain total heat supplied.
Obtains 1.26 × 10⁴ J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the total mechanical work done on the gas ΔW along path A → B → C (including its sign).
Calculate the total change in internal energy ΔU of the monatomic gas between state A and state C.
workingSteps: For a monatomic ideal gas, U = (3/2) PV, so ΔU_AC = (3/2)(P_C V_C − P_A V_A).

parts.prompt: Determine the total thermal energy ΔQ supplied to the gas over the complete path A → B → C.
workingSteps: By the first law of thermodynamics (ΔU = ΔQ + ΔW), ΔQ = ΔU_AC − ΔW = 8.568 × 10³ − (-4.032 × 10³) = 1.26 × 10⁴ J.

items.stem: Why is it unnecessary to know the heat capacity of the glass jacket or heater wire in a properly conducted continuous-flow calorimetry experiment?
items.workedSolution: At steady state the outlet temperature remains constant over time indicating thermal equilibrium before recording mass flow rate, so the apparatus stores zero net energy. Therefore the correct statement is: Once the outlet temperature remains constant over time indicating thermal equilibrium before recording mass flow rate, the apparatus temperature is unchanging so it absorbs no further thermal energy.

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: outlet temperature remains constant over time indicating thermal equilibrium before recording mass flow rate.

options.label: A
options.text: Once the liquid starts flowing, glass acts as a perfect thermal insulator with zero specific heat capacity.
options.distractorRationale: Glass has finite specific heat capacity and conducts heat.

options.label: B
options.text: Once the heater current doubles, the heat absorbed by the glass becomes negative and cancels out.
options.distractorRationale: Apparatus thermal capacity never becomes negative.

options.label: C
options.text: Once the vacuum jacket is evacuated, the heater wire stops transferring energy to the glass entirely.
options.distractorRationale: Radiation and conduction along supports still occur; steady temperature is what eliminates apparatus heat storage.

options.label: D
options.text: Once the outlet temperature remains constant over time indicating thermal equilibrium before recording mass flow rate, the apparatus temperature is unchanging so it absorbs no further thermal energy.

items.stem: A closed heat engine (a laboratory heat-engine indicator rig with low-friction seals) takes 1.2 mol of monatomic ideal gas (γ = 5/3) from A (5.5 × 10⁵ Pa, 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³) adiabatically to V_B = 5.0 × 10⁻³ m³, compresses it at constant pressure back to V_C = 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³, and heats it isochorically back to A. Find the net work done by the gas per cycle (work by gas positive).
items.workedSolution: At B, P_B = P_A (V_A / V_B)^(5/3) = 1.732 × 10⁵ Pa. Adiabatic work W_AB = (3/2)(P_A V_A − P_B V_B) = 763.2 J, and isobaric compression work W_BC = P_B(V_C − V_B) = -433.1 J (W_CA = 0). Thus W_net = W_AB + W_BC = 330 J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates the closed adiabatic heat-engine cycle to obtain 330 J (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes only the magnitude of the isobaric compression work P_B(V_B − V_C).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Computes only the adiabatic expansion work W_AB and forgets to subtract the isobaric compression work |W_BC|.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates total heat input Q_CA along the isochoric leg instead of net work W_net.

items.stem: Thermalised Xenon-131 (Xe) vapour of molar mass 0.1313 kg mol⁻¹ fills a thermostatted noble-gas reference bulb at a uniform temperature of 310 K. Given k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ and 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, Determine the mean kinetic energy per atom expressed in eV.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes T = 310 K into the monatomic kinetic-theory energy relation to obtain 0.0401 eV (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Evaluates (1/2) k_B T / e for a single degree of freedom instead of three.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes k_B T / e and omits the 3/2 translational factor.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Doubles the 3/2 factor to 3 k_B T / e by omitting the 1/2 in kinetic energy.

items.stem: Starting at 551 K in a ceramic-lined materials characterization furnace, 1.25 kg of lead absorbs heat, crosses its 600.6 K melting point (specific latent heat of fusion L_f = 2.3 × 10⁴ J kg⁻¹), and finishes as liquid at 646 K. With c_solid = 128 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and c_liquid = 147 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, how much energy was supplied?

markScheme.criterion: Sums sensible mcΔT stages and latent heat mL to obtain 4.50 × 10⁴ J (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Omits the isothermal latent-heat plateau m L during the phase transition and sums only the mcΔT stages.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Treats the entire process as single-phase sensible heating m c_liquid ΔT with zero latent heat.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Computes only the phase-transition latent energy m L and omits both sensible heating intervals.

items.stem: Operating at 1200 K with effective blackbody emissivity 1 and area 1.5 × 10⁻³ m², a nearby solar-type star modelled as an ideal spherical radiator irradiates a sensor located 1.5 m away in vacuum. Taking Wien's constant b = 2.90 × 10⁻³ m K, what is the peak emission wavelength λ_max in nanometres?
items.workedSolution: By Wien's displacement law, λ_max = b / T = (2.90 × 10⁻³) / 1200 = 2.417 × 10⁻⁶ m = 2.42 × 10³ nm.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates the blackbody radiation law in SI units to obtain 2.42 × 10³ nm (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Inverts Wien's displacement law by dividing T by b instead of b by T.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts 273.15 from the kelvin temperature before applying Wien's law.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies Wien's constant b by T instead of dividing b by T.

items.stem: A Carnot engine modelled in a closed-cycle Stirling regenerator test cell uses 1 mol of ideal gas operating between a hot reservoir at 608 K and a cold sink at 380 K. During the high-temperature isothermal stage A → B, the volume increases from 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ to 7.0 × 10⁻³ m³. Taking net work done by the gas as positive (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹), what is the net work output W_net per cycle?
items.workedSolution: Q_H = nRT_H ln(V_B / V_A) = 6.330 × 10³ J and η = 1 − T_C / T_H = 0.3750. Net work output W_net = η Q_H = nR(T_H − T_C) ln(V_B / V_A) = 2.37 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Carnot thermodynamics in kelvin to obtain 2.37 × 10³ J (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses base-10 log₁₀(V_B / V_A) instead of natural logarithm ln(V_B / V_A).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the rejected heat Q_C = nRT_C ln(V_B / V_A) instead of net work Q_H − Q_C.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates total heat input Q_H = nRT_H ln(V_B / V_A) without multiplying by Carnot efficiency (1 − T_C / T_H).

items.stem: Engineers charge a high-vacuum synchrotron beamline gas target (capacity 0.045 m³) with 1.6 mol of Helium-4 (He) of molar mass 4 g mol⁻¹ at an equilibrium temperature of 87 °C (take T(K) = θ(°C) + 273.15) (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹). Determine the density of the confined gas.
items.workedSolution: Total gas mass m = nM = 1.6 × 4.0 × 10⁻³ = 6.400 × 10⁻³ kg. Density ρ = m / V = 6.400 × 10⁻³ / 0.045 = 0.142 kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Applies ρ = nM / V in SI units to obtain 0.142 kg m⁻³ (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies total gas mass nM by container volume V instead of dividing by V.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Computes molar concentration n / V (mol m⁻³) and omits multiplication by molar mass M.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Leaves molar mass in g mol⁻¹ instead of converting to kg mol⁻¹, overestimating density by a factor of 1000.

items.stem: A heated brass block of mass 0.28 kg and specific heat capacity 380 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ at 410 K is plunged into 0.42 kg of water (c = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) initially at 285 K inside a precision isothermal-jacket mixing cup. During mixing, 1600 J of thermal energy escapes to the surroundings. How much thermal energy is released by the brass block in reaching equilibrium?
items.workedSolution: Enthalpy balance: m_s c_s (T_s − T_eq) = m_l c_l (T_eq − T_l) + 1600, giving T_eq = 291.3 K. Heat released by the solid Q_lost = m_s c_s (T_s − T_eq) = 1.26 × 10⁴ J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies calorimetry energy balance to obtain 1.26 × 10⁴ J (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Assumes the final equilibrium temperature is the unweighted midpoint (T_solid + T_liquid) / 2.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes only the heat gained by the liquid bath without adding the heat lost to the surroundings.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Assumes the solid cools all the way down to the initial bath temperature T_liquid instead of T_eq.

items.stem: Why is the indicated power measured from a real four-stroke petrol engine always substantially lower than the theoretical ideal Otto cycle prediction?
items.workedSolution: Finite combustion time, early/late valve opening, heat loss to the coolant, and gas pumping work mean the real indicator loop has rounded corners and a lower pumping loop reducing net enclosed work area.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that real indicator loop has rounded corners and a lower pumping loop reducing net enclosed work area.

items.stem: During a timed run in a spacecraft latent-heat thermal-buffer canister, a Peltier extraction module rated at 1600 W with coupling efficiency 0.75 removes thermal energy on 0.2 kg of water between 333 K and 245 K. Given melting point 273.15 K, L_f = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹, c_s = 2100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, and c_l = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, determine the constant-temperature arrest time.
items.workedSolution: Effective thermal power P_eff = η P = 0.75 × 1600 = 1.200 × 10³ W. Plateau latent energy Q_f = m L_f = 6.680 × 10⁴ J, giving Δt_plateau = Q_f / P_eff = 55.7 s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses P_eff = η P and divides required thermal energy to obtain 55.7 s (C).

items.stem: Operating clockwise between 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³ and 0.012 m³ and between 1.8 × 10⁵ Pa and 5.4 × 10⁵ Pa, 1.5 mol of monatomic ideal gas in a magnetically coupled piston calorimeter chamber completes cycle A → B → C → D → A. What is the total thermal energy Q_in absorbed by the monatomic gas during the heating legs D → A and A → B?
items.workedSolution: Heat enters on D → A (isochoric, W = 0): Q_DA = (3/2)(P_high − P_low)V_min = 2.160 × 10³ J, and on A → B (isobaric): Q_AB = (5/2)P_high(V_max − V_min) = 1.080 × 10⁴ J. Total Q_in = Q_DA + Q_AB = 1.30 × 10⁴ J.

markScheme.criterion: Computes heatInputJ correctly for the closed rectangular cycle to obtain 1.30 × 10⁴ J (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Confuses net cycle heat Q_net = W_net with total heat input Q_in absorbed from the hot source.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omits the 3/2 factor in monatomic ΔU on both heating legs.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Includes only the heat absorbed during isobaric expansion A → B and omits the isochoric heating D → A.

items.stem: A thermal laboratory tests a solid block of bismuth-tin eutectic alloy of mass 0.55 kg initially at 18 °C. The figure displays its temperature–time heating curve through its melting point of 96 °C. The solid has specific heat capacity 420 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and specific latent heat of fusion 4.80 × 10⁴ J kg⁻¹. An electrical immersion heater rated at 135 W transfers energy to the sample with thermal efficiency 85%. In a separate pressure-law check, a sealed argon laboratory flask contains a fixed mass of ideal gas at pressure 112 kPa and temperature 18 °C, before being heated at constant volume to 128 °C (use T / K = θ / °C + 273.2).
items.workedSolution: (a)(i) Q₁ = m c Δθ = 0.55 × 420 × (96 − 18) = 1.802 × 10⁴ J ≈ 1.80 × 10⁴ J. (a)(ii) Q_melt = m L_f = 2.640 × 10⁴ J; Q_total = 4.442 × 10⁴ J; t = Q_total / (η P) = 387.1 s ≈ 387 s. (a)(iii) mean molecular kinetic energy stays constant while intermolecular potential energy changes to overcome or form intermolecular bonds. (a)(iv) thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings and absorbed by the container. (b)(i) T₁ = 291.2 K, T₂ = 401.2 K, so p₂ = 112 × (401.2 / 291.2) = 154.3 kPa ≈ 154 kPa. (b)(ii) faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Q = m c Δθ = 0.55 × 420 × 78.
Correctly computes 1.80 × 10⁴ J (4 s.f. 1.802 × 10⁴ J).
Computes Q_melt = 2.640 × 10⁴ J, Q_total = 4.442 × 10⁴ J, and substitutes t = Q_total / (η P).
Shows 4 s.f. value 387.1 s rounding cleanly to 387 s.
States that temperature and mean molecular kinetic energy remain constant along the plateau.
Explains that intermolecular potential energy changes as bonds are weakened, broken, or formed.
States accurately that thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings and absorbed by the container.
Converts both temperatures using T = θ + 273.2 (291.2 K and 401.2 K) and applies p₂ = p₁ T₂ / T₁.
Evaluates final gas pressure = 154 kPa (4 s.f. 154.3 kPa).

Explains via Newton second law that faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area (no credit for quoting pV = nRT alone).

Referring to the horizontal phase-change plateau QR on the figure, explain in terms of molecular energies why the temperature stays constant while internal energy changes. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: During the plateau, mean molecular kinetic energy stays constant while intermolecular potential energy changes to overcome or form intermolecular bonds.
workingSteps: State that temperature measures mean random molecular kinetic energy which stays constant.
Explain that latent thermal energy changes intermolecular potential energy as bonds are broken or formed.

parts.prompt: State one physical reason why the measured heating time in the laboratory exceeds the ideal value calculated assuming perfect efficiency. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings and absorbed by the container.

parts.prompt: Calculate the new pressure of the ideal gas in the sealed argon laboratory flask at 128 °C using T / K = θ / °C + 273.2. [2]
Explain in terms of kinetic theory and Newton's second law (without using the ideal gas equation) why heating the gas at constant volume increases its pressure. [1]

items.stem: Inside a frictionless piston-cylinder assembly on a thermodynamics test bench, 0.25 mol of an ideal monatomic gas (adiabatic index γ = 5/3) initially at P_A = 3.2 × 10⁵ Pa and V_A = 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³ is reversibly and adiabatically expanded to V_B = 6.0 × 10⁻³ m³. Take R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the final pressure P_B in state B?
items.workedSolution: For a monatomic adiabatic process, P_B = P_A (V_A / V_B)^(5/3) = 3.2 × 10⁵ × (3.0 × 10⁻³ / 6.0 × 10⁻³)^(5/3) = 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Applies P V^(5/3) = const to obtain 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses the diatomic adiabatic index γ = 7/5 instead of γ = 5/3 for a monatomic gas.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Treats the process as isothermal (P_A V_A = P_B V_B) rather than adiabatic (P_A V_A^(5/3) = P_B V_B^(5/3)).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the adiabatic exponent, using 3/5 instead of γ = 5/3.

items.stem: In the AQA Engineering Physics sign convention $Q = \Delta U + W$, what is the exact physical statement of the First Law of Thermodynamics?
items.workedSolution: In AQA Engineering Physics ($Q = \Delta U + W$), heat supplied to the gas equals increase in internal energy plus work done by the gas (so $W < 0$ on compression).

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that heat supplied to the gas equals increase in internal energy plus work done by the gas.

options.label: A
options.text: Heat supplied to the gas equals the decrease in internal energy minus work done on the gas.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses signs of $\Delta U$ and $W$.

options.label: B
options.text: Work done on the gas equals heat leaving the gas plus increase in internal energy.
options.distractorRationale: Confuses work done ON versus BY the gas.

options.label: C
options.text: Internal energy is conserved whenever mechanical work is performed by an expanding gas.
options.distractorRationale: Internal energy changes unless $Q = W$.

options.label: D
options.text: Heat supplied to the gas equals increase in internal energy plus work done by the gas.

items.stem: As shown in the cutaway diagram, an open rectangular storage tank with horizontal base area 1.8 m² holds two immiscible liquids at rest: an upper layer of vegetable oil (ρ₁ = 910 kg m⁻³, depth h₁ = 1.6 m) resting above a lower layer of concentrated brine (ρ₂ = 1160 kg m⁻³, depth h₂ = 1 m). Atmospheric pressure at the open top surface is 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa and g = 9.81 m s⁻². What is the total hydrostatic gauge pressure at point Y due to the two liquid layers combined?
items.workedSolution: Upper layer Δp₁ = 910 × 9.81 × 1.6 = 1.428 × 10⁴ Pa. Lower layer Δp₂ = 1160 × 9.81 × 1 = 1.138 × 10⁴ Pa. Total liquid gauge pressure Δp = 2.566 × 10⁴ Pa ≈ 2.57 × 10⁴ Pa. Absolute bottom pressure p_Y = 1.01 × 10⁵ + 2.566 × 10⁴ = 1.267 × 10⁵ Pa = 126.7 kPa ≈ 127 kPa.

markScheme.criterion: Correct verified value = 2.57 × 10⁴ Pa.

items.stem: Even if all mechanical friction and stray conduction losses were eliminated from a cyclic heat engine, why can its thermal efficiency never reach 100%?
items.workedSolution: From $\eta_{\max} = 1 - \frac{T_{\mathrm{C}}}{T_{\mathrm{H}}}$, achieving 100% would require $T_{\mathrm{C}} = 0\text{ K}$: the cold reservoir cannot reach absolute zero so some thermal energy must always be rejected.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that cold reservoir cannot reach absolute zero so some thermal energy must always be rejected.

options.text: Fuel combustion never releases enough chemical energy to raise the hot reservoir temperature.
options.distractorRationale: Carnot efficiency depends on $T_{\mathrm{C}}/T_{\mathrm{H}}$, not on fuel quantity.

options.label: B
options.text: Cold reservoir cannot reach absolute zero so some thermal energy must always be rejected.

options.label: C
options.text: First Law of Thermodynamics forbids converting more than half of input heat into work.
options.distractorRationale: The 100% restriction comes from the Second Law, not an arbitrary 50% First-Law rule.

options.label: D
options.text: Working gas solidifies before it can expand back to atmospheric pressure.
options.distractorRationale: Ideal-gas Carnot limit applies regardless of phase changes.

items.stem: The diagram compares instantaneous molecular arrangements for three samples of the same pure substance kept in identical rigid containers. Which statement best characterizes the arrangement, motion, and intermolecular forces of the particles in the right-hand panel?
items.workedSolution: In the right-hand panel, particles are widely spaced and move rapidly and randomly in all directions with negligible intermolecular forces.

markScheme.criterion: In the right-hand panel, particles are widely spaced and move rapidly and randomly in all directions with negligible intermolecular forces.

options.text: Particles move slowly in uniform parallel streams all pointing in the same direction.
options.distractorRationale: Thermal motion of gas molecules is rapid and isotropic (random in all directions).

options.label: C
options.text: Particles oscillate back and forth about fixed points separated by tiny lattice gaps.
options.distractorRationale: Describes lattice vibration in a crystalline solid.

options.label: D
options.text: Particles remain closely touching in small vibrating clusters held by strong rigid bonds.
options.distractorRationale: Confuses gas behaviour with condensed solid/liquid phases.

items.stem: In a dark-room optics bench demonstration, a glass cell containing trapped smoke and air is illuminated from the side and viewed through a low-power microscope as shown. What is the correct physical explanation for the erratic zig-zag path traced by the illuminated speck?
items.workedSolution: The abrupt changes in direction occur because of uneven rapid random collisions by much smaller invisible moving air molecules transferring momentum to the suspended speck.

markScheme.criterion: The abrupt changes in direction occur because of uneven rapid random collisions by much smaller invisible moving air molecules transferring momentum to the suspended speck.

options.label: A
options.text: Warm convection currents generated by the lamp continuously sweep all specks in smooth circular loops.
options.distractorRationale: Convection produces smooth bulk drift in one direction, not independent erratic zig-zag jumps.

options.label: B
options.text: The abrupt changes in direction occur because of uneven rapid random collisions by much smaller invisible moving air molecules transferring momentum to the suspended speck.

options.label: C
options.text: Photons in the side light beam push the smoke specks erratically sideways whenever they scatter light.
options.distractorRationale: Radiation pressure from a lab lamp is far too weak and uniform to produce random isotropic zig-zags.

options.label: D
options.text: The visible specks themselves are living organisms or electrically charged dust repelling one another.
options.distractorRationale: Inert smoke or pollen specks move passively due to bombardment by invisible fluid molecules.

items.stem: On the pressure–temperature (P–T) diagram, 0.35 mol of an ideal gas in a precision pneumatic actuator chamber sealed with a movable piston starts at state A (2.2 × 10⁵ Pa, 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³), expands at constant pressure to 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³ at state B, and is then heated at constant volume to a final pressure of 3.52 × 10⁵ Pa at state C. Take R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the final temperature T_C at state C?

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates PV / (nR) at the target state to obtain 363 K (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Reports the final temperature converted to °C when the question and options specify kelvin.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes T_B after the isobaric stage and omits the isochoric pressure ratio P_C / P_A.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses the initial volume V_A instead of V_B = V_C when evaluating T_C = P_C V_C / (nR).

items.stem: In a semiconductor lithography purge canister (volume 0.04 m³), 1.2 mol of monatomic Argon-40 (Ar) of molar mass 0.04 kg mol⁻¹ is warmed from T₁ = 320 K to T₂ = 720 K, shifting the Maxwell–Boltzmann speed curve as plotted. Given R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (kinetic-theory pressure relation: pV = ⅓ N m v_rms²), determine v_rms at the higher temperature T₂.
items.workedSolution: Convert molar mass to SI units: M = 0.04 kg mol⁻¹. Using v_rms = √(3RT / M) at T = 720 K gives v_rms = √(3 × 8.31 × 720 / 0.04) = 670 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates √(3RT / M) with M in kg mol⁻¹ to obtain 670 m s⁻¹ (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes molar mass in g mol⁻¹ instead of kg mol⁻¹ into √(3RT / M), underestimating v_rms by a factor of √1000 ≈ 31.6.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 3 from the three translational degrees of freedom, evaluating √(RT / M).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses a factor of 2 instead of 3, computing the most probable speed v_p = √(2RT / M) rather than v_rms.

items.stem: An energy-budget sensor monitors an arid continental land-surface test plot (area 2.5 m², greybody emissivity 0.95) maintained at 314 K within a radiative environment at 286 K. Using σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, calculate P_net = e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴).
items.workedSolution: Net radiative power loss P_net = e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴) = 0.95 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 2.5 × ((314)⁴ − (286)⁴) = 408 W.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴) to obtain 408 W (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Evaluates e σ A (T − T_amb)⁴ instead of e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴), a classic fourth-power algebra error.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits the greybody emissivity factor e (< 1) from P_net = e σ A (T⁴ − T_amb⁴).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates gross emitted power e σ A T⁴ and ignores incoming radiation absorbed from the surroundings at T_amb.

items.stem: Inside a magnetically coupled piston calorimeter chamber, 0.3 mol of ideal gas is held at a constant temperature of 350 K while expanding reversibly from V_A = 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³ to V_B = 5.0 × 10⁻³ m³. Taking work done by the gas as positive and R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, how much work is done by the gas?
items.workedSolution: At constant temperature T = 350 K, ΔU = 0 and W_by = Q = nRT ln(V_B / V_A) = 0.3 × 8.31 × 350 × ln(5.0 × 10⁻³ / 2.5 × 10⁻³) = 605 J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates W = nRT ln(V_B / V_A) to obtain 605 J (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes log₁₀(V_B / V_A) instead of ln(V_B / V_A).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Treats pressure as remaining constant at P_A, computing P_A(V_B − V_A) instead of ∫ P dV = nRT ln(V_B / V_A).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Adds U = (3/2)nRT to isothermal work, overlooking that ΔU = 0 at constant temperature.

items.stem: In a thermally isolated materials-testing bath, 0.34 kg of water cools from 301.15 K down to 273.15 K against 0.3 kg of melting ice initially at 273.15 K (c = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; fusion enthalpy 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹). Find the melted ice mass.
items.workedSolution: Maximum heat released by water cooling to 273.15 K is Q = 0.34 × 4180 × (301.15 − 273.15) = 3.979 × 10⁴ J, which is less than m_ice L_f = 1.002 × 10⁵ J. Mass melted Δm = Q / L_f = 0.119 kg.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Δm = m_water c_water (T_water − 273.15) / L_f to obtain 0.119 kg (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Divides available thermal energy by the latent heat of vaporization (2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹) instead of fusion.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Computes the mass of unmelted ice remaining at 273.15 K rather than the mass of ice that melts.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the dimensionless melted fraction Δm / m_ice instead of the melted mass Δm in kg.

items.stem: The P–V graph shows an isobaric compression of 0.6 mol of ideal monatomic gas inside a variable-volume optical pressure cell at 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa from V_A = 6.5 × 10⁻³ m³ to V_B = 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³. Using the sign convention where work done on the gas is positive, determine the compression work done on the gas.
items.workedSolution: During isobaric compression from 6.5 × 10⁻³ m³ to 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³ at 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa, work done on the gas W_on = −P(V_B − V_A) = 3.0 × 10⁵ × (6.5 × 10⁻³ − 2.5 × 10⁻³) = 1.20 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates the first-law energy transfer with consistent work sign to obtain 1.20 × 10³ J (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the magnitude of internal energy change |ΔU| = (3/2) P |ΔV| instead of boundary work P |ΔV|.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies pressure by initial volume V_A instead of the volume change |V_B − V_A|.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the total heat rejected |Q| = (5/2) P |ΔV| rather than the mechanical work done on the gas.

items.stem: A student attempts to determine the specific heat capacity of oil from a single continuous-flow run using c = V I / (ṁ Δθ) and obtains a value significantly higher than the accepted book value. Why does using two flow rates remove this systematic error?
items.workedSolution: In one run P = ṁcΔθ + H makes V I / (ṁ Δθ) overestimate c; identical inlet and outlet temperatures keep thermal energy loss rate to the surroundings constant so heat loss cancels upon subtraction. Therefore the correct statement is: Using two flow rates with identical inlet and outlet temperatures keep thermal energy loss rate to the surroundings constant so heat loss cancels upon subtraction

markScheme.criterion: Selects correct conceptual explanation: identical inlet and outlet temperatures keep thermal energy loss rate to the surroundings constant so heat loss cancels upon subtraction.

options.label: A
options.text: Using two flow rates with identical inlet and outlet temperatures keep thermal energy loss rate to the surroundings constant so heat loss cancels upon subtraction

options.label: B
options.text: Using two flow rates with different outlet temperatures forces the thermal loss rate H to double proportionally.
options.distractorRationale: Changing Δθ changes H so it cannot cancel cleanly on subtraction.

options.label: C
options.text: Using two flow rates eliminates random timing uncertainty completely without affecting systematic heat losses.
options.distractorRationale: Two flow rates specifically eliminate the systematic heat loss rate H, not random timing error.

options.label: D
options.text: Using two flow rates causes the liquid to absorb thermal energy from the cooler laboratory air.
options.distractorRationale: When the liquid is heated above room temperature, heat flows outward to the surroundings.

items.stem: Inside a micro-electro-mechanical gas spring cavity, 0.4 mol of an ideal monatomic gas (γ = 5/3) performs a closed three-step cycle A → B → C → A: reversible adiabatic expansion from state A (4.5 × 10⁵ Pa, 1.5 × 10⁻³ m³) to volume 3.75 × 10⁻³ m³ at B, isobaric compression from B to volume 1.5 × 10⁻³ m³ at C, and isochoric heating from C back to A. Taking work done by the gas as positive, what is the net work output W_net per cycle?
items.workedSolution: At B, P_B = P_A (V_A / V_B)^(5/3) = 9.772 × 10⁴ Pa. Adiabatic work W_AB = (3/2)(P_A V_A − P_B V_B) = 462.8 J, and isobaric compression work W_BC = P_B(V_C − V_B) = -219.9 J (W_CA = 0). Thus W_net = W_AB + W_BC = 243 J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates the closed adiabatic heat-engine cycle to obtain 243 J (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes only the magnitude of the isobaric compression work P_B(V_B − V_C).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Computes only the adiabatic expansion work W_AB and forgets to subtract the isobaric compression work |W_BC|.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates total heat input Q_CA along the isochoric leg instead of net work W_net.

items.stem: Inside a sealed borosilicate acoustic-thermometry sphere, an ideal monatomic sample of Neon-20 (Ne) (M = 0.0202 kg mol⁻¹) is in thermal equilibrium at 187 °C (take T(K) = θ(°C) + 273.15). Use Boltzmann constant 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ and elementary charge 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Find the average translational kinetic energy of a single atom in eV.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes T = 460.15 K into the monatomic kinetic-theory energy relation to obtain 0.0595 eV (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Evaluates (1/2) k_B T / e for a single degree of freedom instead of three.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Uses temperature in °C rather than absolute temperature in kelvin.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Computes k_B T / e and omits the 3/2 translational factor.

items.stem: Calorimetric heating carries 1.25 kg of lead in a metallurgical vacuum-induction melting pot from an initial solid temperature of 551 K up to 631 K as liquid. Using 600.6 K for the melting point, specific heat capacities 128 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ (solid) and 147 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ (liquid), and specific latent heat of fusion L_f = 2.3 × 10⁴ J kg⁻¹, determine the total enthalpy input.

markScheme.criterion: Sums sensible mcΔT stages and latent heat mL to obtain 4.23 × 10⁴ J (D).

options.distractorRationale: Omits the isothermal latent-heat plateau m L during the phase transition and sums only the mcΔT stages.

options.label: B

items.stem: Modelled as an ideal blackbody (emissivity = 1), a luminous A-type stellar photosphere has surface area 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m², absolute surface temperature 2600 K, and is observed from a distance d = 1.5 m. Taking σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, what is the radiant intensity received at distance d (neglecting intervening absorption)?
items.workedSolution: Radiated luminosity L = σ A T⁴ = 647.8 W. Intensity at distance d is I = L / (4π d²) = 647.8 / (4π × (1.5)²) = 22.9 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates the blackbody radiation law in SI units to obtain 22.9 W m⁻² (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides by 4π d instead of 4π d², omitting the inverse-square exponent.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Divides radiated power by disc area π d² instead of spherical shell area 4π d².

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the geometric factor 4π for isotropic spherical spreading in I = L / (4π d²).

items.stem: The diagram shows a reversible Carnot cycle A → B → C → D → A for 1 mol of monatomic ideal gas in a cryocooler compression cylinder containing monatomic working gas coupled to a hot reservoir at 537 K and a cold sink at 290 K, with isothermal expansion from 1.5 × 10⁻³ m³ to 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³. Taking R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, what magnitude of thermal energy Q_C is rejected to the cold sink per cycle?
items.workedSolution: During isothermal compression C → D at T_C = 290 K, V_C / V_D = V_B / V_A, so heat rejected to the cold sink is Q_C = nRT_C ln(V_B / V_A) = 1.67 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Carnot thermodynamics in kelvin to obtain 1.67 × 10³ J (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses log₁₀(V_B / V_A) instead of ln(V_B / V_A) in Q_C = nRT_C ln(V_B / V_A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes net work W_net = Q_H − Q_C instead of the rejected heat Q_C.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes the heat absorbed Q_H from the hot reservoir instead of the heat Q_C rejected to the cold sink.

items.stem: 0.85 mol of monatomic Krypton-84 (Kr) (molar mass 0.0838 kg mol⁻¹) fills a thick-walled titanium deep-sea pressure housing of volume 0.06 m³ at a steady temperature of 520 K. Take R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Find the gas pressure.
items.workedSolution: From the ideal gas equation p = nRT / V = (0.85 × 8.31 × 520) / 0.06 = 6.12 × 10⁴ Pa.

markScheme.criterion: Applies p = nRT / V in SI units to obtain 6.12 × 10⁴ Pa (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies nRT by volume V instead of dividing nRT by V.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Subtracts 273.15 from an already-kelvin temperature before applying pV = nRT.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Omits the amount of substance n in p = nRT / V, solving for 1 mol instead of the given molar amount.

items.stem: In a calorimetry run using a low-heat-capacity polymeric calorimetry beaker, a 0.28 kg cylinder of copper (c = 385 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 475 K is quenched in 0.32 kg of mineral oil (c = 1960 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) at 298 K. During mixing, 950 J of thermal energy escapes to the surroundings. Find T_eq at thermal equilibrium.
items.workedSolution: Enthalpy balance: m_s c_s (T_s − T_eq) = m_l c_l (T_eq − T_l) + 950, giving T_eq = 322.7 K. Therefore T_eq = 323 K.

markScheme.criterion: Applies calorimetry energy balance to obtain 323 K (B).

items.stem: Why must the crankshaft rotational frequency in revolutions per second be halved when calculating the indicated power of a four-stroke engine from its indicator loop area?
items.workedSolution: Induction, compression, power, and exhaust take four piston strokes (two full turns of the crankshaft), so a four-stroke cylinder completes one power stroke every two crankshaft revolutions.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that a four-stroke cylinder completes one power stroke every two crankshaft revolutions.

items.stem: In a spacecraft latent-heat thermal-buffer canister, an electrical immersion heater of input power 450 W and thermal transfer efficiency 0.9 supplies energy as a 0.55 kg sample of lead goes from 563 K to 661 K across its 600.6 K fusion point (c_solid = 128 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, c_liquid = 147 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, L_f = 2.3 × 10⁴ J kg⁻¹). How long does the isothermal melting plateau last?
items.workedSolution: Effective thermal power P_eff = η P = 0.9 × 450 = 405.0 W. Plateau latent energy Q_f = m L_f = 1.265 × 10⁴ J, giving Δt_plateau = Q_f / P_eff = 31.2 s.

markScheme.criterion: Uses P_eff = η P and divides required thermal energy to obtain 31.2 s (C).

items.stem: The diagram shows a closed four-leg cycle A → B → C → D → A for 0.2 mol of monatomic ideal gas in a laboratory heat-engine indicator rig with low-friction seals, bounded by P_low = 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa, P_high = 5.25 × 10⁵ Pa, V_min = 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³, and V_max = 7.5 × 10⁻³ m³. What is the thermal efficiency η = W_net / Q_in of this rectangular monatomic-gas cycle?
items.workedSolution: W_net = (5.25 × 10⁵ − 1.5 × 10⁵)(7.5 × 10⁻³ − 3.0 × 10⁻³) = 1.688 × 10³ J. Heat enters on D → A and A → B: Q_in = (3/2)(P_high − P_low)V_min + (5/2)P_high(V_max − V_min) = 7.594 × 10³ J. Efficiency η = W_net / Q_in = 0.222.

markScheme.criterion: Computes thermalEfficiency correctly for the closed rectangular cycle to obtain 0.222 (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Divides W_net by Q_AB alone, neglecting the heat input Q_DA on the isochoric leg D → A.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Omits internal energy gain ΔU_AB when computing total heat input Q_in.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes the Carnot efficiency 1 − T_min / T_max between extreme corner temperatures instead of the actual cycle efficiency W_net / Q_in.

items.stem: A thermal laboratory tests a solid block of refined paraffin wax of mass 0.24 kg initially at 20 °C. The figure displays its temperature–time heating curve through its melting point of 64 °C. The solid has specific heat capacity 1850 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ and specific latent heat of fusion 1.48 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. An electrical immersion heater rated at 85 W transfers energy to the sample with thermal efficiency 82%. In a separate pressure-law check, a sealed helium pressure sensor bulb contains a fixed mass of ideal gas at pressure 102 kPa and temperature 20 °C, before being heated at constant volume to 92 °C (use T / K = θ / °C + 273.2).
items.workedSolution: (a)(i) Q₁ = m c Δθ = 0.24 × 1850 × (64 − 20) = 1.954 × 10⁴ J ≈ 1.95 × 10⁴ J. (a)(ii) Q_melt = m L_f = 3.552 × 10⁴ J; Q_total = 5.506 × 10⁴ J; t = Q_total / (η P) = 789.9 s ≈ 790 s. (a)(iii) mean molecular kinetic energy stays constant while intermolecular potential energy changes to overcome or form intermolecular bonds. (a)(iv) thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings and absorbed by the container. (b)(i) T₁ = 293.2 K, T₂ = 365.2 K, so p₂ = 102 × (365.2 / 293.2) = 127.0 kPa ≈ 127 kPa. (b)(ii) faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area.

markScheme.criterion: Applies Q = m c Δθ = 0.24 × 1850 × 44.
Correctly computes 1.95 × 10⁴ J (4 s.f. 1.954 × 10⁴ J).
Computes Q_melt = 3.552 × 10⁴ J, Q_total = 5.506 × 10⁴ J, and substitutes t = Q_total / (η P).
Shows 4 s.f. value 789.9 s rounding cleanly to 790 s.
States that temperature and mean molecular kinetic energy remain constant along the plateau.
Explains that intermolecular potential energy changes as bonds are weakened, broken, or formed.
States accurately that thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings and absorbed by the container.
Converts both temperatures using T = θ + 273.2 (293.2 K and 365.2 K) and applies p₂ = p₁ T₂ / T₁.
Evaluates final gas pressure = 127 kPa (4 s.f. 127.0 kPa).

Explains via Newton second law that faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area (no credit for quoting pV = nRT alone).

parts.prompt: Calculate the thermal energy required to raise the temperature of the solid refined paraffin wax from 20 °C to 64 °C. [2]
Show clearly that the actual time required for the 85 W heater operating at 82% efficiency to warm the solid from 20 °C and melt it completely at 64 °C is approximately 790 s. [2]
Referring to the horizontal phase-change plateau QR on the figure, explain in terms of molecular energies why the temperature stays constant while internal energy changes. [2]
parts.expectedAnswer: During the plateau, mean molecular kinetic energy stays constant while intermolecular potential energy changes to overcome or form intermolecular bonds.
workingSteps: State that temperature measures mean random molecular kinetic energy which stays constant.
Explain that latent thermal energy changes intermolecular potential energy as bonds are broken or formed.

parts.prompt: State one physical reason why the measured heating time in the laboratory exceeds the ideal value calculated assuming perfect efficiency. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings and absorbed by the container.
workingSteps: Apply NCUK calorimetry observation: thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings and absorbed by the container.

parts.prompt: Calculate the new pressure of the ideal gas in the sealed helium pressure sensor bulb at 92 °C using T / K = θ / °C + 273.2. [2]
Explain in terms of kinetic theory and Newton's second law (without using the ideal gas equation) why heating the gas at constant volume increases its pressure. [1]
parts.expectedAnswer: Heating raises molecular speeds so faster molecules undergo a greater momentum change per wall collision and collide more frequently raising average force per unit area.
workingSteps: Link higher molecular speed to larger momentum change per collision, higher collision frequency, and larger force per unit area.

items.stem: The P–V diagram shows a rapid thermally insulated (adiabatic) expansion A → B of 0.25 mol of monatomic ideal gas (γ = 5/3) in an insulated aerospace gas-accumulator cylinder from (4.0 × 10⁵ Pa, 1.6 × 10⁻³ m³) to final volume 4.8 × 10⁻³ m³ (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹). Taking work done by the gas as positive, how much mechanical work is done by the gas during A → B?
items.workedSolution: First find P_B = P_A (V_A / V_B)^(5/3) = 6.410 × 10⁴ Pa. Since Q = 0 in an adiabatic process, W_by = −ΔU = (3/2)(P_A V_A − P_B V_B) = 498 J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies P V^(5/3) = const and Q = 0 to obtain 498 J (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Omits the 3/2 factor in |ΔU| = (3/2)|P_B V_B − P_A V_A| when applying Q = 0 => |W| = |ΔU|.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses the isothermal work formula P_A V_A |ln(V_B / V_A)| instead of adiabatic work.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Treats pressure as constant at P_A, computing P_A |V_B − V_A| instead of adiabatic work.

items.stem: Two expansion curves start from the same state A on a $p$–$V$ diagram: one is isothermal and the other is adiabatic. Which statement correctly distinguishes their gradients?
items.workedSolution: The isothermal gradient is $-p/V$ whereas the adiabatic gradient is $-\gamma p/V$ with $\gamma > 1$: the adiabatic curve has a steeper gradient than an isothermal curve because temperature falls during adiabatic expansion.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that adiabatic curve has a steeper gradient than an isothermal curve because temperature falls during adiabatic expansion.

options.label: A
options.text: Isothermal curve has a steeper gradient than an adiabatic curve because heat leaves the gas.
options.distractorRationale: Reverses the relative steepness of adiabatic versus isothermal curves.

options.label: B
options.text: Both curves have identical gradients at state A because both obey the ideal gas equation.
options.distractorRationale: Ignores the factor of $\gamma > 1$ in the adiabatic slope $-\gamma p/V$.

options.label: C
options.text: Adiabatic curve has a steeper gradient than an isothermal curve because temperature falls during adiabatic expansion.

options.label: D
options.text: Adiabatic curve is flatter because pressure falls more slowly when internal energy decreases.
options.distractorRationale: Falling temperature drops pressure faster, making the adiabatic curve steeper.

items.stem: An open glass U-tube contains freshwater of known density ρ₂ = 1000 kg m⁻³ in its lower bend and right arm. An immiscible sample of paraffin oil of unknown density ρ₁ is poured into the left arm until equilibrium is reached as illustrated. Above the horizontal interface datum P–Q, the left oil column stands h₁ = 0.38 m tall while the right freshwater column stands h₂ = 0.258 m tall (take g = 9.81 m s⁻²). What is the density ρ₁ of the unknown paraffin oil?
items.workedSolution: Pressures at P and Q on the same horizontal datum are equal: p₀ + ρ₁ g h₁ = p₀ + ρ₂ g h₂ ⇒ ρ₁ = ρ₂ (h₂ / h₁) = 1000 × (0.258 / 0.38) = 678.9 kg m⁻³ ≈ 679 kg m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Correct unknown density ρ₁ = 679 kg m⁻³.

items.stem: A domestic heat pump has an operating coefficient of performance $\mathrm{COP}_{\mathrm{hp}} = 3.8$. Why does a value greater than 1 NOT violate the principle of conservation of energy?
items.workedSolution: Because $Q_{\mathrm{H}} = Q_{\mathrm{C}} + W$, a heat pump transfers thermal energy from the cold outdoors in addition to the electrical work input, so $\mathrm{COP}_{\mathrm{hp}} = Q_{\mathrm{H}}/W > 1$ obeys energy conservation.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that heat pump transfers thermal energy from the cold outdoors in addition to the electrical work input.

items.stem: A laboratory wall chart compares the molecular spacing and motion of a pure substance in three physical phases as illustrated. Which statement correctly accounts for why the middle state flows to take the shape of its container while retaining nearly constant volume?
items.workedSolution: In the middle panel representing a liquid, particles are closely packed in an irregular arrangement and can slide past one another.

options.text: Particles are widely spaced with negligible intermolecular forces so the substance easily compresses.
options.distractorRationale: Describes a gas; liquid particles stay almost touching and are nearly incompressible.

options.label: B
options.text: Particles are locked into a rigid repeating crystal lattice and can only vibrate in place.
options.distractorRationale: Describes a solid lattice; liquids lack fixed lattice positions.

options.label: C
options.text: Particles expand to occupy the entire empty upper volume of the sealed container uniformly.
options.distractorRationale: Liquids keep a definite volume and form a free surface under gravity.

options.label: D
options.text: In the middle panel representing a liquid, particles are closely packed in an irregular arrangement and can slide past one another.

items.stem: A physics teacher projects the microscope eyepiece view of an illuminated smoke speck suspended in motionless air inside a sealed glass cell. What fundamental kinetic-theory conclusion is supported by this experiment?
items.workedSolution: This classic experiment provides direct experimental evidence that fluid molecules are in continuous random thermal motion.

options.label: A
options.text: This classic experiment provides direct experimental evidence that fluid molecules are in continuous random thermal motion.

options.label: B
options.text: Direct proof that solids melt whenever exposed to lateral visible light.
options.distractorRationale: Brownian motion demonstrates kinetic molecular agitation in fluids, not phase melting.

options.label: C
options.text: Evidence that gravity does not act on microscopic particles suspended inside sealed cells.
options.distractorRationale: Gravity still acts, but random molecular bombardment dominates the rapid lateral jiggling.

options.label: D
options.text: Proof that air molecules are larger than smoke particles and move only when illuminated.
options.distractorRationale: Air molecules are vastly smaller than smoke specks and move thermally even in total darkness.

items.stem: A sample of 1.2 mol of ideal gas in a solar-thermal helium Brayton demonstrator cylinder undergoes an isobaric expansion from state A (1.6 × 10⁵ Pa, 5.0 × 10⁻³ m³) to state B (0.011 m³), followed by an isochoric rise to 2.24 × 10⁵ Pa at state C. Given R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, find the absolute temperature at B.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates PV / (nR) at the target state to obtain 176 K (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Inverts Charles's law ratio, multiplying T_A by V_A / V_B instead of V_B / V_A.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Stops after computing the initial temperature T_A = P_A V_A / (nR) without scaling by V_B / V_A.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the final temperature T_C at state C rather than the intermediate temperature T_B.

items.stem: In an atmospheric research dropsonde reference chamber (volume 0.04 m³), 1.2 mol of monatomic Helium-4 (He) of molar mass 4.0 × 10⁻³ kg mol⁻¹ is warmed from T₁ = 410 K to T₂ = 615 K, shifting the Maxwell–Boltzmann speed curve as plotted. Given R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (kinetic-theory pressure relation: pV = ⅓ N m v_rms²), determine v_rms at the higher temperature T₂.
items.workedSolution: Convert molar mass to SI units: M = 4.0 × 10⁻³ kg mol⁻¹. Using v_rms = √(3RT / M) at T = 615 K gives v_rms = √(3 × 8.31 × 615 / 4.0 × 10⁻³) = 1.96 × 10³ m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates √(3RT / M) with M in kg mol⁻¹ to obtain 1.96 × 10³ m s⁻¹ (D).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Substitutes molar mass in g mol⁻¹ instead of kg mol⁻¹ into √(3RT / M), underestimating v_rms by a factor of √1000 ≈ 31.6.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Omits the factor of 3 from the three translational degrees of freedom, evaluating √(RT / M).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Uses a factor of 2 instead of 3, computing the most probable speed v_p = √(2RT / M) rather than v_rms.

items.stem: In a planetary energy-balance study, an instrumented rooftop longwave-emissivity test slab of area 2.5 m² and infrared emissivity e = 0.78 is at surface temperature 373 K beneath a radiative environment at 278 K. Taking σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴, what is the gross thermal power radiated per unit area (surface exitance) by this greybody surface?
items.workedSolution: Gross radiated intensity (exitance) M = e σ T⁴ = 0.78 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × (373)⁴ = 856 W m⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates e σ T⁴ to obtain 856 W m⁻² (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Treats the surface as an ideal blackbody (e = 1) and omits the emissivity factor e.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Divides blackbody exitance σ T⁴ by emissivity e instead of multiplying by e.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies by surface area A, reporting total radiated power in watts rather than power per unit area.

items.stem: Maintained in thermal contact with a 450 K bath, 0.6 mol of ideal gas in a high-efficiency reciprocating research engine cylinder expands quasi-statically from 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ to 9.0 × 10⁻³ m³. Using R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, determine ΔS = Q / T for the gas.
items.workedSolution: For a reversible isothermal expansion, ΔU = 0 so Q = W_by = nRT ln(V_B / V_A). Therefore ΔS = Q / T = nR ln(V_B / V_A) = 0.6 × 8.31 × ln(9.0 × 10⁻³ / 2.0 × 10⁻³) = 7.50 J K⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates ΔS = nR ln(V_B / V_A) to obtain 7.50 J K⁻¹ (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Uses base-10 logarithm log₁₀(V_B / V_A) instead of the natural logarithm ln(V_B / V_A).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Replaces ln(V_B / V_A) with the linear fractional change (V_B − V_A) / V_A.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes isothermal heat Q = nRT ln(V_B / V_A) without dividing by T to obtain ΔS = Q / T.

items.stem: In an insulated mixing test within a vacuum-insulated stainless-steel Dewar flask, 0.035 kg of solid H₂O at 263.15 K dissolves thermally into 0.68 kg of water initially at 318.15 K. Data: melting temperature 273.15 K; c_s = 2100 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; c_l = 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹; specific fusion enthalpy 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. Which equilibrium temperature is reached?
items.workedSolution: Energy to warm and melt all ice at 273.15 K: Q_1+2 = 0.035 × 2100 × (273.15 − 263.15) + 0.035 × 3.34 × 10⁵ = 1.243 × 10⁴ J. Energy balance with warm water: m_w c_w (318.15 − T_eq) = Q_1+2 + m_ice c_w (T_eq − 273.15), giving T_eq = 312 K.

markScheme.criterion: Includes sub-zero ice warming, fusion latent heat, and meltwater warming to obtain 312 K (B).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Applies an extra factor of one-half from misremembering the degrees-of-freedom or geometric prefactor.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Introduces an extraneous integer factor when rearranging the governing thermal relation.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Introduces an extraneous integer factor when rearranging the governing thermal relation.

items.stem: The P–V graph shows an isobaric compression of 1.5 mol of ideal monatomic gas inside a precision pneumatic actuator chamber sealed with a movable piston at 2.7 × 10⁵ Pa from V_A = 9.9 × 10⁻³ m³ to V_B = 4.5 × 10⁻³ m³. Using the sign convention where work done on the gas is positive, determine the compression work done on the gas.
items.workedSolution: During isobaric compression from 9.9 × 10⁻³ m³ to 4.5 × 10⁻³ m³ at 2.7 × 10⁵ Pa, work done on the gas W_on = −P(V_B − V_A) = 2.7 × 10⁵ × (9.9 × 10⁻³ − 4.5 × 10⁻³) = 1.46 × 10³ J.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates the first-law energy transfer with consistent work sign to obtain 1.46 × 10³ J (A).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the magnitude of internal energy change |ΔU| = (3/2) P |ΔV| instead of boundary work P |ΔV|.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies pressure by initial volume V_A instead of the volume change |V_B − V_A|.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the total heat rejected |Q| = (5/2) P |ΔV| rather than the mechanical work done on the gas.
